taxonomy.title: Vascular — aortic and peripheral aneurysms
taxonomy.scopeIn: Aneurysm screening, surveillance and repair selection, rupture, aortic dissection and operative/endovascular complications. Peripheral aneurysms stay with this aneurysm lane.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Carotid disease belongs to vascular-carotid. Occlusive limb/mesenteric disease belongs to vascular-limb-mesenteric-arterial. Traumatic aortic injury belongs to trauma-thoracic.
taxonomy.priorityReason: Current AAA recognition covers only a fraction of major aortic surgical decisions.
taxonomy.coverageReason: At most four distinct live clinical concept identities cover this scope. Variants repeat those identities.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

decisionNodes.stem: Which statement should guide this patient's counseling?

answerChoices.label: Women have higher observed perioperative mortality than men
Women have lower operative mortality because rupture occurs at smaller diameters
EVAR eliminates the observed difference in outcomes between sexes
Every risk-adjusted contemporary study reports identical outcomes

decisionNodes.explanation: Contemporary pooled and registry evidence generally shows higher perioperative mortality among women, although the magnitude and mechanisms remain uncertain.
sourceLabels: Pouncey et al., EJVES systematic review and meta-analysis, 2021
Tedjawirja et al., BJS registry study, 2022
2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline
Clinically approved by Melissa Rowland, MD on 2026-08-06

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The counseling discussion recorded lower operative mortality for women instead of higher observed perioperative mortality for women.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: Contemporary pooled and registry evidence generally shows higher perioperative mortality among women, although the magnitude and mechanisms remain uncertain.

decisionNodes.stem: Which statement is appropriate for this patient's counseling?

answerChoices.label: Women have higher observed perioperative mortality after AAA repair
Women may routinely continue surveillance until the aneurysm reaches 6.5 cm
Severe cardiac risk makes EVAR mandatory once the aneurysm reaches 5.0 cm
EVAR's lower early mortality proves benefit for repair below accepted thresholds

decisionNodes.explanation: Current guidelines recommend repair at approximately 5.0 cm in women and 5.5 cm in men, while operative risk still requires individualized assessment. Trials have not demonstrated a survival benefit from routine early repair of smaller asymptomatic AAAs merely because EVAR is available.
sourceLabels: Pouncey et al., EJVES systematic review and meta-analysis, 2021
Tedjawirja et al., BJS registry study, 2022
2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline
Clinically approved by Melissa Rowland, MD on 2026-08-06

rankedConcepts.objective: Use total dissection extent rather than entry-tear location to identify the need for emergency ascending repair.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A distal entry tear can distract from acute ascending involvement; the resulting operative pathway is consequential.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Failure to treat the dangerous acute ascending segment.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old woman, visits clinic after hospitalization for abrupt chest and back pain. The founder reviews her initial CTA: the entry tear lies distal to the left subclavian artery, but the flap extends backward through the arch into the ascending aorta. At that assessment she was alert and normotensive, without abdominal pain or limb deficits.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which definitive hospital plan should have been selected from {patientName}'s initial CTA?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Descending TEVAR directed at the entry tear as the complete treatment.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The flap extends into the ascending aorta, not merely through the descending segment.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Confine the flap to the descending aorta and preserve the uncomplicated physiology: the offered medical plan becomes correct.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Interpret the current perfusion trajectory before choosing planning CTA versus a direct control/resuscitation pathway.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Detection, physiology and repair planning must be separated in a time-critical aneurysm problem.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Failing to define the repair anatomy or contained hemorrhage needed for the definitive strategy.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 73-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for abrupt abdominal and back pain. The initial record shows systolic pressure 78 mm Hg and a 7-cm infrarenal AAA on bedside ultrasound. After initial blood-product resuscitation, three successive assessments show systolic pressures 110, 108 and 116 mm Hg; he is alert, speaking and has warm extremities. The hospital aortic team is preparing definitive care.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which next step should have been selected at {patientName}'s recorded assessment?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Direct open control based solely on the first low pressure despite the subsequent trajectory.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Repeated current pressure and mental-status recovery after initial resuscitation, rather than one isolated reading.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the recovered trajectory with recurrent loss of consciousness and falling pressure despite initial resuscitation: direct hemorrhage control becomes the appropriate offered pathway.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Integrate contained rupture and documented device-compatible anatomy to select an emergency repair approach.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Contained rupture and suitable anatomy test two competing errors: elective delay and automatic open repair.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Choosing a less-favored approach for this supported anatomy, or dangerously delaying repair if containment is mistaken for an intact aneurysm.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 73-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for abrupt abdominal and back pain. At the recorded initial assessment, bedside ultrasound showed a 7-cm infrarenal AAA. He remained alert with systolic pressures between 108 and 116 mm Hg over repeated assessments. The hospital aortic team was preparing definitive treatment.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: CTA shows retroperitoneal hematoma continuous with a posterior aortic-wall defect. The infrarenal neck is parallel-sided, the iliac access vessels are patent, and the vascular planning record confirms the selected graft's instructions-for-use requirements are satisfied. He remains alert with unchanged pressure. The treating hospital performs both open and endovascular aortic repair.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which definitive repair approach should have been selected for {patientName} at that point?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Emergency open repair regardless of suitable endovascular anatomy.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A wall defect with contiguous retroperitoneal blood plus verified graft suitability.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Keep rupture but replace the planning record with no usable proximal seal or iliac access: the offered emergency open approach becomes appropriate. Remove the wall defect/hematoma and make the case asymptomatic: an elective pathway becomes reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize new dissection-related renal malperfusion despite achieved impulse control and escalate to repair.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Treatment response can improve one target while organ perfusion deteriorates.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Prolonged organ ischemia.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Continue the prior infusions and observe renal function because pain and pressure improved.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: New renal dysfunction co-localized with true-lumen compression and weaker kidney enhancement despite achieved impulse control.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If renal function, output and enhancement stayed preserved after treatment, continued monitored medical management would remain appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Distinguish persistent static branch obstruction from resolved central dynamic compression to choose the next endovascular target.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: An apparently successful central repair can leave a distinct fixed branch lesion requiring another target.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Additional intervention at the wrong target while renal ischemia persists.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Distal septal fenestration for presumed continued dynamic obstruction.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Central expansion and entry sealing coexist with fixed renal flap narrowing and persistent gradient.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the branch were patent but central true-lumen collapse and cycling flap prolapse persisted, a pressure-equalizing fenestration could become reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize when new attributable symptoms override the prior small-AAA surveillance plan.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A change in symptoms can overturn a previously correct diameter-based plan.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Delay in evaluating an aneurysm that may be clinically unstable despite an intact image.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic to review serial outside aortic assessments. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the first surveillance visit. The clinic receives the original arterial CT volumes and the measurement records below.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: During a later outside admission he reports new deep abdominal and back pain beginning at rest and persisting through changes in position. Palpation over the pulsatile abdominal mass reproduces the pain. MR angiography measures the infrarenal sac at 4.9 cm without extravasation. A chronic lumbar wedge deformity has the same appearance as on older imaging. His pressure and lower-limb strength remain preserved.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have been selected for {patientName} during that admission?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Spine MRI first because a lumbar deformity appears in the imaging record.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: New persistent rest pain is reproduced over the aortic mass while the competing lumbar structural finding is unchanged.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace aortic tenderness/rest pain with reproducible mechanical back pain and new corresponding spinal findings: the spine-directed investigation becomes reasonable before attributing symptoms to the AAA.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize a direct attachment leak and repair the seal despite stable current sac size.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A dangerous direct-pressure leak should not inherit stable-sac observation rules.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Leaving a direct-pressure leak untreated.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 74-year-old woman, attends clinic to review a later outside CTA after EVAR. The sac diameter is unchanged, but contrast passes directly between the proximal graft edge and native aortic wall during the arterial phase. Modular junctions remain continuous. A healthy neck segment remains between the graft edge and the renal arteries.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s proximal attachment finding?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Surveillance because the sac has not enlarged.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Direct flow at the proximal attachment with an available healthy neck segment.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If contrast arrived through lumbar branches on delayed images with intact seals and a stable sac, continued surveillance would become correct.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Interpret the mechanical source of a junctional leak and distinguish a sealing repair from radial remodelling.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Correct leak recognition must lead to repair at the actual failed graft segment.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: An unclosed sac-pressure source with continuing rupture risk.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: Aortography shows arterial-phase contrast entering the sac between the main body and right iliac limb. Their fabric ends are separated rather than overlapped; the adjacent fabric is intact and the components remain aligned. Proximal and distal native-wall attachment images show no contrast escaping at those sites.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which endovascular repair should have addressed {patientName}'s demonstrated leak?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Balloon remodelling because the contrast focus lies at a modular junction.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The fabric ends have separated and no overlap remains across the leak route.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Maintain a fabric overlap and show incomplete expansion at that junction without an open gap: balloon remodelling becomes an appropriate offered repair.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Reassess an old leak attribution when sac growth and current imaging no longer establish the source.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: An old leak attribution can become unreliable when the sac trajectory changes.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Missing a direct-pressure leak and treating the wrong pathway.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: A later CTA measures the sac at 7.0 cm using the same method. Contrast appears near a graft-limb junction and a lumbar branch, but metal artifact prevents tracing its origin despite arterial and delayed acquisitions. He remains hemodynamically stable without pain.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which angiographic assessment should precede targeted leak treatment for {patientName} now?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Targeted lumbar angiography as if the original attribution were still established.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Large interval sac expansion plus artifact-limited origin near a graft junction despite an adequate multiphase acquisition.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If multiphase imaging conclusively established isolated lumbar inflow with no attachment or junction defect, selective iliolumbar mapping would become reasonable for treatment planning.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Combine branch-flow origin and sac trajectory to avoid unnecessary treatment of an isolated stable type II endoleak.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Avoid treating every persistent post-EVAR contrast focus when the source and trajectory favor observation.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Unnecessary intervention while teaching a mechanism-insensitive rule.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.

exhibit.caption: Constructed outside-record measurements; not a reproduced clinical image

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s later surveillance study?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Lumbar/sac embolization for a persistent but stable leak.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Lumbar continuity with identical full sac diameters and intact attachments/overlaps.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace branch filling with direct proximal attachment inflow: prompt seal treatment replaces surveillance even if size has not yet grown.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize an unaddressed graft-related source when bleeding and infection coexist after aortic reconstruction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Aortic graft history changes the interpretation of otherwise familiar gastrointestinal bleeding and infection.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Delayed recognition of a dangerous graft-related infection or bowel communication.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 75-year-old man, comes to clinic after hospitalization several months after open infrarenal AAA grafting. His outside record describes fever, recurrent positive blood cultures and intermittent melena. Upper endoscopy examined the esophagus, stomach and first two duodenal portions without finding a bleeding source. He was alert with preserved pressure between bleeding episodes.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which investigation should have followed {patientName}'s unrevealing upper endoscopy during that admission?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Push enteroscopy as the entire next workup because the earlier scope did not reach the distal duodenum.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Persistent unexplained bloodstream infection accompanies bleeding after prosthetic aortic reconstruction, while only proximal mucosa has been examined.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the unresolved prosthetic-infection concern with independently localized distal-duodenal mucosal bleeding: the offered distal enteroscopic investigation becomes appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose definitive source control for an infected aortic prosthesis in a patient who can undergo reconstruction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Definitive infection source control differs from hemostatic bridging or suppression.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Persistent infected material and bowel contamination.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 75-year-old man, comes to clinic after hospitalization several months after open infrarenal AAA grafting. His outside record describes fever, recurrent positive blood cultures and intermittent melena. Upper endoscopy examined the esophagus, stomach and first two duodenal portions without finding a bleeding source. He was alert with preserved pressure between bleeding episodes.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: CTA demonstrates a perigraft fluid-and-gas collection with a channel to adjacent duodenum. The same organism persists in repeated blood cultures despite directed intravenous antibiotics. He has preserved pressure and organ function, remains functionally independent, and the multidisciplinary hospital assessment finds no prohibitive operative condition.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Covered relining as definitive treatment because it may arrest bleeding.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A communicating perigraft collection, persistent same-organism cultures and no prohibitive operative condition.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace stable operability with uncontrolled hemorrhage and shock: covered relining as a bridge may become appropriate. Replace it with prohibitive permanent operative risk: suppression may be considered.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Localize a new post-TEVAR neurologic deficit and reverse impaired spinal perfusion rather than extending pressure reduction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: The required direction of pressure treatment changes when postoperative cord perfusion is threatened.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Worsening potentially reversible cord hypoperfusion.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, visits clinic to review an outside elective descending thoracic aneurysm repair. The planned proximal sealing segment spans the left subclavian origin. His CABG record shows a patent pedicled left internal mammary graft arising from the left subclavian artery to the LAD; the native LAD is chronically occluded. Both carotid arteries are patent.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The later outside ICU record describes new bilateral leg weakness after a hypotensive episode following long-segment TEVAR. Both feet remain warm with palpable pulses. Speech, face and arm movement are unchanged. Platelet count and coagulation studies are normal, and no neuraxial drain is present.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Continue esmolol pressure reduction because the patient has an aortic repair.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Bilateral leg deficit after hypotension with warm pulsed feet and preserved face/arm function.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Change the record to cold pulseless legs with confirmed aortoiliac occlusion: the offered limb-ischemia pathway becomes appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Trace LSA-dependent coronary inflow and preserve it before an elective covering graft.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Conduit origin and clamp sequence make a familiar revascularization technique hazardous in a specific patient.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Loss of coronary graft inflow during an otherwise elective procedure.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, visits clinic to review an outside elective descending thoracic aneurysm repair. The planned proximal sealing segment spans the left subclavian origin. His CABG record shows a patent pedicled left internal mammary graft arising from the left subclavian artery to the LAD; the native LAD is chronically occluded. Both carotid arteries are patent.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Choose transposition without accounting for interruption of the pedicled LIMA during proximal clamping.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Patent LIMA-to-LAD graft with native LAD occlusion and planned LSA-origin coverage.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the LIMA were a free graft arising from the aorta rather than a patent pedicled subclavian conduit, transposition could become a reasonable pre-coverage technique; the specific bypass-over-transposition constraint would be removed.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Identify an embolizing small PAA and choose repair planning rather than size-only or medication-only follow-up.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Complications override a memorized asymptomatic diameter rule.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Continued distal embolization and possible limb injury.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aneurysm plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s right popliteal lesion?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Anticoagulation and duplex as the definitive plan without a source-repair assessment.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Repeated distal embolic findings coexist with mural thrombus in the 18-mm lesion.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Remove thrombus and the embolic history while preserving a small stable asymptomatic PAA: annual surveillance becomes reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Identify symptomatic sac compression after successful exclusion/bypass rather than treating graft patency as resolution of the entire lesion.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Conduit patency does not establish that an excluded aneurysm no longer causes harm.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Persisting venous/neurologic compression despite attention to blood flow.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: After outside popliteal exclusion and vein bypass, he develops progressive calf swelling and plantar numbness. Duplex shows a widely patent bypass and persistent flow within an enlarging excluded sac. The sac displaces the popliteal vein and tibial nerve. Venous duplex shows compression without thrombus.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which procedure should have addressed {patientName}'s new postoperative problem?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Genicular inflow embolization as the entire treatment for the current compressive symptoms.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: An enlarging sac visibly displaces vein and nerve while the bypass is patent and the vein has no thrombus.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the patent bypass with a flow-limiting graft lesion and remove mass effect: bypass revision becomes the appropriate offered procedure.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Interpret pelvic inflow patency and choose an exclusion strategy preserving the remaining direct hypogastric supply.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Repair planning must account for the only remaining pelvic inflow and real landing anatomy.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Avoidable pelvic ischemia risk or failure to seal in a healthy segment.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 71-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside aortic measurement and treatment-planning record. She had no abdominal or back symptoms, remained independent in daily activities and had no major life-limiting illness. The original ultrasound measurements are shown below.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The repair-planning CTA shows enlargement of both common iliac arteries through their bifurcations. Contrast fills the right internal-iliac trunk and its divisions. At the left internal-iliac origin, arterial and delayed images show calcified occlusion without a continuous distal lumen. Both external iliac arteries have nonaneurysmal distal segments. The planned distal graft seals lie in the external iliac arteries.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which pelvic-inflow strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s planned distal seals?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Apply a nominal left-sided preservation policy while the patent right origin is excluded.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Right internal-iliac opacification with an occluded left channel, coupled with distal seals beyond both origins.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Reverse the observed patency so the left side supplies the pelvis and the right channel is occluded: left-sided preservation becomes the appropriate offered strategy.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose a durable repair approach for an operable heritable native-aorta TAAA rather than extending routine degenerative-aneurysm EVAR preferences.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A heritable substrate changes the applicability of an ordinary degenerative endovascular preference.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Extending a degenerative-aneurysm procedural preference without accounting for the heritable substrate.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 43-year-old man with genetically confirmed Marfan syndrome, attends clinic to review an outside aortic-team plan. An enlarging intact thoracoabdominal aneurysm includes the visceral origins; both potential endograft sealing regions are native aorta. He is active without major cardiac, pulmonary or renal dysfunction. Repair has been recommended, and both open and branched endovascular reconstruction are technically possible.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which repair approach should have been preferred for {patientName}'s intact thoracoabdominal aneurysm?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Branched endovascular repair because both procedures are technically feasible.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Confirmed Marfan syndrome with native sealing regions and no prohibitive open risk.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace Marfan with a degenerative aneurysm and substantially elevated open operative risk: branched endovascular repair becomes a reasonable preferred alternative after aortic-team assessment.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Determine whether an apparent six-month change is valid enough to support a growth-based repair decision.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Measurement-plane validity must precede a growth-based treatment conclusion.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Radiation/contrast exposure while leaving the growth inference unresolved.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic to review serial outside aortic assessments. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the first surveillance visit. The clinic receives the original arterial CT volumes and the measurement records below.

exhibit.caption: Constructed outside CT acquisition and measurement records
cells: 4.6 cm, outer wall to outer wall
5.3 cm, outer wall to outer wall
Short-axis reformat across local vessel path
Axial image across a curved segment

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which next aortic plan should have followed {patientName}'s serial CT reports?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Repair referral based on the apparent six-month enlargement as if it were confirmed.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Different image planes despite adequate complete source volumes from both time points.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Make both values matched orthogonal outer-wall measurements at the same landmark: the confirmed six-month increase supports the offered repair-evaluation plan.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Select the relevant full aneurysm dimension and apply the female repair-assessment boundary without mandating an operation.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A stable aneurysm can still cross a sex-specific repair-assessment boundary.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Delayed specialist repair evaluation.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 71-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside aortic measurement and treatment-planning record. She had no abdominal or back symptoms, remained independent in daily activities and had no major life-limiting illness. The original ultrasound measurements are shown below.

exhibit.caption: Constructed outside aortic ultrasound measurements

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aortic plan should have followed {patientName}'s measured result?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Use the full size but apply a male threshold and defer assessment for six months.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm outer contour surrounds a smaller flowing channel in a woman.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Change the patient to a man with the same asymptomatic full dimensions: six-month ultrasound becomes an appropriate offered plan. Change the female full sac to 4.2 cm: annual follow-up becomes appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use full sac size rather than a thrombus-lined lumen to determine referral for an intact 6-cm AAA.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Residual flowing lumen is not the full aneurysm diameter used for repair assessment.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Deferring assessment of an aneurysm already warranting repair consideration.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic to review his outside preventive-care records. He stopped smoking after 20 pack-years. At the first visit he had no abdominal or back symptoms. His previous chest CTA ended at the diaphragm; he had never had abdominal aortic imaging.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The next outside record contains an ultrasound with an outer-wall infrarenal aortic diameter of 6.0 cm and a flowing lumen of 3.1 cm surrounded by mural thrombus. He had no pain, remained independent, and had no life-limiting illness or major cardiopulmonary impairment.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s ultrasound result at that asymptomatic visit?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Annual surveillance based on the patent lumen.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The 6.0-cm outer wall surrounds a smaller lumen and mural thrombus.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Change the full sac to 4.7 cm with documented stability: annual ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose a usable surveillance modality after ultrasound becomes nondiagnostic in a patient with a serious iodinated-contrast reaction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Reconciled dimensions, population and adequate modality determine a concrete follow-up plan.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Unnecessary short-interval testing; a three-year error would under-surveil.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic to review serial outside aortic assessments. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the first surveillance visit. The clinic receives the original arterial CT volumes and the measurement records below.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The matched CT measurements are 4.6 and 4.7 cm, six months apart. At the following annual surveillance visit, ultrasound displays the anterior wall but cannot trace the posterior sac boundary through bowel gas on the acquired supine and lateral views. During the last iodinated-contrast injection he developed wheezing, generalized hives and hypotension requiring epinephrine. He has no new pain.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which study should have completed {patientName}'s current aortic surveillance assessment?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Order CTA after correctly recognizing that ultrasound is inadequate.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The posterior sac boundary is not measurable on the current views, and the prior iodinated injection produced an immediate systemic reaction.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Provide complete reproducible current ultrasound visualization of the sac: duplex becomes the appropriate offered study despite the contrast history.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Interpret the response of heart rate versus pressure to beta blockade and select the next infusion change.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Extent and current organ function distinguish initial impulse therapy from immediate repair.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Premature invasive treatment or failure to institute appropriate impulse control.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside aortic admission. His initial CTA showed a dissection flap beginning distal to the left subclavian artery without ascending extension or extravasation. The record below documents the subsequent monitored infusion response.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The outside monitored-treatment record shows sinus rate falling from 108 to 64/min during esmolol infusion, while arterial pressure remains 184/96 mm Hg. PR interval remains unchanged, the extremities are warm, urine output is maintained and echocardiography shows preserved systolic function without advanced aortic stenosis.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which infusion change should have followed {patientName}'s recorded treatment response?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Increase esmolol because blood pressure is still high.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Sinus rate is now 64/min while arterial pressure remains 184/96 with preserved perfusion.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Keep pressure elevated but leave the sinus rate at 108/min without a limiting beta-blocker effect: further esmolol titration becomes a reasonable offered next change before adding vasodilation.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Distinguish inflammatory wall disruption from a small true aneurysm when choosing whether to treat a visceral arterial lesion.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Wall-disruption mechanism changes management despite a small apparent lesion.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Leaving an acquired wall defect at risk while waiting for size growth.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside pancreatitis admission. Follow-up CTA shows a new 12-mm contrast-filled cavity outside the pancreas, continuous with the splenic artery through a focal wall defect beside an inflammatory collection. Earlier imaging showed that arterial segment without a cavity. He is stable and has no active bleeding.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which vascular plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s new splenic-artery lesion?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Annual size surveillance after applying a small true-aneurysm rule.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A new extra-organ cavity connected through a focal arterial wall defect after pancreatitis.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the lesion with a small contained intraparenchymal defect selected by specialists for strict observation: interval imaging can become appropriate. A stable small true aneurysm would require a separate policy decision, not this pseudoaneurysm rule.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use the associated aneurysm pattern and actual prior imaging coverage to complete an aneurysm survey without repeating an adequate examination.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: An association becomes useful when combined with the actual coverage of prior studies.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Duplicate testing while leaving the contralateral aneurysm site unassessed.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The outside file contains the following acquired studies and observations from that same workup.

exhibit.caption: Constructed original acquisition and observation log
cells: Outer aortic contours traced; maximum 2.5 cm
Deep venous compression and Doppler sequences

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which additional aneurysm study should have been selected after review of {patientName}'s original acquisitions?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Choose abdominal ultrasound after assuming the left-leg study already assessed the contralateral aneurysm site.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The apparently reassuring left-leg record consists of venous sequences, whereas the aortic outer contours were actually imaged.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Make the left examination a complete arterial duplex and the CT a pelvis-only acquisition: abdominal aortic ultrasound becomes the appropriate additional study.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Interpret actual inferior scan coverage before applying abdominal-aortic screening eligibility.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Preventive eligibility and prior scan coverage are a more useful application than repeating a modality label.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Missing an indicated abdominal-aortic screen.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside preventive-care visit. He stopped smoking after 20 pack-years and had no abdominal or back symptoms at that visit. The archived study is titled aortic CTA; its acquisition runs from the arch to the celiac origin.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aortic imaging plan should have been selected at {patientName}'s preventive visit?

rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The repair-planning CTA shows enlargement of both common iliac arteries through their bifurcations. Contrast fills the right internal-iliac trunk and its divisions. At the left internal-iliac origin, arterial and delayed images show calcified occlusion without a continuous distal lumen. Both external iliac arteries have nonaneurysmal distal segments. The planned distal graft seals lie in the external iliac arteries.
decisionNodes.stem: Which pelvic-inflow strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s planned distal seals?

answerChoices.label: Preserve right internal-iliac inflow during bilateral external-iliac extension
answerChoices.rationale: The right internal iliac is the remaining direct pelvic inflow. An exclusion strategy should preserve it when feasible rather than intentionally eliminating that route.

answerChoices.label: Preserve left internal-iliac inflow during bilateral external-iliac extension
answerChoices.rationale: The left channel is already occluded; assigning preservation to that side does not protect the patent right pelvic supply from the planned coverage.

answerChoices.label: Exclude both internal-iliac origins during bilateral external-iliac extension
answerChoices.rationale: This would intentionally interrupt the remaining right-sided route instead of preserving at least one direct hypogastric inflow when feasible.

decisionNodes.explanation: The current imaging leaves the right internal iliac as the remaining direct pelvic inflow. Preserve that route as part of exclusion planning when feasible. This is a strategy decision: the scan does not by itself establish eligibility for a particular iliac branch device, and the final preserving reconstruction requires separate anatomic planning.

decisionNodes.stem: Which endovascular repair should have addressed {patientName}'s demonstrated leak?

answerChoices.label: Covered stent-graft bridging at the modular junction
answerChoices.rationale: A fabric gap provides a direct route into the sac. A covered bridge restores the missing barrier between the aligned components.

answerChoices.label: Balloon remodelling at the modular junction
answerChoices.rationale: Expansion can improve apposition where fabric overlaps, but cannot supply the absent covering between separated ends.

answerChoices.label: Bare-metal stent reinforcement at the leaking segment
answerChoices.rationale: Radial scaffolding does not add a covering across the demonstrated open channel to the sac.

decisionNodes.explanation: The problem is loss of covered continuity, not simply insufficient expansion. A covered bridge can close a separated modular junction. Balloon remodelling or bare-metal reinforcement addresses other apposition/support problems but does not itself cover a fabric gap.
sourceLabels: Joo-Young Chun et al. (2024). CIRSE Standards of Practice on Management of Endoleaks Following Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.

record.title: Reassessing an enlarging EVAR sac with uncertain inflow
fairness: The meaningful decision is to question the earlier branch-leak attribution when a larger sac and indeterminate graft-junction flow appear, then investigate a potential direct graft-related source before selective branch treatment.

The three choices are angiographic assessments at the same stage. Aortography is a defensible first offered assessment; selective collateral studies might subsequently be needed but do not replace assessment of the uncertain graft interface.

The update supplies the current uncertainty even if earlier feedback is not recalled. Prior advice that source and sac behavior matter is general scaffolding, not disclosure of this selected assessment.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between an earlier documented pattern and an uncertain current source. Do not convert the task into an unsupported universal rule that selective studies are never useful.

contextAudit.carriedFacts: The 5.8-cm outer-sac value is from the original prior-node exhibit. Delayed lumbar-associated filling and intact attachments/overlaps are from the original header. No new measurement or growth cutoff is invented.
contextAudit.cueRecheck: The header gives the earlier observations without a type-II label or a treatment instruction. The current arterial/delayed acquisition remains indeterminate despite adequate phases, so source reassessment still competes with two credible selective branch studies.
contextAudit.sequenceRecheck: Both the prior stable-sac scored turn and the later component-repair turn are absent. Earlier raw measurements are supplied directly; no prior key or feedback is needed to interpret the changed source uncertainty.

authorGate.cueAttack: The header gives the earlier observations without a type-II label or a treatment instruction. The current arterial/delayed acquisition remains indeterminate despite adequate phases, so source reassessment still competes with two credible selective branch studies.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Define the inflow source during catheter workup before selecting targeted treatment.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that a new expanding sac invalidates automatic reassurance from prior stable branch flow.
Choose central graft/seal assessment before committing to one collateral route.
authorGate.difficulty: Hard prediction: the earlier correct surveillance decision and branch finding create a credible anchoring error; nearby lumbar contrast is not proof of causal inflow.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Large interval sac expansion plus artifact-limited origin near a graft junction despite an adequate multiphase acquisition.
authorGate.closestError: Targeted lumbar angiography as if the original attribution were still established.
authorGate.consequence: Missing a direct-pressure leak and treating the wrong pathway.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the growth and new uncertainty restores the earlier surveillance rationale. Phase acquisition details distinguish actual ambiguity from a merely missing export.
authorGate.counterfactual: If multiphase imaging conclusively established isolated lumbar inflow with no attachment or junction defect, selective iliolumbar mapping would become reasonable for treatment planning.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Both the prior stable-sac scored turn and the later component-repair turn are absent. Earlier raw measurements are supplied directly; no prior key or feedback is needed to interpret the changed source uncertainty.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: The later 7.0-cm measurement needs an actual earlier diameter and prior source pattern. decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
answerChoices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.

choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic 3.1-cm full aneurysm, rather than a 3.1-cm lumen inside a 6-cm sac, could support this interval.

decisionNodes.stem: Which study should have completed {patientName}'s current aortic surveillance assessment?

answerChoices.label: MRI of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The current ultrasound does not define full sac size; MRI provides cross-sectional assessment without requiring the iodinated-contrast exposure implicated in his prior reaction.

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging addresses the inadequate ultrasound, but this proposed contrast examination disregards the serious prior immediate reaction when MRI is a supported alternative.

answerChoices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The prior success of ultrasound does not establish a usable current outer-wall measurement through the documented acoustic limitation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Current ultrasound adequacy matters more than the fact that ultrasound was useful previously. Cross-sectional assessment is needed when the sac is not defined, and MRI is reasonable when CT is contraindicated. The earlier matched measurements do not establish the current sac size after an inadequate examination.

fairness: Reformatting and comparable orthogonal measurements are a defensible best answer. The issue is low discrimination rather than a demonstrated wrong key.
Elapsed time would be needed to judge a growth rate, but this task appropriately stops before that judgment. Do not invent a growth threshold.
suggestions: Make the resident interpret a concise measurement/acquisition exhibit and decide whether the apparent change warrants additional acquisition or a change in management. Compare credible approaches to the actual uncertainty rather than repeating the stated problematic protocol as a foil.
Preserve dataset adequacy and availability when necessary; removing those facts without replacing them would make retrieval versus repeat acquisition unfair.

reviews.title: Surveillance after matched AAA measurements
clarityIssues: The time between the two matched studies is not stated. The node should not imply that a growth-rate assessment has been completed from diameters alone.
fairness: Annual ultrasound is consistent with the intended uncomplicated male AAA diameter-band rule. The item supplies the corrected size and adequate ultrasound visualization, so selecting among intervals is essentially single-rule recall.

The sequence is coherent, but the preceding feedback has already taught the measurement correction. This node does not independently retest that inference, and the corrected current diameter alone selects the intended answer.
suggestions: If routine surveillance eligibility depends on the serial comparison, state its actual interval and relevant trajectory without inventing a growth cutoff.

Add a clinically consequential competing surveillance consideration or seek explicit acceptance as foundational interval practice. Do not count the prior node's measurement inference as this node's second step.

reviews.title: New pain in a smaller intact AAA

cues.phrase: should have replaced surveillance
cues.why: The task rules out both surveillance options before the learner interprets the symptoms. Only the repair-evaluation answer can satisfy the wording.

cues.phrase: the hospital evaluation identifies no competing abdominal or spinal cause
cues.why: This broad authored exclusion further supplies the attribution instead of showing the observations that distinguish the closest competing explanation.

fairness: New persistent aortic-localized pain and tenderness support inpatient repair assessment despite intact imaging and a diameter below the usual asymptomatic threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The chronology clearly changes the earlier asymptomatic premise, and the update contains the new decision-critical findings. The task itself, however, defeats the options.
suggestions: Ask neutrally which plan was appropriate at that admission; remove the instruction that surveillance must be replaced.

Retain genuine safety findings and use concrete relevant evaluation findings instead of a blanket exclusion of other causes. Compare credible plans at that stage rather than one active plan against two unsupported delays.

reviews.title: Repair evaluation for an asymptomatic woman
fairness: Repair evaluation is a defensible offered plan at the stated size and functional status. This wording does not mandate a specific operation.

The exact strength of sex-specific size recommendations and the boundary with continued surveillance require clinician/source confirmation; this offline review does not establish a universal mandatory repair threshold.
As written, sex plus an explicitly established diameter selects a familiar threshold rule. Stable serial size adds a misconception but little independent interpretation.
suggestions: If retained as resident application, introduce a real competing consideration that changes the referral decision and is resolved by observations, rather than adding more statements of fitness.

Explain the actual source-supported recommendation and its limitations after answering. Preserve evaluation-versus-mandatory-operation distinctions and avoid presenting all women's thresholds as a universal rule.

reviews.title: Iliac repair with one remaining pelvic inflow artery
clarityIssues: Nonaneurysmal distal landing segments establish a useful principle, but do not clearly establish that the right iliac branch device can be deployed in this anatomy.

cues.phrase: both common iliac arteries enlarged through their bifurcations
cues.why: The bilateral distal-common-iliac landing foil directly contradicts the stated extent of disease and is much weaker than a genuine competing pelvic-inflow strategy.

fairness: Recognizing that left internal-iliac occlusion leaves the right artery as the remaining direct pelvic inflow and preserving it during exclusion is a worthwhile two-step decision.

The keyed configuration is defensible if branch-device anatomy is suitable; nonaneurysmal landing zones alone leave uncertainty about that specific technical selection. This is an adequacy concern, not a claim that the proposed device is contraindicated.
The node follows the prior referral coherently, and the update restates the relevant planning anatomy without needing the earlier answer.
suggestions: Supply only the relevant branch-device anatomic observations needed to establish suitability, with supported criteria; alternatively test the inflow-preservation strategy without overcommitting to a particular device.
Replace the clearly aneurysmal landing-zone foil with a plausible configuration error. Keep the occluded-versus-patent side distinction and re-solve all options.

reviews.title: Branch-associated flow with an unchanged EVAR sac
fairness: The learner must interpret the delayed branch-associated route and then use unchanged sac size to distinguish surveillance from embolization. The leak description does not itself prescribe treatment.
Intact attachments weaken the cuff option for a clinical reason, not a grammatical shortcut. Continued surveillance is the defensible best offered action.
The explanation does not disclose the next node's angiographic plan or the later component failure.
suggestions: Keep the source-and-sac-behavior combination. The constructed table is appropriately labeled; avoid adding a universal intervention cutoff without direct supporting evidence.

reviews.title: Reassessing an enlarging EVAR sac with uncertain inflow
fairness: The meaningful decision is to question the earlier branch-leak attribution when a larger sac and indeterminate graft-junction flow appear, then investigate a potential direct graft-related source before selective branch treatment.

The three choices are angiographic assessments at the same stage. Aortography is a defensible first offered assessment; selective collateral studies might subsequently be needed but do not replace assessment of the uncertain graft interface.

The update supplies the current uncertainty even if earlier feedback is not recalled. Prior advice that source and sac behavior matter is general scaffolding, not disclosure of this selected assessment.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between an earlier documented pattern and an uncertain current source. Do not convert the task into an unsupported universal rule that selective studies are never useful.

reviews.title: Repairing a separated EVAR component

cues.phrase: Adequate overlap can be obtained between the existing components with an additional covered limb
cues.why: The update states the corrective device and successful bridging mechanism before the learner chooses the covered-graft bridge.

cues.phrase: Both attachment sites remain sealed
cues.why: This is clinically useful localization, but in this option set it also explicitly removes the proximal-cuff alternative, leaving little work after the supplied bridge plan.

fairness: A covered bridging repair is defensible for a demonstrated component separation with suitable overlap. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The evolution from initially intact overlaps to a later separation is coherent. The current update stands alone; the difficulty problem is the supplied repair, not missing chronology.
suggestions: Replace the sentence prescribing an additional covered limb with neutral anatomic observations sufficient to assess repair feasibility.

Use credible alternative repairs of the demonstrated defect, or change the task to make distinguishing the defect from another plausible source consequential. Do not remove necessary seal information merely to obscure the answer.

reviews.title: Proximal attachment leak despite stable sac size
fairness: The learner must infer an attachment-related leak from its route and act despite unchanged sac diameter. This contrasts meaningfully with surveillance for stable branch-associated flow.

A remaining healthy proximal segment makes extension a defensible best offered plan; actual device sizing is outside this strategy question. The task's proximal localization is necessary context rather than a sufficient nonmedical answer rule.
No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally appropriate offered alternative identified.
suggestions: Preserve the unchanged-sac distractor premise and the actual contrast route. Keep detailed device feasibility subject to normal clinical planning rather than implying that any healthy neck length is sufficient.

reviews.title: Imaging at a stable suspected rupture assessment

cues.phrase: recorded stable assessment
cues.why: The task supplies the stability classification instead of leaving interpretation of repeated pressure and mental status to the learner.

fairness: Urgent CTA for planning in the described stable suspected rupture is a defensible best answer. No confident inaccuracy identified.

Restricting the task to imaging and offering repeat duplex after an already diagnostic bedside ultrasound removes much of the consequential imaging-versus-immediate-treatment decision. The remaining task is largely modality recall.
The later confirmed rupture is not disclosed here, and this explanation does not give away the subsequent repair approach.
suggestions: Use a neutral next-step task if the intended inference is whether the patient's trajectory permits planning imaging. Retain observed physiology rather than announcing stability in the lead-in.
Compare credible actions at that actual stage without inventing a pressure cutoff or stripping out necessary urgency information.

reviews.title: Repair approach after confirmed rupture

cues.phrase: Emergency endovascular aneurysm repair
cues.why: Convergence: emergency occurs in two options and endovascular occurs in two options; the key uniquely combines the repeated components.

cues.phrase: the selected graft's instructions-for-use requirements are satisfied
cues.why: This supplies the procedural-eligibility inference. Together with the stated availability of both methods, the remaining distinction is the guideline preference.

fairness: Rupture, preserved pressure, suitable anatomy and expertise support emergency EVAR as the intended best offered approach. Preserved pressure does not make elective repair appropriate.
The third choice is a plainly inappropriate delay after rupture is established, rather than a serious competing repair decision.
The node follows CTA coherently and contains the relevant new findings, but the option matrix undermines independent reasoning.
suggestions: Remove the convergence pattern and replace the elective-repair foil with a credible same-stage alternative, or redesign the decision so urgency itself must be inferred with balanced options.
Where technical suitability is the intended inference, supply the supported observations rather than a completed eligibility conclusion. Do not replace it with arbitrary device thresholds.

reviews.title: Distal entry tear with ascending extension
fairness: The distal entry and ascending extension create a real classification trap. The learner must classify by involved aorta and choose the corresponding emergency pathway despite preserved pressure.

The medical option is not an equivalent definitive plan for the supplied acute ascending involvement. Interim impulse therapy remains compatible with arranging surgery and is not negated by this task.
No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical option-selection shortcut identified.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between entry location and ascending involvement. The word 'founder' is unnecessary framing but does not change the answer; a plain reference to reviewing the admission CTA would be cleaner.

reviews.title: Initial treatment of uncomplicated descending dissection

cues.phrase: He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure
cues.why: This clustered medication-permission sentence points toward the only drug regimen, while neither competing answer contains medication.

cues.phrase: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
cues.why: The key is the only medical option and uniquely contains an ordered, conditional plan; the two alternatives are short urgent operations. Choosing medical care automatically answers the untested sequencing detail.

fairness: Initial monitored impulse control is defensible for the supplied descending dissection without rupture or malperfusion, and the drug sequence is clinically coherent.

The question cannot discriminate knowledge of beta blockade before vasodilation because no competing medical sequence is offered. Several normal findings establish uncomplicated disease, but the choices make the final selection elementary.
suggestions: Choose one focused objective: medical-versus-interventional management with a genuine competing complication, or initial drug sequencing with comparable regimens. Do not claim the unopposed sequencing detail as a second tested inference.
Retain contraindication information only to the extent needed for the selected close alternatives, preferably as ordinary clinical observations rather than an option-specific permission list.

reviews.title: New renal malperfusion despite improved pressure and pain
fairness: The clinical response and new organ dysfunction pull in different directions. Urine output, creatinine and new asymmetric renal enhancement with true-lumen compression support a clinically consequential malperfusion inference rather than nonspecific creatinine attribution.
Intervention with TEVAR and reassessment is the defensible best offered plan given the stated access and sealing anatomy. Continuing observation misses the new complication.

The update clearly changes the original uncomplicated course. Prior explanation teaches initial therapy but does not supply the current intervention. Its own feedback anticipates reassessment, not the later branch-stent answer.
suggestions: Preserve both the apparent symptomatic improvement and objective new perfusion failure. Avoid making creatinine rise by itself diagnostic of malperfusion.

reviews.title: Persistent renal branch obstruction after central repair
fairness: The learner must distinguish a fixed intrabranch lesion from persistent central dynamic obstruction using the response to TEVAR, branch flap, nonvarying narrowing and pressure gradient, then select the corresponding intervention.

Branch stenting is the defensible best offered treatment. Septal fenestration is a credible competing mechanism-specific action; extending an already effective proximal repair does not address the demonstrated branch lesion.

The update restates the completed repair and residual findings sufficiently to stand alone. Prior feedback mentions central dynamic compression and reassessment but does not name the static lesion or its treatment.
suggestions: Retain the response-to-treatment observations and branch pressure evidence. The technical detail is justified by a consequential mechanism-specific action; do not add unsupported numeric gradients.

reviews.title: Preserving pedicled LIMA inflow during elective TEVAR
fairness: The learner must infer coronary dependence on subclavian inflow and then distinguish two prophylactic revascularization techniques, rather than merely recognize the risk of arm ischemia.

A patent pedicled LIMA and occluded native LAD provide a defensible reason to prefer bypass over transposition involving proximal subclavian interruption. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the exact technique comparison remains a specialist clinical-sign-off point in this offline review.
The delayed-bypass option is less appropriate because arm symptoms do not monitor the threatened coronary territory. The two before-coverage options prevent timing alone from identifying the key.
suggestions: Retain the pedicled graft origin, patency and native LAD status. Keep the explanation specific to this coronary-dependent anatomy rather than declaring transposition universally unsuitable.

reviews.title: Neurologic rescue after TEVAR and hypotension
fairness: Bilateral leg findings, preserved limb pulses and unchanged cranial/upper-limb function require localization before choosing cord-perfusion rescue rather than limb reperfusion or renewed pressure reduction.

Hypotension is a necessary causal observation, not a removable cue. The rescue activation is defensible; the explanation appropriately calls for specialist drainage assessment rather than claiming that normal coagulation tests establish every condition for immediate drain insertion.
The long-segment postoperative phase is coherent after elective TEVAR planning and is understandable from the update. The preceding LIMA explanation does not teach this neurologic rescue answer.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between activating perfusion/drainage rescue and inserting a drain without procedural assessment. If a future version asks specifically for drain placement, supply relevant antithrombotic exposure and other procedural safety information rather than relying solely on platelet count and coagulation tests.

reviews.title: Small popliteal aneurysm with distal embolization
clarityIssues: The task asks for an aneurysm plan, but the key selects a particular operation while the explanation says the exact operation still depends on assessment and conduit anatomy.
fairness: Blue toes with preserved pedal pulses, mural thrombus and digital occlusions support distal embolization; the complication changes the significance of the small aneurysm diameter. That is a useful two-step objective.

The case supports repair evaluation more clearly than it establishes exclusion and bypass as the selected operation. Operative fitness, suitable conduit and reconstruction anatomy are not supplied. This is overspecification of the key rather than a confident assertion that bypass would be wrong.
The alternative anticoagulation plan is a meaningful temptation, but its lack of definitive source treatment should be explained after answering.
suggestions: Either provide the decision-critical assessment supporting the named operation or make every option a comparably specific strategy at the repair-versus-surveillance stage. Avoid a generic individualized-planning key.
Explain why treating embolic risk without addressing the aneurysm source is less appropriate here, and preserve the distinction between an embolizing viable limb and an acutely threatened limb.

reviews.title: Completing the associated aneurysm survey

cues.phrase: Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
cues.why: The label announces repetition immediately after a complete normal abdominal CTA is supplied. It advertises why the option is unnecessary.

cues.phrase: right lower extremity from common femoral to pedal vessels
cues.why: Combined with the complete abdominal study, this leaves the left-sided option as the obvious missing counterpart. The record interpretation is mostly a coverage checklist rather than two consequential clinical inferences.

fairness: Contralateral popliteal screening is the defensible best offered study. The associated AAA/PAA concept is high yield, and no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
The acquisition records avoid mistaking absent exported images for absent acquisition, but the completeness statements and repeat-test foil make the item easy.
The workup is chronologically coherent and the update is sufficient with the shared PAA presentation. Prior repair feedback does not disclose the screening association.
suggestions: Keep an authentic acquisition-adequacy distinction if that is the objective, but compare equally plausible additional studies without labeling one as a redundant repeat.
If the purpose remains simple associated-aneurysm recall, request explicit foundational acceptance rather than asserting two-step resident difficulty.

reviews.title: Compressive excluded popliteal sac after bypass
clarityIssues: The sequence moves from an 18-mm aneurysm to an enlarging sac causing neural and venous symptoms without an interval or current size. It is plausible, but the compressed chronology makes the evolution difficult to picture.
fairness: The learner must distinguish a functioning bypass from a still-perfused excluded sac and address the compressive consequence. The closest competitor is residual-branch embolization, not revision of the patent bypass.

Symptomatic compression supports decompression, but the explanation only rejects bypass revision and never explains why branch embolization is less appropriate for this patient's current symptoms. I am not asserting that decompression is an incorrect key; the exact ranking against embolization needs clinician confirmation and clearer justification.
The update identifies the completed operation and current anatomy sufficiently to stand alone, although the time course should be clearer.
suggestions: Add a clinically plausible interval and observed progression sufficient to establish the current compressive problem; do not invent a size threshold.

Have the clinician adjudicate decompression versus inflow embolization for the stated severity, then explain the closest alternative explicitly. Name control of persistent inflow as part of the operative strategy if required by the intended procedure, rather than suggesting decompression without treatment of the perfused source.

reviews.title: Bleeding and bacteremia after aortic grafting

cues.phrase: Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
cues.why: The record just states that this scope was examined without a source; no change in examination adequacy or target is offered. The word repeat advertises the same already-completed workup as a weak foil.

cues.phrase: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
cues.why: Only this option names both salient structures in the presentation, while the competing endoscopy repeats the explicitly completed region. This creates a partial wording shortcut even before the graft-enteric complication is inferred.

fairness: Prior grafting, bacteremia and melena warrant concern for an infected graft-enteric complication; CTA is the defensible best offered investigation in the stated stable interval.

A limited negative endoscopy does not exclude that complication. The task has a valid diagnostic inference followed by a test-selection decision, but the closest endoscopic alternative is deliberately restricted to the already examined target.
The explanation does not disclose the definitive source-control answer in the next node.
suggestions: Compare credible investigations of the remaining uncertainty and label their scope in a parallel way. Do not use an identical completed examination as a disposable foil unless an actual reason to repeat it is supplied.
Retain hemodynamic context, the graft history and the actual endoscopic coverage; do not turn the negative examination into an exclusion of graft-enteric disease.

reviews.title: Definitive treatment of infected graft-enteric communication
fairness: The learner must interpret persistent infection plus a graft-to-bowel channel and distinguish definitive source control from hemorrhage bridging or suppressive therapy.

Graft removal with vascular and bowel reconstruction is the defensible best offered definitive strategy in the stated operable patient. The alternatives can have roles in other settings, which makes stability and operability necessary information rather than gratuitous permission.

The update follows imaging coherently and contains enough current information to answer independently. Earlier feedback identifies concern for a complication but does not prescribe this definitive operation.
suggestions: Keep the explicit definitive-treatment task and persistent-infection observations. Do not imply that suppressive treatment or endovascular bridging has no role in inoperable or unstable patients.

reviews.title: Repair strategy for native-aortic Marfan TAAA
fairness: A known syndrome is appropriate because this is a management task. Native landing-zone tissue, intact aneurysm, fitness and technical feasibility of alternatives require the resident to separate technical possibility from long-term preferred strategy.
Open repair is a defensible preferred approach in this supplied setting. Branched and hybrid alternatives are specific same-stage competitors, not nonsensical options.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The exact recommendation remains subject to clinician review; this offline PASS does not freshly verify the cited guideline or make open repair universal for every patient with heritable disease.
