suggestions: Retain native-versus-prosthetic landing-zone information and the intact, operable context. Keep explanation language about preference within this setting rather than an absolute prohibition of endovascular treatment.

reviews.title: New splenic arterial cavity after pancreatitis
clarityIssues: The explanation gives 'extra-organ location' diagnostic or management weight without making clear why location outside the pancreas matters independently of the demonstrated arterial wall defect.

cues.phrase: Prompt splenic-artery embolization assessment
cues.why: This is the sole active treatment pathway and an assessment-level label, whereas both competitors commit to specific imaging-surveillance policies. That asymmetry makes the key easier to select than a comparison of equally concrete plans.

fairness: The new arterial communication through a wall defect after pancreatitis supports a pseudoaneurysm inference, and its small size and current stability do not make ordinary true-aneurysm size surveillance the best offered plan.

The intended treatment-assessment key is defensible. I do not identify a confident clinical inaccuracy, but extra-pancreatic location should not be taught as an independent defining criterion without a clear supported reason.
The two surveillance distractors test essentially the same delay error rather than two distinct close alternatives.
suggestions: Focus the explanation on acquired wall disruption and arterial communication; remove or substantiate the claimed role of extra-organ location.

Compare plans at the same decision stage and specificity, with one credible size-based surveillance error and another genuinely distinct alternative. Preserve the small-size/stability conflict rather than making the item harder through unsupported embolization anatomy or thresholds.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic to review his outside preventive-care records. He stopped smoking after 20 pack-years. At the first visit he had no abdominal or back symptoms. His previous chest CTA ended at the diaphragm; he had never had abdominal aortic imaging.

nodes.objective: Apply ever-smoker eligibility and the actual scope of prior imaging to choose an initial abdominal aortic screen.
nodes.stem: Which imaging plan should have been selected at {patientName}'s asymptomatic preventive visit?

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound
choices.rationale: He was an eligible previously unscreened man; chest imaging did not examine the abdominal aorta.
choices.temptation: Selects the recommended screening modality after checking prior coverage.
choices.counterfactual: An adequate previous abdominal aortic screen would remove the indication for a new one-time screen.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic CT angiography
choices.rationale: CTA can define repair anatomy but is not the routine first screen for this asymptomatic eligible man.
choices.temptation: Treats the greater anatomic detail of CTA as a reason to use it for screening.
choices.counterfactual: New pain with suspected symptomatic AAA would favor diagnostic CT rather than preventive ultrasound.

choices.label: No additional aortic imaging
choices.rationale: The previous study ended before the abdominal aorta, and remote smoking still counts as ever smoking.
choices.temptation: Counts any previous aortic scan or remote cessation as a completed screen.
choices.counterfactual: A documented adequate prior abdominal aortic screen could make no repeat one-time screening appropriate.

nodes.explanation: An ever-smoker in the eligible age range still needs a first abdominal aortic screen when prior imaging covered the chest. Ultrasound is the initial screening modality.

gate.cueAttack: The complaint names the organ, not the modality. Chest CTA is retained because its inferior coverage boundary changes whether screening is complete. Three imaging plans use similar scope; both offered tests have wait metadata.
gate.stageAndCategory: Initial preventive abdominal-aortic imaging plans; no repair or rupture action competes at this stage.
reasoningSteps: Infer that the infrarenal aorta was not assessed by the prior chest acquisition.
Apply age and ever-smoking eligibility to choose ultrasound rather than repeat chest work or diagnostic CTA.
gate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: an otherwise prepared PGY-2/3 may mistake remote cessation or prior thoracic CTA for completed screening. The ultrasound-versus-CTA distinction remains a narrower rule than the later complications.
gate.decidingObservation: The prior acquisition stops at the diaphragm and he has never had abdominal imaging.
gate.closestError: No additional imaging because an aortic CTA already exists.
gate.consequence: Missing an indicated abdominal-aortic screen.
gate.deletionTest: Removing prior-coverage information leaves uncertainty about a completed screen. Removing smoking or age changes eligibility. The number of pack-years is a fictional exposure, not an eligibility cutoff.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the chest study with a documented completed adequate abdominal aortic screen: no additional one-time screen becomes the best offered plan.
gate.sequenceReview: The first explanation gives no repair diameter or subsequent result. The later ultrasound appears only after this answer as a separate outside record; no test is executed in clinic.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed radiography and transthoracic echo foils and the one-time-test lead-in. Re-solved with the earlier scan's actual field of view; all three plans have a real screening/diagnostic role.

nodes.objective: Use full sac size rather than a thrombus-lined lumen to determine referral for an intact 6-cm AAA.
nodes.update: The next outside record contains an ultrasound with an outer-wall infrarenal aortic diameter of 6.0 cm and a flowing lumen of 3.1 cm surrounded by mural thrombus. He had no pain, remained independent, and had no life-limiting illness or major cardiopulmonary impairment.
nodes.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s ultrasound result at that asymptomatic visit?

choices.label: Refer for elective vascular repair evaluation
choices.rationale: Repair assessment uses the outer aneurysm diameter; the patent channel understates sac size.
choices.temptation: Recognizes that thrombus does not remove the surrounding sac from size assessment.
choices.counterfactual: A small stable full sac diameter would support surveillance instead.

choices.label: Arrange annual aortic ultrasound surveillance
choices.rationale: A 3.1-cm patent lumen is not the relevant aneurysm diameter; the full sac is 6.0 cm.
choices.temptation: Uses the smaller channel as the aneurysm measurement.
choices.counterfactual: A stable 4.7-cm full sac in an asymptomatic man would support annual ultrasound.

choices.label: Arrange three-year aortic ultrasound surveillance
choices.rationale: A surveillance schedule for a much smaller AAA is inappropriate for this full sac size.
choices.temptation: Treats thrombus as an exclusion of the aneurysmal wall and follows a small-AAA interval.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic 3.1-cm full aneurysm, rather than a 3.1-cm lumen inside a 6-cm sac, could support this interval.

nodes.explanation: Use the full outer-wall aneurysm diameter. A stable acceptable-risk man with a 6-cm fusiform AAA needs elective vascular repair evaluation; mural thrombus does not reduce that diameter to the flowing channel.

gate.cueAttack: The update provides both competing measurements without identifying the one to use. Removed 'acceptable operative-risk candidate' as an authored eligibility conclusion; ordinary function and absence of life-limiting illness supply context. Surveillance choices carry identical ultrasound profiles.
gate.stageAndCategory: Plans after an intact asymptomatic aneurysm result: repair referral or specified imaging surveillance.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish full sac diameter from residual flowing lumen.
Apply the full 6-cm size and patient context to elective repair referral.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: a plausible lumen-versus-sac error now competes with the correct referral; no emergency-exploration or discharge caricature remains.
gate.decidingObservation: The 6.0-cm outer wall surrounds a smaller lumen and mural thrombus.
gate.closestError: Annual surveillance based on the patent lumen.
gate.consequence: Deferring assessment of an aneurysm already warranting repair consideration.
gate.deletionTest: Without the paired measurements, the distinctive interpretation step disappears. Symptoms and general fitness establish an elective, rather than emergent or futile, evaluation.
gate.counterfactual: Change the full sac to 4.7 cm with documented stability: annual ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
gate.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback covers eligibility and screening modality only. It does not teach sac measurement or a repair threshold. This later decision changes care.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced ruptured-exploration and no-follow-up foils with credible surveillance plans. Both wrong intervals now reflect the supplied smaller measurement; the outside ultrasound is a completed record, not a fabricated pending result gate.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, comes to clinic to review serial outside aortic studies. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the surveillance visit. The prior CTA measured 4.6 cm perpendicular to the aortic centerline; the new report lists 5.3 cm on an axial image across a curved segment. Both original CT datasets are available.

nodes.objective: Resolve noncomparable serial dimensions before treating an apparent diameter increase as rapid growth.
nodes.stem: Which imaging action should precede a growth-based repair decision for {patientName} at that visit?

choices.label: Re-measure both CT datasets perpendicular to the centerline
choices.rationale: Different measurement planes can create an apparent increase; the acquired data permit a comparable assessment.
choices.temptation: Checks measurement validity before assigning growth.
choices.counterfactual: If matched orthogonal measurements confirmed enlargement, reassessment rather than another reformat would be needed.

choices.label: Acquire another contrast CT using the new axial protocol
choices.rationale: Another noncomparable acquisition does not resolve the existing plane mismatch.
choices.temptation: Mistakes measurement inconsistency for a need to repeat acquisition.
choices.counterfactual: An unavailable or technically inadequate existing acquisition could require new CT imaging.

choices.label: Replace the CT comparison with a new ultrasound diameter
choices.rationale: A new modality does not establish how the two existing CT measurements relate.
choices.temptation: Uses a third number to arbitrate a methodological discrepancy.
choices.counterfactual: Once a comparable small stable AAA is established, ultrasound is suitable for ongoing surveillance.

nodes.explanation: Compare the same anatomic site with reproducible orthogonal measurements. Reformat the available acquisitions before labeling the difference as growth; repeating the scan is not necessary just to correct a measurement plane.

gate.cueAttack: The exhibit-free imaging record contains acquisition observations, not the conclusion 'measurement artifact.' The key is longest by a few words but all labels name a concrete imaging action; re-measure versus re-acquire is the tested distinction, not a caution cue.
gate.stageAndCategory: Resolve the validity of a serial imaging comparison before any growth-based repair decision.
reasoningSteps: Identify noncomparable axial and centerline-perpendicular measurements.
Choose re-analysis of already acquired images rather than another acquisition or cross-modality comparison.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: apparent threshold crossing tempts escalation, while a repeat scan feels more definitive than reviewing the adequate acquisition.
gate.decidingObservation: Different planes across a curved segment, with both datasets available.
gate.closestError: Repeat contrast CT under the same new axial protocol.
gate.consequence: Radiation/contrast exposure while leaving the growth inference unresolved.
gate.deletionTest: The whole update is required: removing the planes or availability of datasets changes the comparison. No report conclusion supplies the answer.
gate.counterfactual: If the original acquisitions were unavailable or inadequate for the needed landmarks, new appropriate cross-sectional acquisition would become reasonable.
gate.sequenceReview: Later annual-surveillance and symptom decisions receive new observations after this answer. This explanation does not specify an interval or symptom-triggered operation.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Rejected an initial immediate-repair foil because it compared another care stage. All three final choices address imaging validity; both new acquisitions have wait metadata.

nodes.objective: Use matched serial diameter and symptom status to select an appropriate small-AAA follow-up interval.
nodes.update: Matched outer-wall orthogonal measurements are 4.6 cm on the prior CTA and 4.7 cm on the current study. He remains free of abdominal or back symptoms. The entire infrarenal sac is consistently visualized on ultrasound.
nodes.stem: Which aortic surveillance schedule should have been selected for {patientName} after that comparison?

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 12 months
choices.rationale: The matched size places this asymptomatic man in the annual-ultrasound group.
choices.temptation: Integrates comparable size, absence of symptoms and usable ultrasound.
choices.counterfactual: A larger diameter near the male repair threshold would shorten surveillance.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 6 months
choices.rationale: This follows a larger-AAA schedule rather than the supported schedule for his matched 4.7-cm diameter.
choices.temptation: Uses the unreconciled 5.3-cm report or applies the female size bands to this man.
choices.counterfactual: A stable asymptomatic man with a 5.2-cm AAA could reasonably receive six-month surveillance.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 3 years
choices.rationale: This is too long for the measured 4.7-cm sac.
choices.temptation: Applies a small-AAA surveillance interval to the wrong size band.
choices.counterfactual: A stable asymptomatic 3.5-cm AAA would support a three-year interval.

nodes.explanation: The matched study establishes a 4.7-cm AAA, not a confirmed jump to 5.3 cm. Annual ultrasound is the guideline schedule for an asymptomatic man in this diameter band when ultrasound defines the sac adequately.

gate.cueAttack: All options are the same modality and comparable length, with the same wait profile. Neither the complaint nor earlier explanation provides the interval. The previously larger number is intentionally retained in history as the competing error.
gate.stageAndCategory: Imaging-surveillance schedules, not repair modalities.
reasoningSteps: Use the valid matched measurements instead of the initial oblique report.
Apply the male diameter band and adequate imaging window to a surveillance interval.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: applying the unreconciled report or the wrong sex-specific band is plausible despite knowing that surveillance is indicated.
gate.decidingObservation: A reproducible 4.7-cm sac in an asymptomatic man with an adequate ultrasound window.
gate.closestError: Six-month ultrasound based on the original 5.3-cm report.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary short-interval testing; a three-year error would under-surveil.
gate.deletionTest: Delete the new comparison and the six-month schedule could follow from the earlier report; the update changes the answer. Ultrasound adequacy earns its role in modality choice.
gate.counterfactual: A matched 5.2-cm sac in the same asymptomatic man changes the preferred offered interval to six months.
gate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback requires comparable planes but gives no interval. This node supplies the corrected result only now. Subsequent feedback does not anticipate the later pain episode.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed elective repair from this interval task and balanced all labels to modality plus interval. Clinical follow-up intervals are evidence-backed; they are distinct from gameplay wait placeholders.

nodes.objective: Recognize when new attributable symptoms override the prior small-AAA surveillance plan.
nodes.update: A later outside admission documents persistent new deep abdominal and back pain, focal tenderness over the aorta and no relation to movement. CTA shows a 4.9-cm intact fusiform AAA; the hospital evaluation identifies no competing abdominal or spinal cause. He is normotensive and otherwise fit for repair.
nodes.stem: Which hospital aortic plan should have replaced surveillance for {patientName} during that admission?

choices.label: Inpatient vascular assessment for aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The new pain pattern and localized findings support aneurysm-attributable symptoms despite a subthreshold asymptomatic diameter.
choices.temptation: Reassesses the earlier plan when the care phase changes.
choices.counterfactual: Reproducible mechanical pain with a separate established cause would support returning to size-based surveillance.

choices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in six months
choices.rationale: A shorter surveillance interval does not address the new symptomatic aneurysm assessment.
choices.temptation: Treats the earlier size-based plan as valid despite the new symptom evidence.
choices.counterfactual: A larger but asymptomatic unrepaired AAA can merit six-month follow-up.

choices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in twelve months
choices.rationale: The old annual plan was for an asymptomatic patient; the current observations change that premise.
choices.temptation: Anchors on the earlier node's correct annual interval.
choices.counterfactual: With an independently established nonaneurysmal pain cause and no AAA symptoms, annual surveillance of a stable 4.9-cm male AAA would be reasonable.

nodes.explanation: A symptomatic intact AAA is assessed for repair even below the usual asymptomatic diameter threshold. The new localized persistent pain changes the previous surveillance premise; hemodynamic stability and absence of a CT leak do not restore that premise.

gate.cueAttack: No pre-answer sentence labels the aneurysm 'symptomatic' or 'the cause.' The pain attribution observations and competing-cause evaluation are necessary for fairness. All options are aortic care plans at this admission; no reassuring discharge or emergency laparotomy caricature is used.
gate.stageAndCategory: Aortic disposition/management plans after a new hospital evaluation.
reasoningSteps: Infer a clinically attributable aneurysm symptom pattern despite no visible rupture.
Replace the earlier asymptomatic surveillance strategy with inpatient repair assessment.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: anchoring on the just-learned size interval and interpreting intact CTA as permission for continued surveillance are credible errors.
gate.decidingObservation: A new persistent localized pain syndrome without another identified cause, rather than size change alone.
gate.closestError: Annual surveillance based on the earlier 4.7-cm classification.
gate.consequence: Delay in evaluating an aneurysm that may be clinically unstable despite an intact image.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the whole symptom update restores the prior annual key, so the later node earns a new inference. Normotension and repair fitness define the available hospital options.
gate.counterfactual: If the pain were reproducible with movement and a separate spinal cause were established, size-based outpatient surveillance could again be appropriate.
gate.sequenceReview: Earlier explanations discuss measurement and asymptomatic intervals only; they do not announce symptoms as a repair trigger. This is a historical admission reviewed in clinic, not an ICU or ED encounter generated in the clinic.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a generic 'urgent referral' key with a concrete inpatient vascular repair assessment. Retained pain attribution and urgent warning observations; no exact deadline or drug regimen invented.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 71-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside vascular consultation. She was asymptomatic and independent in daily activities. Serial orthogonal measurements showed a fusiform infrarenal AAA of 5.1 cm, unchanged from the preceding study. No major life-limiting illness was identified.

nodes.objective: Apply the female repair-assessment threshold without treating stable size or female sex as a reason to defer assessment.
nodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been offered after {patientName}'s 5.1-cm result?

choices.label: Elective vascular evaluation for aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The size meets the female repair-assessment boundary even without interval growth.
choices.temptation: Uses the appropriate population and leaves the actual procedure to anatomic and operative assessment.
choices.counterfactual: A smaller asymptomatic sac would favor continued imaging surveillance.

choices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every six months
choices.rationale: A male size band should not postpone this woman's repair assessment.
choices.temptation: Applies the male threshold and waits for growth to establish eligibility.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic woman with a 4.7-cm AAA could receive six-month surveillance.

choices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every twelve months
choices.rationale: Annual follow-up does not address a woman's aneurysm already at the repair-assessment boundary.
choices.temptation: Assumes stability negates a size indication or applies the wrong surveillance band.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic woman with a 4.2-cm AAA could receive annual surveillance.

nodes.explanation: A stable diameter can still warrant repair evaluation. The guideline boundary is lower in women than men, but it does not prescribe a procedure or an individual mortality estimate.

gate.cueAttack: Sex and full measured size are necessary eligibility data, not deterministic risk language. The stem does not ask for a sex association or announce a lower threshold. All choices name concrete plans, and both surveillance choices have ultrasound wait metadata.
gate.stageAndCategory: Elective aortic management after an established intact aneurysm result.
reasoningSteps: Separate absence of growth from being below a size threshold.
Apply the female diameter boundary to repair assessment rather than borrowing the male band.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: stable size and remembered male thresholds are two credible competing errors. This is a practical replacement for repeating an epidemiologic association.
gate.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm full sac in a woman without a life-limiting condition.
gate.closestError: Six-month surveillance until the male repair threshold is reached.
gate.consequence: Delayed specialist repair evaluation.
gate.deletionTest: Removing sex or the measured diameter makes the interval/referral ranking indeterminate. Ordinary function supplies fitness context without assigning an invented mortality score.
gate.counterfactual: Change the diameter to 4.7 cm while retaining the asymptomatic female profile: six-month ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
gate.sequenceReview: The subsequent iliac decision uses a new CTA planning record. This explanation does not teach hypogastric preservation.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Created a separate meaning; no FSRS history from the approved sex-outcome association is transferred. Replaced unqualified mandatory EVAR with assessment rather than asserting that diameter determines the operation.

nodes.objective: Choose an iliac repair configuration that preserves the only remaining internal-iliac inflow.
nodes.update: The outside repair-planning CTA shows both common iliac arteries enlarged through their bifurcations. The left internal iliac artery is chronically occluded. The right internal iliac and both external iliac arteries are patent, with nonaneurysmal distal landing segments. A standard bifurcated infrarenal main body can be used.
nodes.stem: Which iliac configuration should have been selected for {patientName}'s planned endovascular repair?

choices.label: Right iliac branch graft; left external-iliac extension
choices.rationale: This preserves the patent right internal iliac route while excluding the aneurysmal common iliac segments.
choices.temptation: Maps inflow, outflow and the remaining pelvic circulation.
choices.counterfactual: If no right internal-iliac landing segment existed, a different reconstruction would need assessment.

choices.label: Bilateral external-iliac extensions; right internal-iliac embolization
choices.rationale: This would eliminate the remaining direct internal-iliac inflow when a preserving option is anatomically described.
choices.temptation: Prioritizes simple exclusion of both common iliac aneurysms without accounting for the contralateral occlusion.
choices.counterfactual: Loss of an internal-iliac artery can be acceptable when the other remains patent and preservation is not feasible.

choices.label: Bilateral limb landings within the distal common iliac arteries
choices.rationale: The proposed landing regions remain aneurysmal through the bifurcations and do not supply a healthy distal seal.
choices.temptation: Avoids internal-iliac interruption by retaining the usual common-iliac landing position.
choices.counterfactual: Nonaneurysmal common iliac landing segments could permit this configuration.

nodes.explanation: The left internal iliac artery is already occluded. Use a configuration that excludes the aneurysms while preserving the patent right pelvic inflow when feasible; landing within an aneurysmal common iliac segment does not solve exclusion.

gate.cueAttack: The update gives each relevant vessel's patency and landing-segment anatomy without naming pelvic ischemia or a preserving technique. Every option is a graft configuration; no uniquely cautious counseling label appears.
gate.stageAndCategory: Distal graft configuration after an elective EVAR plan, not selection of whether to repair.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that the right internal iliac is the remaining direct pelvic inflow and that both usual distal landing regions are aneurysmal.
Choose an excluding configuration that preserves that inflow.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a technically simple bilateral external extension is tempting, as is retaining common-iliac landings to avoid branch work.
gate.decidingObservation: Left internal-iliac occlusion plus right internal-iliac and external-iliac distal landing segments.
gate.closestError: Bilateral external extension with embolization of the remaining internal iliac.
gate.consequence: Avoidable pelvic ischemia risk or failure to seal in a healthy segment.
gate.deletionTest: The entire new vessel map is needed; without it, no configuration is uniquely preferred. No arbitrary device dimension is imposed.
gate.counterfactual: Restore nonaneurysmal distal common iliac landing zones: standard common-iliac limb landings become appropriate. Remove the right branch landing zone: the exact chosen branch configuration is no longer established.
gate.sequenceReview: The preceding size decision does not disclose this vessel map or preservation rule. A new clinical decision is made at the planning stage.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a fourth implausible remote-vessel operation. Kept three actual configurations and a source limitation: final device suitability requires the treating vascular team, not this synthetic map.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.

nodes.objective: Combine branch-flow origin and sac trajectory to avoid unnecessary treatment of an isolated stable type II endoleak.

exhibit.caption: Constructed outside-record measurements; not a reproduced clinical image

nodes.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s later surveillance study?

choices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
choices.rationale: The branch origin and unchanged sac support observation with continued imaging.
choices.temptation: Interprets both the leak route and sac behavior.
choices.counterfactual: A direct attachment leak or a growing sac would require a different evaluation or intervention.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: A visible branch leak does not by itself establish a treatment benefit when the sac is stable.
choices.temptation: Treats persistence of any contrast outside the graft as a repair indication.
choices.counterfactual: A persistent proven branch leak with consequential sac growth can merit embolization after other sources are excluded.

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: The observed inflow is from lumbar branches, not the proximal attachment.
choices.temptation: Confuses every leak with a proximal seal failure.
choices.counterfactual: A proximal attachment leak with a usable extra landing segment would favor cuff extension.

nodes.explanation: Delayed branch-associated flow with an unchanged sac supports continued surveillance. A visible leak is not enough to choose its treatment; source and sac behavior matter.

gate.cueAttack: The record never calls the flow benign or supplies a type label. The table requires the learner to compare diameter across time. Each option names one plan; the key is not the most detailed or only cautious phrase. Its ultrasound wait is explicit.
gate.stageAndCategory: Management of a known post-EVAR sac-flow finding at surveillance.
reasoningSteps: Infer retrograde side-branch inflow from phase and continuity.
Use unchanged serial sac size to favor surveillance rather than treating every leak.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: embolization feels appropriate when contrast persists, and a proximal cuff is a real treatment for the competing leak mechanism.
gate.decidingObservation: Lumbar continuity with identical full sac diameters and intact attachments/overlaps.
gate.closestError: Lumbar/sac embolization for a persistent but stable leak.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary intervention while teaching a mechanism-insensitive rule.
gate.deletionTest: Without the diameter comparison, the branch leak might coexist with enlargement and the management ranking would be incomplete. Attachment observations exclude a different dangerous source without interpreting them for the learner.
gate.counterfactual: Replace branch filling with direct proximal attachment inflow: prompt seal treatment replaces surveillance even if size has not yet grown.
gate.sequenceReview: Feedback does not name component separation or its treatment. Subsequent growth and new angiographic anatomy are withheld until their nodes.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the label 'isolated type II' from the visible context and replaced it with raw phase/continuity observations. The constructed table is numerical evidence rather than a promised scan asset.

nodes.objective: Reassess an old leak attribution when sac growth and current imaging no longer establish the source.
nodes.update: A later CTA measures the sac at 7.0 cm using the same method. Contrast appears near a graft-limb junction and a lumbar branch, but metal artifact prevents tracing its origin despite arterial and delayed acquisitions. He remains hemodynamically stable without pain.
nodes.stem: Which angiographic assessment should precede targeted leak treatment for {patientName} now?

choices.label: Aortography across the seal zones and graft junctions
choices.rationale: The enlarging sac and uncertain source require reassessment for direct graft or attachment inflow before targeting a branch.
choices.temptation: Questions whether the old branch label explains the current growth.
choices.counterfactual: A clearly established enlarging isolated branch leak could move directly to targeted branch mapping and embolization.

choices.label: Selective mesenteric-to-inferior-mesenteric collateral angiography
choices.rationale: This maps a branch route but does not resolve the possible attachment or component defect producing the current sac growth.
choices.temptation: Extends the previous type-II attribution to a new scan without validating it.
choices.counterfactual: Proven inferior-mesenteric branch inflow into a growing sac can justify this approach.

choices.label: Selective iliolumbar-to-lumbar collateral angiography
choices.rationale: The lumbar branch near the contrast focus does not establish that it is the only source.
choices.temptation: Anchors on the branch seen on the earlier surveillance images.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed isolated lumbar leak with sac growth can be mapped for targeted embolization.

nodes.explanation: Do not carry forward a branch-leak label when a growing sac has an uncertain current inflow source. Problem-solving aortography can assess the attachments and modular junctions before choosing a branch-directed treatment.

gate.cueAttack: All three choices are equally specific catheter-angiographic assessments and share a wait profile. The update describes both candidate sites and actual acquired phases; it does not say a series is missing or name an omitted action.
gate.stageAndCategory: Define the inflow source during catheter workup before selecting targeted treatment.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that a new expanding sac invalidates automatic reassurance from prior stable branch flow.
Choose central graft/seal assessment before committing to one collateral route.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: the earlier correct surveillance decision and branch finding create a credible anchoring error; nearby lumbar contrast is not proof of causal inflow.
gate.decidingObservation: Large interval sac expansion plus artifact-limited origin near a graft junction despite an adequate multiphase acquisition.
gate.closestError: Targeted lumbar angiography as if the original attribution were still established.
gate.consequence: Missing a direct-pressure leak and treating the wrong pathway.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the growth and new uncertainty restores the earlier surveillance rationale. Phase acquisition details distinguish actual ambiguity from a merely missing export.
gate.counterfactual: If multiphase imaging conclusively established isolated lumbar inflow with no attachment or junction defect, selective iliolumbar mapping would become reasonable for treatment planning.
gate.sequenceReview: The first explanation teaches source/trajectory assessment but does not identify this new source. This node's explanation names possible categories but gives no repair configuration for the later demonstrated defect.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced 'obtain more information' versus repair options with three same-stage angiographic targets. No universal growth threshold is inferred from the constructed large change.

nodes.objective: Use direct junctional flow and component separation to choose a repair that closes the actual graft defect.
nodes.update: Aortography shows contrast passing through a gap between the main body and right iliac limb into the sac during the arterial phase. Both attachment sites remain sealed. Adequate overlap can be obtained between the existing components with an additional covered limb.
nodes.stem: Which endovascular repair should have been selected for {patientName}'s demonstrated defect?

choices.label: Bridge the separated components with a covered graft
choices.rationale: The source is the modular gap; a bridging covered component restores continuity.
choices.temptation: Matches the repair to the observed mechanical failure.
choices.counterfactual: A branch-fed leak without component disruption would require a different strategy.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: Branch embolization does not close the direct connection through the separated graft components.
choices.temptation: Persists with the earlier lumbar explanation despite new central findings.
choices.counterfactual: A proven isolated growing lumbar leak can warrant embolization.

choices.label: Extend the proximal attachment with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: The proximal seal is intact; extending it does not cover the limb junction gap.
choices.temptation: Recognizes a high-pressure leak but repairs the wrong level.
choices.counterfactual: A proximal attachment defect with additional landing length could be treated by a cuff.

nodes.explanation: The direct component gap is a type III mechanism and requires prompt repair. A covered bridge across the separation closes the source; branch embolization or a remote proximal extension would not.

gate.cueAttack: The update supplies raw defect anatomy instead of a type-III label. 'Covered graft' is one specific repair among parallel actual endovascular actions; no uniquely elaborate plan or rationale appears in its label.
gate.stageAndCategory: Select the site-specific endovascular repair after definitive angiography.
reasoningSteps: Infer a direct-pressure modular graft failure from arterial-phase passage through the component gap.
Choose a covered bridge across that site rather than a branch or attachment procedure.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: prior branch attribution can persist, while a resident may identify a dangerous leak yet choose a proximal cuff for the wrong anatomic defect.
gate.decidingObservation: Flow traverses the main-body/limb gap, with intact seals and a feasible bridging overlap.
gate.closestError: Proximal cuff extension after correctly recognizing a high-pressure leak.
gate.consequence: An unclosed sac-pressure source with continuing rupture risk.
gate.deletionTest: Remove the actual gap and there is no basis to select bridging over the two other repairs; intact seal observations distinguish the closest wrong repair.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the junction gap with direct inflow at the proximal attachment and an available healthy landing segment: proximal cuff extension becomes appropriate.
gate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback requires source confirmation but never gives this bridging answer. The new angiographic relationship, not a repeated type label, determines the repair.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Kept attachment and overlap facts because they establish one feasible repair. Did not use an unsafe default that every component defect can be managed with a generic new limb.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 74-year-old woman, attends clinic to review a later outside CTA after EVAR. The sac diameter is unchanged, but contrast passes directly between the proximal graft edge and native aortic wall during the arterial phase. Modular junctions remain continuous. A healthy neck segment remains between the graft edge and the renal arteries.

nodes.objective: Recognize a direct attachment leak and repair the seal despite stable current sac size.
nodes.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s proximal attachment finding?

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: Direct attachment inflow requires prompt seal correction; the remaining healthy segment supports a cuff.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes a sealing defect from a stable branch leak.
choices.counterfactual: Absent a usable neck, a more complex reconstruction would need consideration.

choices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
choices.rationale: Stable sac size does not justify observation of an established late direct attachment leak.
choices.temptation: Overgeneralizes conservative care for stable type-II flow.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed isolated branch leak with stable sac size supports surveillance.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: The demonstrated source is the proximal attachment, not a side branch.
choices.temptation: Treats contrast in the sac as a branch-leak problem regardless of its observed source.
choices.counterfactual: A growing isolated branch leak could support branch/sac embolization.

nodes.explanation: This arterial-phase attachment route represents a type I sealing failure. Prompt seal repair is appropriate even before the sac enlarges; the available healthy neck makes proximal extension a supported option.

gate.cueAttack: The unchanged diameter is a real competing datum, not reassurance supplied by the author. No type label or urgency phrase appears before answering. All choices are post-EVAR management plans with similar specificity.
gate.stageAndCategory: Treat or observe a documented late leak, using its anatomic source.
reasoningSteps: Infer a sealing failure from direct arterial-phase attachment flow.
Apply its pressure-risk significance rather than letting stable sac size determine observation.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: a resident may correctly remember stable-sac observation but apply it to the wrong leak origin.
gate.decidingObservation: Direct flow at the proximal attachment with an available healthy neck segment.
gate.closestError: Surveillance because the sac has not enlarged.
gate.consequence: Leaving a direct-pressure leak untreated.
gate.deletionTest: The source and healthy landing anatomy are necessary; removing them prevents selecting the cuff. Stable diameter earns its role as the competing misconception.
gate.counterfactual: If contrast arrived through lumbar branches on delayed images with intact seals and a stable sac, continued surveillance would become correct.
gate.sequenceReview: Standalone exact context; not dependent on the other endoleak case or its explanation. No cross-case exposure is assumed.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced 'repair immediately' with a concrete anatomically possible cuff plan. Restricted the case to an established late leak rather than a transient intraoperative blush.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 73-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for abrupt abdominal and back pain. At the recorded initial assessment, bedside ultrasound showed a 7-cm infrarenal AAA. He remained alert with systolic pressures between 108 and 116 mm Hg over repeated assessments. The hospital aortic team was preparing definitive treatment.

nodes.objective: Choose urgent cross-sectional planning in a stable suspected rupture without misusing a repeat size-only study.
nodes.stem: Which imaging study should have been selected at {patientName}'s recorded stable assessment?

choices.label: CT angiography of the aorta and iliac access vessels
choices.rationale: Urgent CT can identify contained rupture and the anatomy needed for the repair strategy while he remains stable.
choices.temptation: Uses current physiology and the information required for repair, rather than repeating aneurysm detection.
choices.counterfactual: A patient unable to sustain circulation for imaging would need immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.

choices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta and iliac vessels
choices.rationale: Another sonographic survey does not provide the same cross-sectional rupture and repair-planning information.
choices.temptation: Extends the correct screening modality to a suspected-rupture planning problem.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic small AAA being surveilled is appropriately assessed by ultrasound.

choices.label: Catheter aortography of the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels
choices.rationale: Initial catheter luminal imaging does not replace CT mapping of the sac, surrounding hemorrhage and access anatomy in this stable setting.
choices.temptation: Treats proximity to an endovascular procedure as a reason to skip cross-sectional planning.
choices.counterfactual: Catheter angiography is useful during an intervention or for an unresolved post-EVAR leak source.

nodes.explanation: At the recorded stable assessment, urgent CT supplies cross-sectional repair-planning anatomy in suspected rupture rather than repeating the already demonstrated aneurysm diameter.

gate.cueAttack: The care frame is a retrospective clinic review. Serial pressure and alertness are constructed physiologic observations, not an invented stability cutoff. No sentence promises that CT is available or will not delay care. Every option names a vascular imaging study and has a wait profile.
gate.stageAndCategory: Imaging to plan hospital repair after aneurysm detection, not initial screening or the final repair procedure.
reasoningSteps: Interpret preserved serial perfusion as allowing urgent planning despite a possible contained rupture.
Choose imaging that supplies surrounding hemorrhage, sealing and access anatomy.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: equating rupture with inevitable immediate collapse or reusing ultrasound after detection are credible errors.
gate.decidingObservation: Preserved serial circulation after a large aneurysm is demonstrated in a painful presentation.
gate.closestError: Repeat duplex because it already identified the AAA and avoids contrast.
gate.consequence: Failing to define the repair anatomy or contained hemorrhage needed for the definitive strategy.
gate.deletionTest: Removing physiologic trajectory makes a CT-planning decision unsafe; removing the completed ultrasound changes the stage from planning to initial evaluation.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the painful admission with an asymptomatic small-AAA surveillance visit: duplex becomes the best offered study. Refractory shock would invalidate the entire stable-imaging task and require immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.
gate.sequenceReview: The first explanation avoids the later EVAR-versus-open ranking. CTA findings appear only after answering, and no hospital service is executed by the clinic runtime.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a transfer-permission sentence with serial physiology and removed 'most informative' from the task. Timing estimates are placeholders, not authorization to delay real emergency care.

nodes.objective: Integrate contained rupture and documented device-compatible anatomy to select an emergency repair approach.
nodes.update: CTA shows retroperitoneal hematoma continuous with a posterior aortic-wall defect. The infrarenal neck is parallel-sided, the iliac access vessels are patent, and the vascular planning record confirms the selected graft's instructions-for-use requirements are satisfied. He remains alert with unchanged pressure. The treating hospital performs both open and endovascular aortic repair.
nodes.stem: Which definitive repair approach should have been selected for {patientName} at that point?

choices.label: Emergency endovascular aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The record demonstrates rupture and device-suitable anatomy; guideline recommendations favor EVAR in that setting.
choices.temptation: Recognizes containment as rupture rather than a reason to delay and uses the documented anatomic suitability.
choices.counterfactual: An unsuitable proximal seal or access anatomy could favor open repair instead.

choices.label: Emergency open aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: Open repair is a real alternative, but the guideline favors EVAR for the documented suitable anatomy.
choices.temptation: Treats rupture as an automatic indication for open exposure.
choices.counterfactual: Inability to achieve an endovascular seal or obtain access could make open repair the appropriate choice.

choices.label: Elective endovascular aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The wall defect and retroperitoneal hematoma establish rupture despite current preserved pressure.
choices.temptation: Misinterprets containment and stable circulation as an intact elective aneurysm.
choices.counterfactual: An intact asymptomatic qualifying aneurysm could undergo elective repair planning.

nodes.explanation: The wall defect and contiguous hematoma establish rupture. Preserved pressure does not make it elective. With documented suitable anatomy and treating-hospital expertise, the guideline favors emergency EVAR over open repair.

gate.cueAttack: All choices specify approach and urgency at the same definitive-treatment stage. Availability of both approaches is a necessary resource constraint that privileges neither. Device suitability is documented rather than fabricated from an invented neck cutoff; actual dimensions are not supplied as unsourced eligibility rules.
gate.stageAndCategory: Definitive repair approach and timing after completed hospital CTA.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the wall-defect/hematoma relationship as rupture despite maintained pressure.
Apply documented endovascular suitability to an emergency repair strategy.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: open-first reflex and treating a contained leak as elective are plausible but separable errors.
gate.decidingObservation: A wall defect with contiguous retroperitoneal blood plus verified graft suitability.
gate.closestError: Emergency open repair regardless of suitable endovascular anatomy.
gate.consequence: Choosing a less-favored approach for this supported anatomy, or dangerously delaying repair if containment is mistaken for an intact aneurysm.
gate.deletionTest: Rupture evidence determines urgency; suitability and hospital capabilities determine the comparison between the emergency approaches. Each changes the decision.
gate.counterfactual: Keep rupture but replace the planning record with no usable proximal seal or iliac access: the offered emergency open approach becomes appropriate. Remove the wall defect/hematoma and make the case asymptomatic: an elective pathway becomes reasonable.
gate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback teaches the role of CT, not the EVAR preference. The new scan changes both the diagnosis boundary and treatment selection.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed unsupported anatomy numbers and any claim that the game executes hospital repair. Retained an explicit limitation: the device suitability judgment is outside the scored objective and must be checked by clinical reviewers.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old woman, visits clinic after hospitalization for abrupt chest and back pain. The founder reviews her initial CTA: the entry tear lies distal to the left subclavian artery, but the flap extends backward through the arch into the ascending aorta. At that assessment she was alert and normotensive, without abdominal pain or limb deficits.

nodes.objective: Use total dissection extent rather than entry-tear location to identify the need for emergency ascending repair.
nodes.stem: Which definitive hospital plan should have been selected from {patientName}'s initial CTA?

choices.label: Emergency open ascending aortic repair
choices.rationale: Ascending involvement places this in the type-A pathway despite a descending entry tear.
choices.temptation: Classifies by the involved segment and applies its urgent surgical consequence.
choices.counterfactual: A flap confined distal to the left subclavian without complications would favor initial medical treatment.

choices.label: Urgent descending thoracic endovascular repair
choices.rationale: Treating the distal tear as a type-B problem does not address the acute ascending involvement.
choices.temptation: Classifies the dissection by the tear location alone.
choices.counterfactual: A complicated dissection confined to the descending aorta with suitable anatomy can favor TEVAR.

choices.label: Intravenous esmolol with CT angiographic follow-up
choices.rationale: Impulse control is background stabilization but not definitive treatment of acute ascending dissection.
choices.temptation: Uses normotension and absence of malperfusion to choose an uncomplicated type-B pathway.
choices.counterfactual: An uncomplicated dissection confined to the descending aorta initially receives medical therapy and monitoring.

nodes.explanation: Ascending involvement determines the type-A pathway even when the entry tear is distal. Stable current pressure does not remove the need for emergency surgical treatment of acute ascending dissection.

gate.cueAttack: The CTA relationship is described without naming type A or assigning an author interpretation. The tear and flap extent deliberately conflict. Every option is a definitive hospital treatment plan; the medical plan's imaging component has timing metadata.
gate.stageAndCategory: Definitive plan after a completed acute aortic CTA; impulse control remains background stabilization for surgical patients.
reasoningSteps: Separate entry-tear location from ascending involvement in classification.
Apply the ascending extent to immediate operative management despite stable physiology.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: both the distal tear and normal pressure can wrongly steer an otherwise knowledgeable resident toward a type-B strategy.
gate.decidingObservation: The flap extends into the ascending aorta, not merely through the descending segment.
gate.closestError: Descending TEVAR directed at the entry tear as the complete treatment.
gate.consequence: Failure to treat the dangerous acute ascending segment.
gate.deletionTest: The distal tear creates the meaningful competing error; ascending extent changes the answer. Preserved perfusion keeps a separate contested malperfusion-first question out of this item.
gate.counterfactual: Confine the flap to the descending aorta and preserve the uncomplicated physiology: the offered medical plan becomes correct.
gate.sequenceReview: Standalone; no other dissection case's feedback is assumed visible. No new ICU setting, bedside treatment execution or live consultation is required.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed an initial pure Stanford-label task and made classification consequential to treatment. The explanation does not claim every distal tear with retrograde extension can be managed with one generic operation.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.

nodes.objective: Interpret descending extent and preserved organ perfusion to choose initial impulse control instead of immediate repair.
nodes.stem: Which initial hospital treatment plan should have been selected for {patientName} at that assessment?

choices.label: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
choices.rationale: The observed extent and perfusion support initial medical treatment; rate/impulse control precedes added vasodilation.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes initial hypertension from persistent complications despite adequate treatment.
choices.counterfactual: New organ malperfusion despite treatment would change the need for intervention.

choices.label: Urgent thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
choices.rationale: The admission record has not demonstrated rupture, malperfusion or failure of medical treatment that would establish an immediate repair indication.
choices.temptation: Treats every acute dissection or first elevated pressure as complicated disease.
choices.counterfactual: A suitable type-B dissection with new organ malperfusion generally warrants intervention.

choices.label: Urgent open descending aortic graft replacement
choices.rationale: An open replacement is not the initial treatment for this uncomplicated descending presentation.
choices.temptation: Overextends the acute ascending-dissection operation rule to a different extent and physiology.
choices.counterfactual: Complicated disease unsuitable for endovascular treatment can require open reconstruction.

nodes.explanation: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated.

gate.cueAttack: No type-B or 'uncomplicated' label is visible. The key is not the only specific plan: all labels identify actual hospital treatments. Organ findings and beta-blocker safety checks are retained because they determine management and the named regimen, rather than merely decorating a high blood pressure.
gate.stageAndCategory: Initial hospital treatment strategy for newly evaluated acute dissection.
reasoningSteps: Infer descending-only dissection without demonstrated organ compromise or rupture.
Choose monitored impulse therapy and appropriate infusion sequence rather than immediate repair.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: applying an all-dissection surgical reflex or calling an untreated first high pressure 'refractory' are credible errors. The named drug sequence is an additional treatment detail, not a separate scored question.
gate.decidingObservation: Descending confinement with preserved kidney enhancement, urine output and limb/abdominal examination before treatment.
gate.closestError: Urgent TEVAR for the first high-pressure reading.
gate.consequence: Premature invasive treatment or failure to institute appropriate impulse control.
gate.deletionTest: Extent and organ-perfusion observations determine the strategy. Conduction, bronchospasm and heart-failure checks earn their place because the key names a beta blocker. Numeric vitals are fictional observations, not new cutoffs.
gate.counterfactual: Replace preserved renal perfusion with new oliguria, falling renal enhancement and true-lumen collapse despite treatment: urgent endovascular repair becomes the preferred offered strategy.
gate.sequenceReview: The explanation does not name the later kidney complication or its intervention. Later anatomy and response are not visible at admission.
gate.repairAndRecheck: An initial pure infusion-order question was rejected as too narrow. The revised neutral treatment-plan task requires extent/perfusion interpretation before drug selection. No dose or numeric treatment target is added.

nodes.objective: Recognize new dissection-related renal malperfusion despite achieved impulse control and escalate to repair.
nodes.update: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.
nodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?

choices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
choices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.
choices.temptation: Uses organ trajectory rather than the improved pain or blood pressure as the endpoint.
choices.counterfactual: Preserved renal perfusion and function would support continued medical monitoring.

choices.label: Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
choices.rationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.
choices.temptation: Attributes the creatinine change to treatment or contrast and remains anchored on an initially uncomplicated course.
choices.counterfactual: An uncomplicated course without malperfusion can continue monitored medical therapy.

choices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
choices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.
choices.temptation: Correctly escalates care but treats all organ malperfusion as requiring open aortic exposure.
choices.counterfactual: Unsuitable sealing/access anatomy or relevant heritable disease could shift toward open repair.

nodes.explanation: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.

gate.cueAttack: The update supplies renal function, enhancement and true-lumen geometry without using 'complicated' or 'malperfusion.' All plans include their relevant reassessment scope; the key is not a uniquely complete combined plan.
gate.stageAndCategory: Aortic treatment strategy after a documented new complication during medical therapy.
reasoningSteps: Integrate oliguria/creatinine change with new regional inflow and enhancement changes rather than assuming nonspecific renal injury.
Escalate from medical therapy to a suitable endovascular central repair.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: symptom and pressure improvement can falsely reassure, while contrast exposure can divert interpretation of the renal trajectory.
gate.decidingObservation: New renal dysfunction co-localized with true-lumen compression and weaker kidney enhancement despite achieved impulse control.
gate.closestError: Continue the prior infusions and observe renal function because pain and pressure improved.
gate.consequence: Prolonged renal ischemia despite a treatable inflow obstruction.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the regional CTA relationship makes nonspecific renal injury more credible; deleting the functional trajectory leaves an image without demonstrated organ consequence. Both are needed.
gate.counterfactual: If renal function, output and enhancement stayed preserved after treatment, continued monitored medical management would remain appropriate.
gate.sequenceReview: The admission explanation does not identify this organ complication or promise that TEVAR will solve all branch disease. This node's feedback states reassessment but not the next fixed branch intervention.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a bowel operation outside this scored lane and balanced reassessment across the operative options. TEVAR suitability is documented by the outside team; no exact device thresholds are fabricated.

nodes.objective: Distinguish persistent static branch obstruction from resolved central dynamic compression to choose the next endovascular target.
nodes.update: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.
nodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

choices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
choices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.
choices.temptation: Localizes the residual obstruction after observing the central repair response.
choices.counterfactual: If branch flow recovered after central true-lumen expansion, an additional renal stent would not follow from these findings.

choices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
choices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.
choices.temptation: Carries forward the original dynamic-compression mechanism despite the documented response.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent dynamic aortic flap-related obstruction after entry treatment can merit fenestration.

choices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
choices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.
choices.temptation: Assumes every perfusion failure after TEVAR reflects inadequate central sealing.
choices.counterfactual: An incompletely sealed entry with persistent central compression could require graft revision.

nodes.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

gate.cueAttack: No static/dynamic diagnosis is supplied. The current response, branch anatomy and persistent gradient must be read together. All three choices are specific endovascular actions and have comparable length; none adds explanatory warnings.
gate.stageAndCategory: Adjunctive endovascular treatment after a completed central repair, with ongoing documented organ inflow compromise.
reasoningSteps: Use central lumen expansion plus unchanged intrabranch narrowing to distinguish a residual fixed lesion from the earlier central mechanism.
Select the branch target rather than repeat central sealing or pressure equalization.
gate.difficulty: Hard: recognizing the initial mechanism does not establish the cause of the residual deficit; the current response must revise the anatomic target.
gate.decidingObservation: Central expansion and entry sealing coexist with fixed renal flap narrowing and persistent gradient.
gate.closestError: Distal septal fenestration for presumed continued dynamic obstruction.
gate.consequence: Additional intervention at the wrong target while renal ischemia persists.
gate.deletionTest: Delete the post-TEVAR response and the initial central strategy may still be appropriate. Delete the persistent functional/pressure defect and an incidental branch flap would not establish a need for treatment.
gate.counterfactual: If the branch were patent but central true-lumen collapse and cycling flap prolapse persisted, a pressure-equalizing fenestration could become reasonable.
gate.sequenceReview: The previous explanation warns to reassess without teaching that this specific branch is fixed or naming renal stenting. This node requires new response interpretation.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced an implausible dialysis-as-repair foil with a credible dynamic-obstruction procedure. Kept renal anatomy in the aortic-complication lane and left non-aortic AKI management unscored.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, visits clinic to review an outside elective descending thoracic aneurysm repair. The planned proximal sealing segment spans the left subclavian origin. His CABG record shows a patent pedicled left internal mammary graft arising from the left subclavian artery to the LAD; the native LAD is chronically occluded. Both carotid arteries are patent.

nodes.objective: Trace LSA-dependent coronary inflow and preserve it before an elective covering graft.
nodes.stem: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.
choices.temptation: Follows the coronary conduit back to its inflow origin.
choices.counterfactual: If no LSA-dependent coronary or other critical inflow existed, timing and need could differ, particularly in an emergency.

choices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
choices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.
choices.temptation: Treats upper-extremity symptoms as the only meaningful consequence of LSA interruption.
choices.counterfactual: Selective delayed revascularization may fit some emergency coverings without critical LSA-dependent inflow.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.
choices.temptation: Chooses a durable LSA revascularization while overlooking its proximal clamp sequence.
choices.counterfactual: Without a patent pedicled LIMA or another clamp-dependent inflow, transposition can be a reasonable LSA revascularization technique.

nodes.explanation: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

gate.cueAttack: The CABG anatomy is necessary raw conduit information; the presentation does not state that bypass is required. The transposition foil is a real durable revascularization, while deferred rescue is a separate timing policy. The first label is not uniquely cautious or longer than the alternatives.
gate.stageAndCategory: LSA management strategy around an elective covering repair.
reasoningSteps: Trace the patent LIMA-to-LAD graft's dependence on the LSA with an occluded native LAD.
Choose pre-coverage inflow preservation that avoids the proximal clamp required for transposition, rather than waiting for arm symptoms.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a durable transposition is tempting until its clamp sequence is considered alongside the pedicled coronary conduit.
gate.decidingObservation: Patent LIMA-to-LAD graft with native LAD occlusion and planned LSA-origin coverage.
gate.closestError: Choose transposition without accounting for interruption of the pedicled LIMA during proximal clamping.
gate.consequence: Loss of coronary graft inflow during an otherwise elective procedure.
gate.deletionTest: Delete the CABG conduit or native LAD finding and the key's patient-specific urgency weakens. Elective timing distinguishes this from unavoidable emergency coverage.
gate.counterfactual: If the LIMA were a free graft arising from the aorta rather than a patent pedicled subclavian conduit, transposition could become a reasonable pre-coverage technique; the specific bypass-over-transposition constraint would be removed.
gate.sequenceReview: This explanation focuses on coronary supply and does not teach spinal-cord rescue. A later postoperative neurologic event is revealed only in the next record.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Rejected the initial low-value post-coverage assessment foil. Targeted STS guideline verification established the transposition-clamp issue; replaced the foil with pre-coverage transposition and re-solved the exact three strategies.

nodes.objective: Localize a new post-TEVAR neurologic deficit and reverse impaired spinal perfusion rather than extending pressure reduction.
nodes.update: The later outside ICU record describes new bilateral leg weakness after a hypotensive episode following long-segment TEVAR. Both feet remain warm with palpable pulses. Speech, face and arm movement are unchanged. Platelet count and coagulation studies are normal, and no neuraxial drain is present.
nodes.stem: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?

choices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
choices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.
choices.temptation: Links bilateral motor findings with the hypotensive trigger and preserved limb inflow.
choices.counterfactual: A focal cerebral syndrome or arterial inflow loss would require a different rescue target.

choices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
choices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.
choices.temptation: Carries an acute aortic impulse-reduction plan into a phase where low pressure is the precipitating problem.
choices.counterfactual: An unrepaired hypertensive acute aortic syndrome without cord hypoperfusion supports impulse control.

choices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
choices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.
choices.temptation: Interprets leg weakness after endovascular repair as an access or limb-occlusion complication.
choices.counterfactual: Sudden cold pulseless legs with demonstrated aortoiliac occlusion could require this pathway.

nodes.explanation: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.

gate.cueAttack: The update contains no spinal diagnosis or target pressure. Warm pulses and preserved upper-body examination are necessary localization data, not blanket exclusions. All labels name an immediate medication/procedure pathway; no option says 'alone' or labels its own error.
gate.stageAndCategory: Immediate postoperative rescue strategies after a new neurologic deficit.
reasoningSteps: Localize the deficit to spinal perfusion rather than limb inflow or a focal cerebral syndrome.
Reverse the low-perfusion state and consider intrathecal-pressure reduction rather than continuing the earlier impulse goal.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: the conflict between protecting an aortic repair from pressure and maintaining cord perfusion creates a consequential treatment-direction error.
gate.decidingObservation: Bilateral leg deficit after hypotension with warm pulsed feet and preserved face/arm function.
gate.closestError: Continue esmolol pressure reduction because the patient has an aortic repair.
gate.consequence: Worsening potentially reversible cord hypoperfusion.
gate.deletionTest: Remove the hypotensive trigger or localization findings and the rescue target is less defensible. Coagulation data inform drain safety; they do not guarantee that placement has no risk.
gate.counterfactual: Change the record to cold pulseless legs with confirmed aortoiliac occlusion: the offered limb-ischemia pathway becomes appropriate.
gate.sequenceReview: The prior LSA explanation concerns LIMA coronary supply and does not give this neurologic rescue plan. The actual postoperative trigger changes the decision.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a numeric MAP/CSF target because source protocols differ. The label activates a rescue pathway, with specialist drain safety assessment in feedback; this is not automatic drain placement or routine prophylactic drainage.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.

nodes.objective: Use embolic complications rather than diameter alone to choose repair evaluation for a small PAA.
nodes.stem: Which aneurysm plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s right popliteal lesion?

choices.label: Plan popliteal aneurysm exclusion and bypass
choices.rationale: The thrombus and distal embolic findings make size-only observation inadequate despite a diameter below 20 mm.
choices.temptation: Recognizes the symptomatic source while preserving the distinction from a threatened limb emergency.
choices.counterfactual: A small asymptomatic lesion without thrombus or poor runoff could remain under surveillance.

choices.label: Arrange annual popliteal duplex surveillance
choices.rationale: A diameter-only policy overlooks the repeated embolic complications documented here.
choices.temptation: Applies the usual asymptomatic small-PAA pathway to a symptomatic source.
choices.counterfactual: A small asymptomatic PAA without thrombus or embolic findings can be monitored.

choices.label: Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up
choices.rationale: Medical suppression does not remove the aneurysmal thrombus source; the supported next strategy includes repair consideration.
choices.temptation: Treats the embolic event without addressing its persistent source.
choices.counterfactual: A patient in whom repair must be deferred for prohibitive risk may require an interim specialist-directed medical plan.

nodes.explanation: The relevant problem is distal embolization from a thrombus-containing PAA, not diameter alone. Repair is considered even below 20 mm when embolic complications are present; the exact operation still depends on operative assessment and conduit anatomy.

gate.cueAttack: The presentation gives symptoms, distal occlusions and aneurysmal thrombus rather than calling the lesion symptomatic or high-risk. All options are vascular management plans. The key is shorter than the two surveillance labels; every testing plan has duplex metadata.
gate.stageAndCategory: Nonemergent source management of a PAA with embolic findings, not acute threatened-limb salvage.
reasoningSteps: Connect digital occlusions and episodic blue toes with the mural-thrombus source despite palpable foot pulses.
Override an asymptomatic diameter-only surveillance rule and plan source repair.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a remembered 20-mm threshold and normal pedal pulses both invite reassurance despite distal embolization.
gate.decidingObservation: Repeated distal embolic findings linked to thrombus in the 18-mm popliteal lesion.
gate.closestError: Annual surveillance because the diameter is below the usual asymptomatic repair threshold.
gate.consequence: Continued distal embolization and possible limb injury.
gate.deletionTest: Without digital findings the small lesion could be observed; without the mural-thrombus source an alternative embolic workup would be needed. Normal strength/sensation keeps acute limb-threat treatment out of scope.
gate.counterfactual: Remove thrombus and embolic symptoms while keeping a small stable PAA: annual surveillance becomes reasonable.
gate.sequenceReview: The next node concerns a new record's survey coverage, not another repair threshold. No contralateral screening answer appears in this feedback.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Changed a simple size-threshold recall draft into an embolic-complication decision. The key states a repair plan, not a claim that open bypass is invariably superior; the exact conduit/procedure is a clinical-review boundary.

nodes.objective: Use the associated aneurysm pattern and actual prior imaging coverage to complete an aneurysm survey without repeating an adequate examination.
nodes.update: The same outside workup includes a complete abdominal-aortic CTA with outer diameters under 3 cm throughout the abdominal aorta. The arterial duplex acquisition is labeled right lower extremity from common femoral to pedal vessels. The clinic receives the original images and acquisition records.
nodes.stem: Which additional aneurysm study should have completed {patientName}'s survey after review of these records?

choices.label: Left popliteal arterial duplex ultrasound
