choices.rationale: The abdominal aorta has been assessed, while the associated contralateral popliteal site is outside the documented unilateral acquisition.
choices.temptation: Combines the PAA association with the actual tested territory.
choices.counterfactual: If the left popliteal artery were already imaged adequately and the aorta were not, an abdominal aortic study would be appropriate.

choices.label: Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: The complete adequate abdominal CTA already addresses the aortic component of the associated-aneurysm survey.
choices.temptation: Recalls the AAA association but ignores the existing acquisition's scope.
choices.counterfactual: An incomplete abdominal assessment would support a dedicated aortic study.

choices.label: Thoracic aortic CT angiography
choices.rationale: The specific routinely recommended associated sites are the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta, not a substitute thoracic survey.
choices.temptation: Generalizes aneurysm association into an unrestricted whole-arterial imaging search.
choices.counterfactual: An independent thoracic aneurysm or heritable-aortopathy indication could justify thoracic imaging.

nodes.explanation: PAA prompts an opposite-leg and abdominal-aortic aneurysm survey. Review what was actually acquired: a complete abdominal CTA already evaluates the aorta, but a right-leg-only duplex does not evaluate the left popliteal artery.

gate.cueAttack: No sentence says 'the left side was not done.' Acquisition labels and the available original studies establish coverage. Each choice is a named arterial imaging study with a wait profile, and the key has no uniquely comprehensive bundle.
gate.stageAndCategory: Complete associated-aneurysm imaging after reviewing existing acquisitions.
reasoningSteps: Identify the relevant associated aneurysm territories for a PAA.
Subtract the adequately imaged territory and choose the remaining targeted study.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: rote recall of an AAA association can lead to duplicate abdominal imaging rather than actual survey completion.
gate.decidingObservation: A complete abdominal CTA paired with a unilateral right-leg arterial acquisition.
gate.closestError: Repeat abdominal ultrasound after recalling the AAA association.
gate.consequence: Duplicate testing while leaving the contralateral aneurysm site unassessed.
gate.deletionTest: Delete the acquisition record and both aortic and opposite-leg screening could be needed; the update determines which single study completes the current workup.
gate.counterfactual: Provide adequate bilateral popliteal imaging but only a pelvis-only CT: abdominal aortic ultrasound becomes the appropriate additional survey study.
gate.sequenceReview: The first feedback concerns embolic repair below a diameter boundary; it does not teach associated-site screening. The new acquisition record is necessary to select one study.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a one-step 'what is associated with PAA' question with survey-completeness reasoning. A missing exported image is not equated with an unperformed acquisition; original acquisition records are explicitly available.

nodes.objective: Identify symptomatic sac compression after successful exclusion/bypass rather than treating graft patency as resolution of the entire lesion.
nodes.update: After outside popliteal exclusion and vein bypass, he develops progressive calf swelling and plantar numbness. Duplex shows a widely patent bypass and persistent flow within an enlarging excluded sac. The sac displaces the popliteal vein and tibial nerve. Venous duplex shows compression without thrombus.
nodes.stem: Which procedure should have addressed {patientName}'s new postoperative problem?

choices.label: Surgical decompression of the excluded aneurysm sac
choices.rationale: The symptomatic enlarging sac is the compressive target even though bypass inflow and outflow remain patent.
choices.temptation: Separates revascularization success from continued local aneurysm effects.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic stable excluded sac would not establish a decompression indication.

choices.label: Revision of the popliteal bypass graft
choices.rationale: The bypass is patent; revising it does not remove the compressive sac.
choices.temptation: Treats new postoperative limb symptoms as graft failure.
choices.counterfactual: A demonstrated flow-limiting graft stenosis or occlusion could require revision.

choices.label: Embolization of residual genicular branch inflow
choices.rationale: Inflows can contribute to sac persistence, but the demonstrated symptomatic compression calls for decompression of the enlarged sac.
choices.temptation: Focuses on recurrent sac flow while overlooking the current compressive effect.
choices.counterfactual: Residual flow without symptomatic mass effect can prompt assessment of an inflow-directed strategy.

nodes.explanation: A patent bypass does not remove an enlarging excluded sac. When that sac causes neural or venous compression, surgical decompression addresses the current problem rather than revising a patent conduit.

gate.cueAttack: Raw duplex geometry links sac, vein and nerve without labeling a compression syndrome. The options are three actual procedures of comparable scope; the key is not a combined diagnosis-plus-treatment label.
gate.stageAndCategory: Procedure for a new post-exclusion sac complication with known graft patency.
reasoningSteps: Localize the new swelling/numbness to the expanding sac rather than venous thrombus or bypass occlusion.
Select decompression for symptomatic mass effect instead of treating patency or inflow alone.
gate.difficulty: Hard prediction: a resident may stop at the successful bypass result or regard residual flow as a purely embolization problem.
gate.decidingObservation: An enlarging sac visibly displaces vein and nerve while the bypass is patent and the vein has no thrombus.
gate.closestError: Genicular inflow embolization as the entire treatment for the current compressive symptoms.
gate.consequence: Persisting venous/neurologic compression despite attention to blood flow.
gate.deletionTest: Without symptomatic displacement, sac-flow management could differ. Without demonstrated bypass patency, graft revision would remain a genuine contender.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the patent bypass with a flow-limiting graft lesion and remove mass effect: bypass revision becomes the appropriate offered procedure.
gate.sequenceReview: Earlier PAA feedback does not teach that exclusion may leave a symptomatic mass. This new postoperative anatomy creates a distinct decision.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a venous thrombolysis foil that was already ruled out by the duplex. The remaining embolization comparator is clinically plausible; the exact preference for decompression is supported by SVS recommendation 6 and needs clinician confirmation for this version.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 75-year-old man, comes to clinic after hospitalization several months after open infrarenal AAA grafting. His outside record describes fever, recurrent positive blood cultures and intermittent melena. Upper endoscopy examined the esophagus, stomach and first two duodenal portions without finding a bleeding source. He was alert with preserved pressure between bleeding episodes.

nodes.objective: Recognize an unaddressed graft-related source when bleeding and infection coexist after aortic reconstruction.
nodes.stem: Which investigation should have followed {patientName}'s unrevealing upper endoscopy during that admission?

choices.label: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
choices.rationale: The graft history plus infection and bleeding warrants cross-sectional assessment of the reconstructed aorta and its bowel interface.
choices.temptation: Does not treat a negative proximal endoscopy as exclusion of a graft complication.
choices.counterfactual: A directly demonstrated ordinary mucosal bleeding lesion without graft-related findings could redirect the workup.

choices.label: Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
choices.rationale: Repeating the same examined mucosal territory does not evaluate the prosthetic graft or its extraluminal interface.
choices.temptation: Anchors on melena as necessarily a lesion within the already examined lumen.
choices.counterfactual: Recurrent bleeding from a known treatable proximal mucosal lesion could warrant repeat endoscopy.

choices.label: Tagged-red-cell scintigraphy for gastrointestinal bleeding
choices.rationale: Bleed localization does not assess the graft infection concern raised by the combined history and cultures.
choices.temptation: Seeks the intermittent bleeding site while treating bacteremia as an unrelated problem.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent intermittent bleeding after graft pathology has been excluded may need a separate bleeding-localization strategy.

nodes.explanation: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal.

gate.cueAttack: The context never labels graft infection or fistula. The endoscopy's actual examined territory is specified rather than saying 'all tests negative.' Every option is a named bleeding/graft investigation with complete wait metadata.
gate.stageAndCategory: Next diagnostic investigation after a completed unrevealing proximal endoscopy in a stable hospital assessment.
reasoningSteps: Integrate graft history, infection and bleeding as a possible linked vascular complication.
Choose cross-sectional graft-interface evaluation rather than re-examining the same mucosal territory or only localizing bleeding.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: melena invites a standard luminal workup, while intermittent stability and an unrevealing endoscopy can falsely reassure.
gate.decidingObservation: Unexplained infection and bleeding months after aortic grafting, with only proximal mucosa examined.
gate.closestError: Repeat the same upper-endoscopic territory to explain the melena.
gate.consequence: Delayed recognition of a dangerous graft-related infection or bowel communication.
gate.deletionTest: Without the graft/culture history this could be an ordinary obscure-bleeding workup. Precise endoscopic scope preserves provenance; no hidden fourth-duodenal examination is assumed.
gate.counterfactual: If the prior endoscopy instead showed a recurrent treatable proximal ulcer with no graft-related infection concern, repeat endoscopy would become reasonable.
gate.sequenceReview: The first explanation indicates the diagnostic target but does not choose a source-control operation. Definitive graft findings appear only next.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a generic 'urgent review' key and used actual investigations. The CTA preference is a targeted application of a single checked guideline; it is flagged for exact clinical review rather than claiming that every intermittent GI bleed must have this scan.

nodes.objective: Choose definitive source control for an infected aortic prosthesis in a patient who can undergo reconstruction.
nodes.update: CTA demonstrates a perigraft fluid-and-gas collection with a channel to adjacent duodenum. The same organism persists in repeated blood cultures despite directed intravenous antibiotics. He has preserved pressure and organ function, remains functionally independent, and the multidisciplinary hospital assessment finds no prohibitive operative condition.
nodes.stem: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?

choices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
choices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes definitive source control from bridging or suppression.
choices.counterfactual: Prohibitive operative risk could change the balance toward nonoperative suppression or a limited strategy.

choices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
choices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.
choices.temptation: Uses rapid bleeding control as though it establishes durable infection source control.
choices.counterfactual: Uncontrolled hemorrhage in an unstable patient can make an endovascular bridge reasonable.

choices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
choices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Equates a temporary physiologic response to antibiotics with eradication of an infected prosthesis.
choices.counterfactual: A patient who cannot tolerate reconstruction may need a suppression-based strategy after specialist review.

nodes.explanation: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

gate.cueAttack: All options are concrete source-control strategies and have comparable scope. Operative physiology and functional context are necessary ranking information; no vague individualized-care option carries the key.
gate.stageAndCategory: Definitive source-control strategy after diagnostic confirmation, with antimicrobials common background care.
reasoningSteps: Recognize persistent prosthesis/bowel infection despite directed treatment rather than an isolated bloodstream episode.
Use current operative suitability to choose removal/reconstruction over bridging or suppression.
gate.difficulty: Hard: rapid endovascular control and antibiotic response can be mistaken for definitive treatment of an infected prosthesis.
gate.decidingObservation: A communicating perigraft collection, persistent same-organism cultures and no prohibitive operative condition.
gate.closestError: Covered relining as definitive treatment because it may arrest bleeding.
gate.consequence: Persistent infected material and bowel contamination.
gate.deletionTest: Without operative suitability, suppression or endovascular treatment may become defensible; without the persistent source, an immediate major reconstruction would not be established.
gate.counterfactual: Replace stable operability with uncontrolled hemorrhage and shock: covered relining as a bridge may become appropriate. Replace it with prohibitive permanent operative risk: suppression may be considered.
gate.sequenceReview: The preceding answer does not supply the operation, and new anatomy/culture response determines this stage. The clinic reviews a hospital operation plan rather than performing it.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Did not rank in-situ against extra-anatomic reconstruction or invent an antibiotic duration. Both belong to specialist/clinician decisions beyond the scored source-control objective.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 43-year-old man with genetically confirmed Marfan syndrome, attends clinic to review an outside aortic-team plan. An enlarging intact thoracoabdominal aneurysm includes the visceral origins; both potential endograft sealing regions are native aorta. He is active without major cardiac, pulmonary or renal dysfunction. Repair has been recommended, and both open and branched endovascular reconstruction are technically possible.

nodes.objective: Choose a durable repair approach for an operable heritable native-aorta TAAA rather than extending routine degenerative-aneurysm EVAR preferences.
nodes.stem: Which repair approach should have been preferred for {patientName}'s intact thoracoabdominal aneurysm?

choices.label: Open thoracoabdominal graft replacement
choices.rationale: Heritable native-aorta disease in an operable patient favors open reconstruction when repair is required.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes the tissue disease from an ordinary degenerative aneurysm.
choices.counterfactual: Severe operative prohibitions or emergency bridging needs can change the balance.

choices.label: Branched endovascular thoracoabdominal repair
choices.rationale: Technical feasibility does not erase the guideline preference for open repair in this heritable native-aorta setting.
choices.temptation: Generalizes the lower initial invasiveness of endovascular repair to all aneurysm substrates.
choices.counterfactual: An appropriate degenerative TAAA patient with higher open risk may be considered for branched repair.

choices.label: Visceral debranching with thoracic endografting
choices.rationale: A hybrid operation still relies on endograft sealing in the diseased native aorta rather than providing the preferred open reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Assumes adding open visceral bypasses resolves the native-seal concern.
choices.counterfactual: Selected patients unsuitable for conventional open repair can require alternative hybrid strategies.

nodes.explanation: For an intact TAAA requiring repair in Marfan syndrome, the checked multisociety guideline favors open repair. Native-aortic tissue disease and long-term durability matter even when branched or hybrid reconstruction is technically possible.

gate.cueAttack: The known genetic diagnosis is a legitimate prerequisite for this management objective; no approach is named as preferred in the presentation. All options are specific thoracoabdominal reconstructions of comparable scope, not an operation versus an obviously premature scan.
gate.stageAndCategory: Definitive repair approach after the need for repair is established.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that native aortic sealing regions in heritable tissue disease differ from the degenerative anatomy commonly used for endovascular repair.
Apply that durability boundary and current operability to the approach preference.
gate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: technical feasibility and lower initial invasiveness make branched repair credible, and hybrid debranching may appear to remove the endograft durability issue.
gate.decidingObservation: Confirmed Marfan syndrome with native sealing regions and no prohibitive open risk.
gate.closestError: Branched endovascular repair because both procedures are technically feasible.
gate.consequence: Extending a degenerative-aneurysm procedural preference without accounting for the heritable substrate.
gate.deletionTest: Without the genetic/native-aorta findings, the preference is not established. Fitness and an already accepted repair indication prevent this becoming an unsupported size-threshold or surveillance question.
gate.counterfactual: Replace Marfan with a degenerative aneurysm and substantially elevated open operative risk: branched endovascular repair becomes a reasonable preferred alternative after aortic-team assessment.
gate.sequenceReview: Standalone exact context. No root/ascending threshold, prophylactic family surgery or traumatic injury objective is imported.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Removed an unverified exact diameter and a surveillance foil. Kept three actual reconstructions. The newer ESVS 2026 PDF was inaccessible; this single-guideline preference requires exact clinician review rather than claiming exhaustive current agreement.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside pancreatitis admission. Follow-up CTA shows a new 12-mm contrast-filled cavity outside the pancreas, continuous with the splenic artery through a focal wall defect beside an inflammatory collection. Earlier imaging showed that arterial segment without a cavity. He is stable and has no active bleeding.

nodes.objective: Distinguish inflammatory wall disruption from a small true aneurysm when choosing whether to treat a visceral arterial lesion.
nodes.stem: Which vascular plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s new splenic-artery lesion?

choices.label: Prompt splenic-artery embolization assessment
choices.rationale: A new extra-organ contained leak through a wall defect is not governed by small true-aneurysm surveillance thresholds.
choices.temptation: Integrates the acquired wall defect and inflammatory setting with the rupture-risk management boundary.
choices.counterfactual: A small stable true aneurysm without symptoms can require a different surveillance decision.

choices.label: CT angiographic surveillance after inflammation resolves
choices.rationale: Waiting for inflammatory resolution leaves the demonstrated arterial wall defect unaddressed.
choices.temptation: Treats the cavity as a transient inflammatory change that can be reassessed with the collection.
choices.counterfactual: Selected small intraparenchymal pseudoaneurysms may be observed only under strict specialist follow-up; this is not that anatomy.

choices.label: Annual CT angiographic surveillance of lesion size
choices.rationale: A diameter-only true-aneurysm policy does not apply to an acquired extra-organ wall disruption.
choices.temptation: Lets the small 12-mm diameter override the lesion's mechanism.
choices.counterfactual: A stable small true visceral aneurysm in an appropriate patient may be surveilled after specialist assessment.

nodes.explanation: A newly acquired cavity communicating through an arterial wall defect after pancreatitis supports a pseudoaneurysm mechanism. Its extra-organ location and wall disruption favor prompt vascular treatment assessment, despite small diameter and current stability.

gate.cueAttack: The context does not use pseudoaneurysm or announce a rupture risk. All options are specific lesion-management plans. The correct label specifies assessment because exact embolization technique depends on vascular anatomy; both imaging alternatives receive equal CT wait metadata.
gate.stageAndCategory: Whether to proceed toward treatment or imaging surveillance after a defined new visceral arterial lesion.
reasoningSteps: Infer an acquired contained wall disruption rather than a chronic small true aneurysm from serial anatomy and the inflammatory setting.
Apply the pseudoaneurysm treatment boundary rather than a true-aneurysm diameter rule.
gate.difficulty: Moderate: the small size and lack of active bleeding are credible reasons to delay if the lesion mechanism is misclassified. The two imaging plans represent different delay rationales; independent review must confirm their discriminating value.
gate.decidingObservation: A new extra-organ cavity connected through a focal arterial wall defect after pancreatitis.
gate.closestError: Annual size surveillance after applying a small true-aneurysm rule.
gate.consequence: Leaving an acquired wall defect at risk while waiting for size growth.
gate.deletionTest: Without the wall/serial findings, the mechanism and prompt-treatment boundary are not established. Extra-organ location excludes the cited narrow intraparenchymal observation exception; small size and stability deliberately test the competing rule.
gate.counterfactual: Replace the lesion with a small contained intraparenchymal defect selected by specialists for strict observation: interval imaging can become appropriate. A stable small true aneurysm would require a separate policy decision, not this pseudoaneurysm rule.
gate.sequenceReview: Standalone; pancreatitis treatment is background. No drain, pancreatic operation or new acute-care runtime setting is proposed.
gate.repairAndRecheck: Kept the specific embolization assessment rather than claiming a universal embolization technique. True splenic/renal aneurysm size thresholds are withheld because CIRSE and SVS differ. This item does not choose between those thresholds.

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic CT angiography
answerChoices.rationale: CTA can define repair anatomy but is not the routine first screen for this asymptomatic eligible man.

answerChoices.label: No additional aortic imaging
answerChoices.rationale: The previous study ended before the abdominal aorta, and remote smoking still counts as ever smoking.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The next outside record contains an ultrasound with an outer-wall infrarenal aortic diameter of 6.0 cm and a flowing lumen of 3.1 cm surrounded by mural thrombus. He had no pain, remained independent, and had no life-limiting illness or major cardiopulmonary impairment.
decisionNodes.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s ultrasound result at that asymptomatic visit?

answerChoices.label: Refer for elective vascular repair evaluation
answerChoices.rationale: Repair assessment uses the outer aneurysm diameter; the patent channel understates sac size.

answerChoices.label: Arrange annual aortic ultrasound surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A 3.1-cm patent lumen is not the relevant aneurysm diameter; the full sac is 6.0 cm.

answerChoices.label: Arrange three-year aortic ultrasound surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A surveillance schedule for a much smaller AAA is inappropriate for this full sac size.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use the full outer-wall aneurysm diameter. A stable acceptable-risk man with a 6-cm fusiform AAA needs elective vascular repair evaluation; mural thrombus does not reduce that diameter to the flowing channel.

answerChoices.label: Re-measure both CT datasets perpendicular to the centerline
answerChoices.rationale: Different measurement planes can create an apparent increase; the acquired data permit a comparable assessment.

answerChoices.label: Acquire another contrast CT using the new axial protocol
answerChoices.rationale: Another noncomparable acquisition does not resolve the existing plane mismatch.

answerChoices.label: Replace the CT comparison with a new ultrasound diameter
answerChoices.rationale: A new modality does not establish how the two existing CT measurements relate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Compare the same anatomic site with reproducible orthogonal measurements. Reformat the available acquisitions before labeling the difference as growth; repeating the scan is not necessary just to correct a measurement plane.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Matched outer-wall orthogonal measurements are 4.6 cm on the prior CTA and 4.7 cm on the current study. He remains free of abdominal or back symptoms. The entire infrarenal sac is consistently visualized on ultrasound.
decisionNodes.stem: Which aortic surveillance schedule should have been selected for {patientName} after that comparison?

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 12 months
answerChoices.rationale: The matched size places this asymptomatic man in the annual-ultrasound group.

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 6 months
answerChoices.rationale: This follows a larger-AAA schedule rather than the supported schedule for his matched 4.7-cm diameter.

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 3 years
answerChoices.rationale: This is too long for the measured 4.7-cm sac.

decisionNodes.explanation: The matched study establishes a 4.7-cm AAA, not a confirmed jump to 5.3 cm. Annual ultrasound is the guideline schedule for an asymptomatic man in this diameter band when ultrasound defines the sac adequately.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later outside admission documents persistent new deep abdominal and back pain, focal tenderness over the aorta and no relation to movement. CTA shows a 4.9-cm intact fusiform AAA; the hospital evaluation identifies no competing abdominal or spinal cause. He is normotensive and otherwise fit for repair.
decisionNodes.stem: Which hospital aortic plan should have replaced surveillance for {patientName} during that admission?

answerChoices.label: Inpatient vascular assessment for aneurysm repair
answerChoices.rationale: The new pain pattern and localized findings support aneurysm-attributable symptoms despite a subthreshold asymptomatic diameter.

answerChoices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in six months
answerChoices.rationale: A shorter surveillance interval does not address the new symptomatic aneurysm assessment.

answerChoices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in twelve months
answerChoices.rationale: The old annual plan was for an asymptomatic patient; the current observations change that premise.

decisionNodes.explanation: A symptomatic intact AAA is assessed for repair even below the usual asymptomatic diameter threshold. The new localized persistent pain changes the previous surveillance premise; hemodynamic stability and absence of a CT leak do not restore that premise.

decisionNodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been offered after {patientName}'s 5.1-cm result?

answerChoices.label: Elective vascular evaluation for aneurysm repair
answerChoices.rationale: The size meets the female repair-assessment boundary even without interval growth.

answerChoices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every six months
answerChoices.rationale: A male size band should not postpone this woman's repair assessment.

answerChoices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every twelve months
answerChoices.rationale: Annual follow-up does not address a woman's aneurysm already at the repair-assessment boundary.

decisionNodes.explanation: A stable diameter can still warrant repair evaluation. The guideline boundary is lower in women than men, but it does not prescribe a procedure or an individual mortality estimate.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside repair-planning CTA shows both common iliac arteries enlarged through their bifurcations. The left internal iliac artery is chronically occluded. The right internal iliac and both external iliac arteries are patent, with nonaneurysmal distal landing segments. A standard bifurcated infrarenal main body can be used.
decisionNodes.stem: Which iliac configuration should have been selected for {patientName}'s planned endovascular repair?

answerChoices.label: Right iliac branch graft; left external-iliac extension
answerChoices.rationale: This preserves the patent right internal iliac route while excluding the aneurysmal common iliac segments.

answerChoices.label: Bilateral external-iliac extensions; right internal-iliac embolization
answerChoices.rationale: This would eliminate the remaining direct internal-iliac inflow when a preserving option is anatomically described.

answerChoices.label: Bilateral limb landings within the distal common iliac arteries
answerChoices.rationale: The proposed landing regions remain aneurysmal through the bifurcations and do not supply a healthy distal seal.

decisionNodes.explanation: The left internal iliac artery is already occluded. Use a configuration that excludes the aneurysms while preserving the patent right pelvic inflow when feasible; landing within an aneurysmal common iliac segment does not solve exclusion.

decisionNodes.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s later surveillance study?

answerChoices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: The branch origin and unchanged sac support observation with continued imaging.

answerChoices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
answerChoices.rationale: A visible branch leak does not by itself establish a treatment benefit when the sac is stable.

answerChoices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
answerChoices.rationale: The observed inflow is from lumbar branches, not the proximal attachment.

decisionNodes.explanation: Delayed branch-associated flow with an unchanged sac supports continued surveillance. A visible leak is not enough to choose its treatment; source and sac behavior matter.
sourceLabels: Joo-Young Chun et al. (2024). CIRSE Standards of Practice on Management of Endoleaks Following Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later CTA measures the sac at 7.0 cm using the same method. Contrast appears near a graft-limb junction and a lumbar branch, but metal artifact prevents tracing its origin despite arterial and delayed acquisitions. He remains hemodynamically stable without pain.
decisionNodes.stem: Which angiographic assessment should precede targeted leak treatment for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Aortography across the seal zones and graft junctions
answerChoices.rationale: The enlarging sac and uncertain source require reassessment for direct graft or attachment inflow before targeting a branch.

answerChoices.label: Selective mesenteric-to-inferior-mesenteric collateral angiography
answerChoices.rationale: This maps a branch route but does not resolve the possible attachment or component defect producing the current sac growth.

answerChoices.label: Selective iliolumbar-to-lumbar collateral angiography
answerChoices.rationale: The lumbar branch near the contrast focus does not establish that it is the only source.

decisionNodes.explanation: Do not carry forward a branch-leak label when a growing sac has an uncertain current inflow source. Problem-solving aortography can assess the attachments and modular junctions before choosing a branch-directed treatment.
sourceLabels: Joo-Young Chun et al. (2024). CIRSE Standards of Practice on Management of Endoleaks Following Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Aortography shows contrast passing through a gap between the main body and right iliac limb into the sac during the arterial phase. Both attachment sites remain sealed. Adequate overlap can be obtained between the existing components with an additional covered limb.
decisionNodes.stem: Which endovascular repair should have been selected for {patientName}'s demonstrated defect?

answerChoices.label: Bridge the separated components with a covered graft
answerChoices.rationale: The source is the modular gap; a bridging covered component restores continuity.

answerChoices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
answerChoices.rationale: Branch embolization does not close the direct connection through the separated graft components.

answerChoices.label: Extend the proximal attachment with an aortic cuff
answerChoices.rationale: The proximal seal is intact; extending it does not cover the limb junction gap.

decisionNodes.explanation: The direct component gap is a type III mechanism and requires prompt repair. A covered bridge across the separation closes the source; branch embolization or a remote proximal extension would not.
sourceLabels: Joo-Young Chun et al. (2024). CIRSE Standards of Practice on Management of Endoleaks Following Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial hospital treatment plan should have been selected for {patientName} at that assessment?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
answerChoices.rationale: The observed extent and perfusion support initial medical treatment; rate/impulse control precedes added vasodilation.

answerChoices.label: Urgent thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
answerChoices.rationale: The admission record has not demonstrated rupture, malperfusion or failure of medical treatment that would establish an immediate repair indication.

answerChoices.label: Urgent open descending aortic graft replacement
answerChoices.rationale: An open replacement is not the initial treatment for this uncomplicated descending presentation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.
decisionNodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?

answerChoices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.

answerChoices.label: Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
answerChoices.rationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.

answerChoices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.

decisionNodes.explanation: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.
decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
answerChoices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

answerChoices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
answerChoices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

decisionNodes.stem: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
answerChoices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.

answerChoices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
answerChoices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
answerChoices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.

decisionNodes.explanation: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

Speech, face and arm movement are unchanged. Platelet count and coagulation studies are normal, and no neuraxial drain is present.
decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?

answerChoices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
answerChoices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
answerChoices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.

answerChoices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.

decisionNodes.explanation: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.

decisionNodes.stem: Which aneurysm plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s right popliteal lesion?

answerChoices.label: Plan popliteal aneurysm exclusion and bypass
answerChoices.rationale: The thrombus and distal embolic findings make size-only observation inadequate despite a diameter below 20 mm.

answerChoices.label: Arrange annual popliteal duplex surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A diameter-only policy overlooks the repeated embolic complications documented here.

answerChoices.label: Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Medical suppression does not remove the aneurysmal thrombus source; the supported next strategy includes repair consideration.

decisionNodes.explanation: The relevant problem is distal embolization from a thrombus-containing PAA, not diameter alone. Repair is considered even below 20 mm when embolic complications are present; the exact operation still depends on operative assessment and conduit anatomy.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The same outside workup includes a complete abdominal-aortic CTA with outer diameters under 3 cm throughout the abdominal aorta. The arterial duplex acquisition is labeled right lower extremity from common femoral to pedal vessels. The clinic receives the original images and acquisition records.
decisionNodes.stem: Which additional aneurysm study should have completed {patientName}'s survey after review of these records?

answerChoices.label: Left popliteal arterial duplex ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: The abdominal aorta has been assessed, while the associated contralateral popliteal site is outside the documented unilateral acquisition.

answerChoices.label: Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: The complete adequate abdominal CTA already addresses the aortic component of the associated-aneurysm survey.

answerChoices.label: Thoracic aortic CT angiography
answerChoices.rationale: The specific routinely recommended associated sites are the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta, not a substitute thoracic survey.

decisionNodes.explanation: PAA prompts an opposite-leg and abdominal-aortic aneurysm survey. Review what was actually acquired: a complete abdominal CTA already evaluates the aorta, but a right-leg-only duplex does not evaluate the left popliteal artery.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After outside popliteal exclusion and vein bypass, he develops progressive calf swelling and plantar numbness. Duplex shows a widely patent bypass and persistent flow within an enlarging excluded sac. The sac displaces the popliteal vein and tibial nerve. Venous duplex shows compression without thrombus.
decisionNodes.stem: Which procedure should have addressed {patientName}'s new postoperative problem?

answerChoices.label: Surgical decompression of the excluded aneurysm sac
answerChoices.rationale: The symptomatic enlarging sac is the compressive target even though bypass inflow and outflow remain patent.

answerChoices.label: Revision of the popliteal bypass graft
answerChoices.rationale: The bypass is patent; revising it does not remove the compressive sac.

answerChoices.label: Embolization of residual genicular branch inflow
answerChoices.rationale: Inflows can contribute to sac persistence, but the demonstrated symptomatic compression calls for decompression of the enlarged sac.

decisionNodes.explanation: A patent bypass does not remove an enlarging excluded sac. When that sac causes neural or venous compression, surgical decompression addresses the current problem rather than revising a patent conduit.
sourceLabels: Alik Farber et al. (2022). SVS clinical practice guidelines on popliteal artery aneurysms.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should have followed {patientName}'s unrevealing upper endoscopy during that admission?

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
answerChoices.rationale: The graft history plus infection and bleeding warrants cross-sectional assessment of the reconstructed aorta and its bowel interface.

answerChoices.label: Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the same examined mucosal territory does not evaluate the prosthetic graft or its extraluminal interface.

answerChoices.label: Tagged-red-cell scintigraphy for gastrointestinal bleeding
answerChoices.rationale: Bleed localization does not assess the graft infection concern raised by the combined history and cultures.

decisionNodes.explanation: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CTA demonstrates a perigraft fluid-and-gas collection with a channel to adjacent duodenum. The same organism persists in repeated blood cultures despite directed intravenous antibiotics. He has preserved pressure and organ function, remains functionally independent, and the multidisciplinary hospital assessment finds no prohibitive operative condition.
decisionNodes.stem: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?

answerChoices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.

answerChoices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
answerChoices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.

answerChoices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

cases.learningSummary: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal. Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

answerChoices.label: Branched endovascular thoracoabdominal repair

answerChoices.label: Visceral debranching with thoracic endografting

answerChoices.label: Prompt splenic-artery embolization assessment
answerChoices.rationale: A new extra-organ contained leak through a wall defect is not governed by small true-aneurysm surveillance thresholds.

answerChoices.label: CT angiographic surveillance after inflammation resolves

answerChoices.label: Annual CT angiographic surveillance of lesion size

questions.stem: Which imaging plan should have been selected at {patientName}'s asymptomatic preventive visit?

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound
Abdominal aortic CT angiography
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CTA can define repair anatomy but is not the routine first screen for this asymptomatic eligible man.

answerChoices.label: No additional aortic imaging
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The previous study ended before the abdominal aorta, and remote smoking still counts as ever smoking.

questions.explanation: An ever-smoker in the eligible age range still needs a first abdominal aortic screen when prior imaging covered the chest. Ultrasound is the initial screening modality.

questions.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s ultrasound result at that asymptomatic visit?

answerChoices.label: Refer for elective vascular repair evaluation
Arrange annual aortic ultrasound surveillance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A 3.1-cm patent lumen is not the relevant aneurysm diameter; the full sac is 6.0 cm.

answerChoices.label: Arrange three-year aortic ultrasound surveillance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A surveillance schedule for a much smaller AAA is inappropriate for this full sac size.

questions.explanation: Use the full outer-wall aneurysm diameter. A stable acceptable-risk man with a 6-cm fusiform AAA needs elective vascular repair evaluation; mural thrombus does not reduce that diameter to the flowing channel.

questions.stem: Which imaging action should precede a growth-based repair decision for {patientName} at that visit?

answerChoices.label: Re-measure both CT datasets perpendicular to the centerline
Acquire another contrast CT using the new axial protocol
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Another noncomparable acquisition does not resolve the existing plane mismatch.

answerChoices.label: Replace the CT comparison with a new ultrasound diameter
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A new modality does not establish how the two existing CT measurements relate.

questions.explanation: Compare the same anatomic site with reproducible orthogonal measurements. Reformat the available acquisitions before labeling the difference as growth; repeating the scan is not necessary just to correct a measurement plane.

questions.stem: Which aortic surveillance schedule should have been selected for {patientName} after that comparison?

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 12 months
Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 6 months
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This follows a larger-AAA schedule rather than the supported schedule for his matched 4.7-cm diameter.

answerChoices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 3 years
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is too long for the measured 4.7-cm sac.

questions.explanation: The matched study establishes a 4.7-cm AAA, not a confirmed jump to 5.3 cm. Annual ultrasound is the guideline schedule for an asymptomatic man in this diameter band when ultrasound defines the sac adequately.

questions.stem: Which hospital aortic plan should have replaced surveillance for {patientName} during that admission?

answerChoices.label: Inpatient vascular assessment for aneurysm repair
Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in six months
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A shorter surveillance interval does not address the new symptomatic aneurysm assessment.

answerChoices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in twelve months
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The old annual plan was for an asymptomatic patient; the current observations change that premise.

questions.explanation: A symptomatic intact AAA is assessed for repair even below the usual asymptomatic diameter threshold. The new localized persistent pain changes the previous surveillance premise; hemodynamic stability and absence of a CT leak do not restore that premise.

questions.stem: Which aortic plan should have been offered after {patientName}'s 5.1-cm result?

answerChoices.label: Elective vascular evaluation for aneurysm repair
Aortic ultrasound surveillance every six months
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A male size band should not postpone this woman's repair assessment.

answerChoices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every twelve months
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Annual follow-up does not address a woman's aneurysm already at the repair-assessment boundary.

questions.explanation: A stable diameter can still warrant repair evaluation. The guideline boundary is lower in women than men, but it does not prescribe a procedure or an individual mortality estimate.

questions.stem: Which iliac configuration should have been selected for {patientName}'s planned endovascular repair?

answerChoices.label: Right iliac branch graft; left external-iliac extension
Bilateral external-iliac extensions; right internal-iliac embolization
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This would eliminate the remaining direct internal-iliac inflow when a preserving option is anatomically described.

answerChoices.label: Bilateral limb landings within the distal common iliac arteries
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The proposed landing regions remain aneurysmal through the bifurcations and do not supply a healthy distal seal.

questions.explanation: The left internal iliac artery is already occluded. Use a configuration that excludes the aneurysms while preserving the patent right pelvic inflow when feasible; landing within an aneurysmal common iliac segment does not solve exclusion.

questions.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s later surveillance study?

exhibit.caption: Constructed outside-record measurements; not a reproduced clinical image

answerChoices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A visible branch leak does not by itself establish a treatment benefit when the sac is stable.

answerChoices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The observed inflow is from lumbar branches, not the proximal attachment.

questions.explanation: Delayed branch-associated flow with an unchanged sac supports continued surveillance. A visible leak is not enough to choose its treatment; source and sac behavior matter.

questions.stem: Which angiographic assessment should precede targeted leak treatment for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Aortography across the seal zones and graft junctions
Selective mesenteric-to-inferior-mesenteric collateral angiography
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This maps a branch route but does not resolve the possible attachment or component defect producing the current sac growth.

answerChoices.label: Selective iliolumbar-to-lumbar collateral angiography
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The lumbar branch near the contrast focus does not establish that it is the only source.

questions.explanation: Do not carry forward a branch-leak label when a growing sac has an uncertain current inflow source. Problem-solving aortography can assess the attachments and modular junctions before choosing a branch-directed treatment.

questions.stem: Which endovascular repair should have been selected for {patientName}'s demonstrated defect?

answerChoices.label: Bridge the separated components with a covered graft
Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Branch embolization does not close the direct connection through the separated graft components.

answerChoices.label: Extend the proximal attachment with an aortic cuff
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The proximal seal is intact; extending it does not cover the limb junction gap.

questions.explanation: The direct component gap is a type III mechanism and requires prompt repair. A covered bridge across the separation closes the source; branch embolization or a remote proximal extension would not.

questions.stem: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s proximal attachment finding?

answerChoices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Stable sac size does not justify observation of an established late direct attachment leak.

answerChoices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The demonstrated source is the proximal attachment, not a side branch.

questions.explanation: This arterial-phase attachment route represents a type I sealing failure. Prompt seal repair is appropriate even before the sac enlarges; the available healthy neck makes proximal extension a supported option.

questions.stem: Which imaging study should have been selected at {patientName}'s recorded stable assessment?

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the aorta and iliac access vessels
Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta and iliac vessels
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Another sonographic survey does not provide the same cross-sectional rupture and repair-planning information.

answerChoices.label: Catheter aortography of the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Initial catheter luminal imaging does not replace CT mapping of the sac, surrounding hemorrhage and access anatomy in this stable setting.

questions.explanation: At the recorded stable assessment, urgent CT supplies cross-sectional repair-planning anatomy in suspected rupture rather than repeating the already demonstrated aneurysm diameter.

questions.stem: Which definitive repair approach should have been selected for {patientName} at that point?

answerChoices.label: Emergency endovascular aneurysm repair
Emergency open aneurysm repair
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Open repair is a real alternative, but the guideline favors EVAR for the documented suitable anatomy.

answerChoices.label: Elective endovascular aneurysm repair
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The wall defect and retroperitoneal hematoma establish rupture despite current preserved pressure.

questions.explanation: The wall defect and contiguous hematoma establish rupture. Preserved pressure does not make it elective. With documented suitable anatomy and treating-hospital expertise, the guideline favors emergency EVAR over open repair.

questions.stem: Which definitive hospital plan should have been selected from {patientName}'s initial CTA?

answerChoices.label: Emergency open ascending aortic repair
Urgent descending thoracic endovascular repair
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Treating the distal tear as a type-B problem does not address the acute ascending involvement.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous esmolol with CT angiographic follow-up
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Impulse control is background stabilization but not definitive treatment of acute ascending dissection.

questions.explanation: Ascending involvement determines the type-A pathway even when the entry tear is distal. Stable current pressure does not remove the need for emergency surgical treatment of acute ascending dissection.

questions.stem: Which initial hospital treatment plan should have been selected for {patientName} at that assessment?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
Urgent thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The admission record has not demonstrated rupture, malperfusion or failure of medical treatment that would establish an immediate repair indication.

answerChoices.label: Urgent open descending aortic graft replacement
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An open replacement is not the initial treatment for this uncomplicated descending presentation.

questions.explanation: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated.

questions.stem: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?

answerChoices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.

answerChoices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.

questions.explanation: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.

questions.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

answerChoices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.

questions.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

questions.stem: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.

questions.explanation: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

questions.stem: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?

answerChoices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.

answerChoices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.

questions.explanation: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.

questions.stem: Which aneurysm plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s right popliteal lesion?

answerChoices.label: Plan popliteal aneurysm exclusion and bypass
Arrange annual popliteal duplex surveillance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A diameter-only policy overlooks the repeated embolic complications documented here.

answerChoices.label: Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Medical suppression does not remove the aneurysmal thrombus source; the supported next strategy includes repair consideration.

questions.explanation: The relevant problem is distal embolization from a thrombus-containing PAA, not diameter alone. Repair is considered even below 20 mm when embolic complications are present; the exact operation still depends on operative assessment and conduit anatomy.

questions.stem: Which additional aneurysm study should have completed {patientName}'s survey after review of these records?

answerChoices.label: Left popliteal arterial duplex ultrasound
Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The complete adequate abdominal CTA already addresses the aortic component of the associated-aneurysm survey.

answerChoices.label: Thoracic aortic CT angiography
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The specific routinely recommended associated sites are the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta, not a substitute thoracic survey.

questions.explanation: PAA prompts an opposite-leg and abdominal-aortic aneurysm survey. Review what was actually acquired: a complete abdominal CTA already evaluates the aorta, but a right-leg-only duplex does not evaluate the left popliteal artery.

questions.stem: Which procedure should have addressed {patientName}'s new postoperative problem?

answerChoices.label: Surgical decompression of the excluded aneurysm sac
Revision of the popliteal bypass graft
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The bypass is patent; revising it does not remove the compressive sac.

answerChoices.label: Embolization of residual genicular branch inflow
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Inflows can contribute to sac persistence, but the demonstrated symptomatic compression calls for decompression of the enlarged sac.

questions.explanation: A patent bypass does not remove an enlarging excluded sac. When that sac causes neural or venous compression, surgical decompression addresses the current problem rather than revising a patent conduit.

questions.stem: Which investigation should have followed {patientName}'s unrevealing upper endoscopy during that admission?

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating the same examined mucosal territory does not evaluate the prosthetic graft or its extraluminal interface.

answerChoices.label: Tagged-red-cell scintigraphy for gastrointestinal bleeding
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bleed localization does not assess the graft infection concern raised by the combined history and cultures.

questions.explanation: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal.

questions.stem: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?

answerChoices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.

answerChoices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.

questions.explanation: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

answerChoices.label: Open thoracoabdominal graft replacement

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Technical feasibility does not erase the guideline preference for open repair in this heritable native-aorta setting.

answerChoices.label: Visceral debranching with thoracic endografting
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A hybrid operation still relies on endograft sealing in the diseased native aorta rather than providing the preferred open reconstruction.

questions.explanation: For an intact TAAA requiring repair in Marfan syndrome, the checked multisociety guideline favors open repair. Native-aortic tissue disease and long-term durability matter even when branched or hybrid reconstruction is technically possible.

authorChecks.cueAttack: The complaint names the organ, not the modality. Chest CTA is retained because its inferior coverage boundary changes whether screening is complete. Three imaging plans use similar scope; both offered tests have wait metadata.
authorChecks.stageAndCategory: Initial preventive abdominal-aortic imaging plans; no repair or rupture action competes at this stage.
reasoningSteps: Infer that the infrarenal aorta was not assessed by the prior chest acquisition.
Apply age and ever-smoking eligibility to choose ultrasound rather than repeat chest work or diagnostic CTA.
authorChecks.difficulty: Moderate prediction: an otherwise prepared PGY-2/3 may mistake remote cessation or prior thoracic CTA for completed screening. The ultrasound-versus-CTA distinction remains a narrower rule than the later complications.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: The prior acquisition stops at the diaphragm and he has never had abdominal imaging.
authorChecks.closestError: No additional imaging because an aortic CTA already exists.
authorChecks.consequence: Missing an indicated abdominal-aortic screen.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Removing prior-coverage information leaves uncertainty about a completed screen. Removing smoking or age changes eligibility. The number of pack-years is a fictional exposure, not an eligibility cutoff.
authorChecks.counterfactual: Replace the chest study with a documented completed adequate abdominal aortic screen: no additional one-time screen becomes the best offered plan.
authorChecks.sequenceReview: The first explanation gives no repair diameter or subsequent result. The later ultrasound appears only after this answer as a separate outside record; no test is executed in clinic.
authorChecks.repairAndRecheck: Removed radiography and transthoracic echo foils and the one-time-test lead-in. Re-solved with the earlier scan's actual field of view; all three plans have a real screening/diagnostic role.

authorChecks.cueAttack: The update provides both competing measurements without identifying the one to use. Removed 'acceptable operative-risk candidate' as an authored eligibility conclusion; ordinary function and absence of life-limiting illness supply context. Surveillance choices carry identical ultrasound profiles.
authorChecks.stageAndCategory: Plans after an intact asymptomatic aneurysm result: repair referral or specified imaging surveillance.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish full sac diameter from residual flowing lumen.
Apply the full 6-cm size and patient context to elective repair referral.
authorChecks.difficulty: Moderate: a plausible lumen-versus-sac error now competes with the correct referral; no emergency-exploration or discharge caricature remains.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: The 6.0-cm outer wall surrounds a smaller lumen and mural thrombus.
authorChecks.closestError: Annual surveillance based on the patent lumen.
authorChecks.consequence: Deferring assessment of an aneurysm already warranting repair consideration.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Without the paired measurements, the distinctive interpretation step disappears. Symptoms and general fitness establish an elective, rather than emergent or futile, evaluation.
authorChecks.counterfactual: Change the full sac to 4.7 cm with documented stability: annual ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
authorChecks.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback covers eligibility and screening modality only. It does not teach sac measurement or a repair threshold. This later decision changes care.
authorChecks.repairAndRecheck: Replaced ruptured-exploration and no-follow-up foils with credible surveillance plans. Both wrong intervals now reflect the supplied smaller measurement; the outside ultrasound is a completed record, not a fabricated pending result gate.

authorChecks.cueAttack: The exhibit-free imaging record contains acquisition observations, not the conclusion 'measurement artifact.' The key is longest by a few words but all labels name a concrete imaging action; re-measure versus re-acquire is the tested distinction, not a caution cue.
authorChecks.stageAndCategory: Resolve the validity of a serial imaging comparison before any growth-based repair decision.
reasoningSteps: Identify noncomparable axial and centerline-perpendicular measurements.
Choose re-analysis of already acquired images rather than another acquisition or cross-modality comparison.
authorChecks.difficulty: Moderate/hard: apparent threshold crossing tempts escalation, while a repeat scan feels more definitive than reviewing the adequate acquisition.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Different planes across a curved segment, with both datasets available.
authorChecks.closestError: Repeat contrast CT under the same new axial protocol.
authorChecks.consequence: Radiation/contrast exposure while leaving the growth inference unresolved.
authorChecks.deletionTest: The whole update is required: removing the planes or availability of datasets changes the comparison. No report conclusion supplies the answer.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the original acquisitions were unavailable or inadequate for the needed landmarks, new appropriate cross-sectional acquisition would become reasonable.
authorChecks.sequenceReview: Later annual-surveillance and symptom decisions receive new observations after this answer. This explanation does not specify an interval or symptom-triggered operation.
authorChecks.repairAndRecheck: Rejected an initial immediate-repair foil because it compared another care stage. All three final choices address imaging validity; both new acquisitions have wait metadata.

authorChecks.cueAttack: All options are the same modality and comparable length, with the same wait profile. Neither the complaint nor earlier explanation provides the interval. The previously larger number is intentionally retained in history as the competing error.
authorChecks.stageAndCategory: Imaging-surveillance schedules, not repair modalities.
reasoningSteps: Use the valid matched measurements instead of the initial oblique report.
Apply the male diameter band and adequate imaging window to a surveillance interval.
authorChecks.difficulty: Moderate: applying the unreconciled report or the wrong sex-specific band is plausible despite knowing that surveillance is indicated.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: A reproducible 4.7-cm sac in an asymptomatic man with an adequate ultrasound window.
authorChecks.closestError: Six-month ultrasound based on the original 5.3-cm report.
authorChecks.consequence: Unnecessary short-interval testing; a three-year error would under-surveil.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Delete the new comparison and the six-month schedule could follow from the earlier report; the update changes the answer. Ultrasound adequacy earns its role in modality choice.
authorChecks.counterfactual: A matched 5.2-cm sac in the same asymptomatic man changes the preferred offered interval to six months.
authorChecks.sequenceReview: Prior feedback requires comparable planes but gives no interval. This node supplies the corrected result only now. Subsequent feedback does not anticipate the later pain episode.
authorChecks.repairAndRecheck: Removed elective repair from this interval task and balanced all labels to modality plus interval. Clinical follow-up intervals are evidence-backed; they are distinct from gameplay wait placeholders.

authorChecks.cueAttack: No pre-answer sentence labels the aneurysm 'symptomatic' or 'the cause.' The pain attribution observations and competing-cause evaluation are necessary for fairness. All options are aortic care plans at this admission; no reassuring discharge or emergency laparotomy caricature is used.
authorChecks.stageAndCategory: Aortic disposition/management plans after a new hospital evaluation.
reasoningSteps: Infer a clinically attributable aneurysm symptom pattern despite no visible rupture.
Replace the earlier asymptomatic surveillance strategy with inpatient repair assessment.
authorChecks.difficulty: Moderate: anchoring on the just-learned size interval and interpreting intact CTA as permission for continued surveillance are credible errors.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: A new persistent localized pain syndrome without another identified cause, rather than size change alone.
authorChecks.closestError: Annual surveillance based on the earlier 4.7-cm classification.
authorChecks.consequence: Delay in evaluating an aneurysm that may be clinically unstable despite an intact image.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Deleting the whole symptom update restores the prior annual key, so the later node earns a new inference. Normotension and repair fitness define the available hospital options.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the pain were reproducible with movement and a separate spinal cause were established, size-based outpatient surveillance could again be appropriate.
authorChecks.sequenceReview: Earlier explanations discuss measurement and asymptomatic intervals only; they do not announce symptoms as a repair trigger. This is a historical admission reviewed in clinic, not an ICU or ED encounter generated in the clinic.
authorChecks.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a generic 'urgent referral' key with a concrete inpatient vascular repair assessment. Retained pain attribution and urgent warning observations; no exact deadline or drug regimen invented.

authorChecks.cueAttack: Sex and full measured size are necessary eligibility data, not deterministic risk language. The stem does not ask for a sex association or announce a lower threshold. All choices name concrete plans, and both surveillance choices have ultrasound wait metadata.
authorChecks.stageAndCategory: Elective aortic management after an established intact aneurysm result.
reasoningSteps: Separate absence of growth from being below a size threshold.
Apply the female diameter boundary to repair assessment rather than borrowing the male band.
authorChecks.difficulty: Moderate: stable size and remembered male thresholds are two credible competing errors. This is a practical replacement for repeating an epidemiologic association.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm full sac in a woman without a life-limiting condition.
authorChecks.closestError: Six-month surveillance until the male repair threshold is reached.
authorChecks.consequence: Delayed specialist repair evaluation.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Removing sex or the measured diameter makes the interval/referral ranking indeterminate. Ordinary function supplies fitness context without assigning an invented mortality score.
authorChecks.counterfactual: Change the diameter to 4.7 cm while retaining the asymptomatic female profile: six-month ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
