sources.authorityAssessment: Specialty consensus standards; not a formal clinical guideline. Directly checks inflammatory arterial wall disruption and prompt pseudoaneurysm treatment. True splenic-artery aneurysm size thresholds conflict with SVS; that separate teaching point is withheld.

claims.statement: Men age 65 through 75 who have ever smoked should receive one-time abdominal ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
claims.limitation: Exact pre-existing atomic statement and stable claim ID retained; source mapping freshly verified. Limited to asymptomatic previously unscreened men; not a diagnostic strategy for symptoms.
claims.applicablePopulation: Asymptomatic men 65-75 with previous tobacco use and no completed abdominal aortic screen.

claims.statement: An acceptable-risk patient with an asymptomatic 6-cm fusiform abdominal aortic aneurysm should receive prompt vascular-surgery evaluation for elective repair rather than routine surveillance alone.
claims.limitation: Exact pre-existing statement/ID retained. Anatomy, life expectancy and operative risk still govern final repair selection.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable acceptable-risk men with intact fusiform AAA.

claims.statement: AAA size assessment includes the outer aneurysm wall, not just the contrast-filled lumen.
claims.limitation: CT measurements must be perpendicular to the aortic path. One directly checked society publication.

claims.statement: Growth assessment requires comparable landmarks and measurement planes.
claims.limitation: A single oblique axial value cannot establish growth against an orthogonal prior value; repeat measurement of existing images can resolve this without repeat acquisition.

claims.statement: For asymptomatic men with a 4.0-4.9-cm AAA, annual ultrasound surveillance is recommended.
claims.limitation: Not a policy for women, symptoms, rapid confirmed growth or poor ultrasound definition.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable asymptomatic men with small fusiform AAA.

claims.statement: A 3.0-3.9-cm AAA can undergo ultrasound surveillance every three years.
claims.limitation: For asymptomatic disease without a separate concerning change.

claims.statement: Six-month ultrasound surveillance applies to unrepaired AAAs at least 5.0 cm in men or 4.5 cm in women.
claims.limitation: Single checked guideline; do not use surveillance to defer an otherwise indicated repair assessment.

claims.statement: For women with a 4.0-4.4-cm AAA, annual ultrasound surveillance is recommended.
claims.limitation: Single checked guideline; symptoms or other concerning findings can change the plan.

claims.statement: An intact AAA of at least 5.0 cm in a woman warrants elective repair assessment.
claims.limitation: Recommendation strength differs by society; diameter does not override operative fitness or preferences.

claims.statement: Symptoms attributable to an intact AAA warrant repair assessment regardless of usual asymptomatic diameter thresholds.
claims.limitation: Pain attribution requires clinical assessment; no universal numeric pain or observation interval is supplied.

claims.statement: Preserve at least one internal iliac inflow when feasible during aortoiliac repair.
claims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline; describes pelvic-perfusion protection, not a universal brand or device choice.
claims.applicablePopulation: AAA repair involving iliac landing zones.

claims.statement: Attachment-site flow into an excluded sac represents a sealing failure.
claims.limitation: Type I origin; one directly checked specialty standard.

claims.statement: An established type I endoleak warrants prompt correction of the seal.
claims.limitation: Cuff extension requires an available healthy landing segment; complex cases may need other repair. One directly checked publication.

claims.statement: Retrograde flow from aortic side branches can fill the excluded sac.
claims.limitation: Type II physiology; other inflow sources must be assessed.

claims.statement: An isolated type II endoleak with stable sac size can undergo imaging follow-up.
claims.limitation: Single publication; requires exclusion of higher-pressure leaks and continued surveillance.
claims.applicablePopulation: Asymptomatic patients with stable post-EVAR sac.

claims.statement: Sac enlargement with uncertain leak origin requires investigation for occult type I or III inflow.
claims.limitation: Catheter angiography with possible cone-beam CT can resolve inconclusive CTA; no disputed growth cutoff is taught.

claims.statement: Separated modular components can directly pressurize the excluded sac.
claims.limitation: Type IIIa mechanism; not retrograde branch flow.

claims.statement: A bridging graft can close a component gap causing a type III endoleak.
claims.limitation: Prompt repair is indicated; anatomy determines the precise device or need for open conversion. One checked publication.

claims.statement: A stable patient with suspected ruptured AAA can undergo urgent CT for repair planning.
claims.limitation: Single checked guideline; do not extend imaging delay to a patient who cannot remain stable.

claims.statement: EVAR is recommended for ruptured AAA when anatomy is suitable.
claims.limitation: Single checked guideline; requires specialist capability, access and device suitability, not diameter alone.

claims.statement: Ascending aortic involvement establishes type A dissection even with a distal entry tear.
claims.limitation: Classification depends on extent, not simply the tear location.

claims.statement: Acute type A dissection requires emergency surgical evaluation and immediate repair.
claims.limitation: Single checked multisociety guideline. This draft does not rank contested mesenteric-first strategies.

claims.statement: Uncomplicated acute type B dissection initially receives medical therapy and close monitoring.
claims.limitation: High-risk morphology and later complications can change the plan; does not ban elective later TEVAR.
claims.applicablePopulation: Acute descending dissection without rupture or malperfusion.

claims.statement: Use intravenous beta blockade first, adding intravenous vasodilation if pressure remains high.
claims.limitation: Single directly checked recommendation; contraindications can favor a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. No dose or numeric target is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Hypertensive acute aortic syndrome without beta-blocker contraindication.

claims.statement: Acute type B dissection with organ malperfusion warrants intervention, commonly TEVAR when suitable.
claims.limitation: Static branch disease can require adjuncts; no automatic bowel resection or non-aneurysm ischemia objective is included.

claims.statement: Sealing a dissection entry can expand the true lumen and relieve dynamic branch obstruction.
claims.limitation: Single current specialty standard; response must be reassessed.

claims.statement: Persistent fixed branch narrowing after central true-lumen expansion may require branch stenting.
claims.limitation: Single specialty standard; the case supplies persistent gradient and flap extension rather than assuming every residual image needs treatment.

claims.statement: Planned left-subclavian coverage should account for a patent LIMA coronary graft by preserving its inflow.
claims.limitation: Elective setting with native landing zones; bypass versus transposition depends on anatomy.
claims.applicablePopulation: TEVAR involving LSA with LIMA-dependent myocardium.

claims.statement: Carotid-subclavian transposition requires temporary proximal subclavian clamping.
claims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline; the anatomy-specific interruption matters for a pedicled LIMA.

claims.statement: A patent pedicled LIMA coronary graft favors bypass over subclavian transposition to avoid interrupting coronary inflow.
claims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline, section on LSA revascularization; other bypass/endovascular configurations remain specialist decisions.
claims.applicablePopulation: LSA revascularization with a patent pedicled LIMA.

claims.statement: New spinal-cord dysfunction after TEVAR calls for perfusion rescue, including pressure support and CSF drainage assessment.
claims.limitation: Rapid specialist response; drainage contraindications must be checked. No invented target, timing, guaranteed recovery or routine prophylactic drain rule.

claims.statement: A small PAA with thrombus and distal embolic findings merits repair consideration despite being below 20 mm.
claims.limitation: Single guideline, weak recommendation/low-quality evidence; excludes acutely threatened limbs requiring an ischemia-specific pathway.
claims.applicablePopulation: PAA under 20 mm with embolic findings.

claims.statement: Finding a PAA warrants screening the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta.
claims.limitation: Single guideline, strong recommendation/moderate evidence; this is aneurysm screening, not broad asymptomatic arterial-stenosis screening.

claims.statement: A symptomatic expanding excluded PAA sac may require decompression despite a patent bypass.
claims.limitation: Single guideline; exclude graft failure and venous thrombosis as the cause of symptoms.

claims.statement: Unexplained infection or gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting warrants cross-sectional graft evaluation.
claims.limitation: Single guideline; imaging and cultures are interpreted together, and an unrevealing endoscopy does not assess the graft.
claims.applicablePopulation: Prosthetic aortic graft with unexplained infection/bleeding.

claims.statement: An operable stable patient with aortic graft infection can undergo graft source-control surgery and arterial reconstruction.
claims.limitation: Specific reconstruction and antimicrobial regimen need specialist judgment; endovascular bridging or suppression may fit other patients.

claims.statement: Open repair is preferred for an intact TAAA requiring repair in Marfan syndrome.
claims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline; does not preclude endovascular rescue or exceptional high-risk situations. Newer ESVS full text was inaccessible.
claims.applicablePopulation: Fit patient with heritable native-aorta TAAA.

claims.statement: Pancreatitis can disrupt an adjacent artery and produce a contained arterial leak.
claims.limitation: One CC BY specialty standard. The synthetic image observations are not a copied figure.

claims.statement: Visceral pseudoaneurysms generally warrant prompt treatment rather than true-aneurysm size surveillance.
claims.limitation: Single standard; small intraparenchymal lesions can be exceptions. This case is an extraparenchymal splenic-artery wall defect; exact true-aneurysm thresholds remain withheld.

authorGate.cueAttack: The complaint names the organ, not the modality. Chest CTA is retained because its inferior coverage boundary changes whether screening is complete. Three imaging plans use similar scope; both offered tests have wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Initial preventive abdominal-aortic imaging plans; no repair or rupture action competes at this stage.
reasoningSteps: Infer that the infrarenal aorta was not assessed by the prior chest acquisition.
Apply age and ever-smoking eligibility to choose ultrasound rather than repeat chest work or diagnostic CTA.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: an otherwise prepared PGY-2/3 may mistake remote cessation or prior thoracic CTA for completed screening. The ultrasound-versus-CTA distinction remains a narrower rule than the later complications.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The prior acquisition stops at the diaphragm and he has never had abdominal imaging.
authorGate.closestError: No additional imaging because an aortic CTA already exists.
authorGate.consequence: Missing an indicated abdominal-aortic screen.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing prior-coverage information leaves uncertainty about a completed screen. Removing smoking or age changes eligibility. The number of pack-years is a fictional exposure, not an eligibility cutoff.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the chest study with a documented completed adequate abdominal aortic screen: no additional one-time screen becomes the best offered plan.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation gives no repair diameter or subsequent result. The later ultrasound appears only after this answer as a separate outside record; no test is executed in clinic.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed radiography and transthoracic echo foils and the one-time-test lead-in. Re-solved with the earlier scan's actual field of view; all three plans have a real screening/diagnostic role.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update provides both competing measurements without identifying the one to use. authorGate.stageAndCategory: Plans after an intact asymptomatic aneurysm result: repair referral or specified imaging surveillance.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish full sac diameter from residual flowing lumen.
Apply the full 6-cm size and patient context to elective repair referral.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: a plausible lumen-versus-sac error now competes with the correct referral; no emergency-exploration or discharge caricature remains.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The 6.0-cm outer wall surrounds a smaller lumen and mural thrombus.
authorGate.closestError: Annual surveillance based on the patent lumen.
authorGate.consequence: Deferring assessment of an aneurysm already warranting repair consideration.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the paired measurements, the distinctive interpretation step disappears. Symptoms and general fitness establish an elective, rather than emergent or futile, evaluation.
authorGate.counterfactual: Change the full sac to 4.7 cm with documented stability: annual ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback covers eligibility and screening modality only. It does not teach sac measurement or a repair threshold. This later decision changes care.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced ruptured-exploration and no-follow-up foils with credible surveillance plans. Both wrong intervals now reflect the supplied smaller measurement; the outside ultrasound is a completed record, not a fabricated pending result gate.

explanation.text: Use the full outer-wall aneurysm diameter. A stable acceptable-risk man with a 6-cm fusiform AAA needs elective vascular repair evaluation; mural thrombus does not reduce that diameter to the flowing channel.

choices.counterfactual: A small stable full sac diameter would support surveillance instead.

choices.label: Arrange annual aortic ultrasound surveillance

choices.counterfactual: A stable 4.7-cm full sac in an asymptomatic man would support annual ultrasound.

choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic 3.1-cm full aneurysm, rather than a 3.1-cm lumen inside a 6-cm sac, could support this interval.

authorGate.cueAttack: The exhibit-free imaging record contains acquisition observations, not the conclusion 'measurement artifact.' The key is longest by a few words but all labels name a concrete imaging action; re-measure versus re-acquire is the tested distinction, not a caution cue.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Resolve the validity of a serial imaging comparison before any growth-based repair decision.
reasoningSteps: Identify noncomparable axial and centerline-perpendicular measurements.
Choose re-analysis of already acquired images rather than another acquisition or cross-modality comparison.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: apparent threshold crossing tempts escalation, while a repeat scan feels more definitive than reviewing the adequate acquisition.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Different planes across a curved segment, with both datasets available.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat contrast CT under the same new axial protocol.
authorGate.consequence: Radiation/contrast exposure while leaving the growth inference unresolved.
authorGate.deletionTest: The whole update is required: removing the planes or availability of datasets changes the comparison. No report conclusion supplies the answer.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the original acquisitions were unavailable or inadequate for the needed landmarks, new appropriate cross-sectional acquisition would become reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Later annual-surveillance and symptom decisions receive new observations after this answer. This explanation does not specify an interval or symptom-triggered operation.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Rejected an initial immediate-repair foil because it compared another care stage. All three final choices address imaging validity; both new acquisitions have wait metadata.

authorGate.cueAttack: No pre-answer sentence labels the aneurysm 'symptomatic' or 'the cause.' The pain attribution observations and competing-cause evaluation are necessary for fairness. All options are aortic care plans at this admission; no reassuring discharge or emergency laparotomy caricature is used.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Aortic disposition/management plans after a new hospital evaluation.
reasoningSteps: Infer a clinically attributable aneurysm symptom pattern despite no visible rupture.
Replace the earlier asymptomatic surveillance strategy with inpatient repair assessment.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: anchoring on the just-learned size interval and interpreting intact CTA as permission for continued surveillance are credible errors.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A new persistent localized pain syndrome without another identified cause, rather than size change alone.
authorGate.closestError: Annual surveillance based on the earlier 4.7-cm classification.
authorGate.consequence: Delay in evaluating an aneurysm that may be clinically unstable despite an intact image.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the whole symptom update restores the prior annual key, so the later node earns a new inference. Normotension and repair fitness define the available hospital options.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the pain were reproducible with movement and a separate spinal cause were established, size-based outpatient surveillance could again be appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Earlier explanations discuss measurement and asymptomatic intervals only; they do not announce symptoms as a repair trigger. This is a historical admission reviewed in clinic, not an ICU or ED encounter generated in the clinic.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a generic 'urgent referral' key with a concrete inpatient vascular repair assessment. Retained pain attribution and urgent warning observations; no exact deadline or drug regimen invented.

authorGate.cueAttack: Sex and full measured size are necessary eligibility data, not deterministic risk language. The stem does not ask for a sex association or announce a lower threshold. All choices name concrete plans, and both surveillance choices have ultrasound wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Elective aortic management after an established intact aneurysm result.
reasoningSteps: Separate absence of growth from being below a size threshold.
Apply the female diameter boundary to repair assessment rather than borrowing the male band.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: stable size and remembered male thresholds are two credible competing errors. This is a practical replacement for repeating an epidemiologic association.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm full sac in a woman without a life-limiting condition.
authorGate.closestError: Six-month surveillance until the male repair threshold is reached.
authorGate.consequence: Delayed specialist repair evaluation.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing sex or the measured diameter makes the interval/referral ranking indeterminate. Ordinary function supplies fitness context without assigning an invented mortality score.
authorGate.counterfactual: Change the diameter to 4.7 cm while retaining the asymptomatic female profile: six-month ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The subsequent iliac decision uses a new CTA planning record. This explanation does not teach hypogastric preservation.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Created a separate meaning; no FSRS history from the approved sex-outcome association is transferred. Replaced unqualified mandatory EVAR with assessment rather than asserting that diameter determines the operation.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update gives each relevant vessel's patency and landing-segment anatomy without naming pelvic ischemia or a preserving technique. Every option is a graft configuration; no uniquely cautious counseling label appears.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Distal graft configuration after an elective EVAR plan, not selection of whether to repair.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that the right internal iliac is the remaining direct pelvic inflow and that both usual distal landing regions are aneurysmal.

authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a technically simple bilateral external extension is tempting, as is retaining common-iliac landings to avoid branch work.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Left internal-iliac occlusion plus right internal-iliac and external-iliac distal landing segments.
authorGate.closestError: Bilateral external extension with embolization of the remaining internal iliac.
authorGate.consequence: Avoidable pelvic ischemia risk or failure to seal in a healthy segment.
authorGate.deletionTest: The entire new vessel map is needed; without it, no configuration is uniquely preferred. No arbitrary device dimension is imposed.
authorGate.counterfactual: Restore nonaneurysmal distal common iliac landing zones: standard common-iliac limb landings become appropriate. Remove the right branch landing zone: the exact chosen branch configuration is no longer established.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding size decision does not disclose this vessel map or preservation rule. A new clinical decision is made at the planning stage.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a fourth implausible remote-vessel operation. Kept three actual configurations and a source limitation: final device suitability requires the treating vascular team, not this synthetic map.

authorGate.cueAttack: The record never calls the flow benign or supplies a type label. The table requires the learner to compare diameter across time. Each option names one plan; the key is not the most detailed or only cautious phrase. Its ultrasound wait is explicit.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Management of a known post-EVAR sac-flow finding at surveillance.
reasoningSteps: Infer retrograde side-branch inflow from phase and continuity.
Use unchanged serial sac size to favor surveillance rather than treating every leak.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: embolization feels appropriate when contrast persists, and a proximal cuff is a real treatment for the competing leak mechanism.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Lumbar continuity with identical full sac diameters and intact attachments/overlaps.
authorGate.closestError: Lumbar/sac embolization for a persistent but stable leak.
authorGate.consequence: Unnecessary intervention while teaching a mechanism-insensitive rule.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the diameter comparison, the branch leak might coexist with enlargement and the management ranking would be incomplete. Attachment observations exclude a different dangerous source without interpreting them for the learner.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace branch filling with direct proximal attachment inflow: prompt seal treatment replaces surveillance even if size has not yet grown.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Feedback does not name component separation or its treatment. Subsequent growth and new angiographic anatomy are withheld until their nodes.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the label 'isolated type II' from the visible context and replaced it with raw phase/continuity observations. The constructed table is numerical evidence rather than a promised scan asset.

explanation.text: Delayed branch-associated flow with an unchanged sac supports continued surveillance. A visible leak is not enough to choose its treatment; source and sac behavior matter.

choices.temptation: Interprets both the leak route and sac behavior.
choices.counterfactual: A direct attachment leak or a growing sac would require a different evaluation or intervention.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: A visible branch leak does not by itself establish a treatment benefit when the sac is stable.
choices.temptation: Treats persistence of any contrast outside the graft as a repair indication.
choices.counterfactual: A persistent proven branch leak with consequential sac growth can merit embolization after other sources are excluded.

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: All three choices are equally specific catheter-angiographic assessments and share a wait profile. The update describes both candidate sites and actual acquired phases; it does not say a series is missing or name an omitted action.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Define the inflow source during catheter workup before selecting targeted treatment.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that a new expanding sac invalidates automatic reassurance from prior stable branch flow.
Choose central graft/seal assessment before committing to one collateral route.
authorGate.difficulty: Hard prediction: the earlier correct surveillance decision and branch finding create a credible anchoring error; nearby lumbar contrast is not proof of causal inflow.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Large interval sac expansion plus artifact-limited origin near a graft junction despite an adequate multiphase acquisition.
authorGate.closestError: Targeted lumbar angiography as if the original attribution were still established.
authorGate.consequence: Missing a direct-pressure leak and treating the wrong pathway.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the growth and new uncertainty restores the earlier surveillance rationale. Phase acquisition details distinguish actual ambiguity from a merely missing export.
authorGate.counterfactual: If multiphase imaging conclusively established isolated lumbar inflow with no attachment or junction defect, selective iliolumbar mapping would become reasonable for treatment planning.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation teaches source/trajectory assessment but does not identify this new source. This node's explanation names possible categories but gives no repair configuration for the later demonstrated defect.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced 'obtain more information' versus repair options with three same-stage angiographic targets. No universal growth threshold is inferred from the constructed large change.

choices.rationale: The enlarging sac and uncertain source require reassessment for direct graft or attachment inflow before targeting a branch.
choices.temptation: Questions whether the old branch label explains the current growth.
choices.counterfactual: A clearly established enlarging isolated branch leak could move directly to targeted branch mapping and embolization.

choices.label: Selective mesenteric-to-inferior-mesenteric collateral angiography
choices.rationale: This maps a branch route but does not resolve the possible attachment or component defect producing the current sac growth.
choices.temptation: Extends the previous type-II attribution to a new scan without validating it.
choices.counterfactual: Proven inferior-mesenteric branch inflow into a growing sac can justify this approach.

choices.label: Selective iliolumbar-to-lumbar collateral angiography
choices.rationale: The lumbar branch near the contrast focus does not establish that it is the only source.
choices.temptation: Anchors on the branch seen on the earlier surveillance images.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed isolated lumbar leak with sac growth can be mapped for targeted embolization.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update supplies raw defect anatomy instead of a type-III label. 'Covered graft' is one specific repair among parallel actual endovascular actions; no uniquely elaborate plan or rationale appears in its label.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Select the site-specific endovascular repair after definitive angiography.
reasoningSteps: Infer a direct-pressure modular graft failure from arterial-phase passage through the component gap.
Choose a covered bridge across that site rather than a branch or attachment procedure.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: prior branch attribution can persist, while a resident may identify a dangerous leak yet choose a proximal cuff for the wrong anatomic defect.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Flow traverses the main-body/limb gap, with intact seals and a feasible bridging overlap.
authorGate.closestError: Proximal cuff extension after correctly recognizing a high-pressure leak.
authorGate.consequence: An unclosed sac-pressure source with continuing rupture risk.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the actual gap and there is no basis to select bridging over the two other repairs; intact seal observations distinguish the closest wrong repair.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the junction gap with direct inflow at the proximal attachment and an available healthy landing segment: proximal cuff extension becomes appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback requires source confirmation but never gives this bridging answer. The new angiographic relationship, not a repeated type label, determines the repair.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Kept attachment and overlap facts because they establish one feasible repair. Did not use an unsafe default that every component defect can be managed with a generic new limb.

authorGate.cueAttack: The unchanged diameter is a real competing datum, not reassurance supplied by the author. No type label or urgency phrase appears before answering. All choices are post-EVAR management plans with similar specificity.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Treat or observe a documented late leak, using its anatomic source.
reasoningSteps: Infer a sealing failure from direct arterial-phase attachment flow.
Apply its pressure-risk significance rather than letting stable sac size determine observation.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: a resident may correctly remember stable-sac observation but apply it to the wrong leak origin.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Direct flow at the proximal attachment with an available healthy neck segment.
authorGate.closestError: Surveillance because the sac has not enlarged.
authorGate.consequence: Leaving a direct-pressure leak untreated.
authorGate.deletionTest: The source and healthy landing anatomy are necessary; removing them prevents selecting the cuff. Stable diameter earns its role as the competing misconception.
authorGate.counterfactual: If contrast arrived through lumbar branches on delayed images with intact seals and a stable sac, continued surveillance would become correct.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone exact context; not dependent on the other endoleak case or its explanation. No cross-case exposure is assumed.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced 'repair immediately' with a concrete anatomically possible cuff plan. Restricted the case to an established late leak rather than a transient intraoperative blush.

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: The care frame is a retrospective clinic review. Serial pressure and alertness are constructed physiologic observations, not an invented stability cutoff. No sentence promises that CT is available or will not delay care. Every option names a vascular imaging study and has a wait profile.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Imaging to plan hospital repair after aneurysm detection, not initial screening or the final repair procedure.
reasoningSteps: Interpret preserved serial perfusion as allowing urgent planning despite a possible contained rupture.
Choose imaging that supplies surrounding hemorrhage, sealing and access anatomy.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: equating rupture with inevitable immediate collapse or reusing ultrasound after detection are credible errors.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Preserved serial circulation after a large aneurysm is demonstrated in a painful presentation.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat duplex because it already identified the AAA and avoids contrast.
authorGate.consequence: Failing to define the repair anatomy or contained hemorrhage needed for the definitive strategy.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing physiologic trajectory makes a CT-planning decision unsafe; removing the completed ultrasound changes the stage from planning to initial evaluation.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the painful admission with an asymptomatic small-AAA surveillance visit: duplex becomes the best offered study. Refractory shock would invalidate the entire stable-imaging task and require immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation avoids the later EVAR-versus-open ranking. CTA findings appear only after answering, and no hospital service is executed by the clinic runtime.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a transfer-permission sentence with serial physiology and removed 'most informative' from the task. Timing estimates are placeholders, not authorization to delay real emergency care.

explanation.text: At the recorded stable assessment, urgent CT supplies cross-sectional repair-planning anatomy in suspected rupture rather than repeating the already demonstrated aneurysm diameter.

choices.label: CT angiography of the aorta and iliac access vessels
choices.rationale: Urgent CT can identify contained rupture and the anatomy needed for the repair strategy while he remains stable.
choices.temptation: Uses current physiology and the information required for repair, rather than repeating aneurysm detection.
choices.counterfactual: A patient unable to sustain circulation for imaging would need immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.

choices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta and iliac vessels
choices.rationale: Another sonographic survey does not provide the same cross-sectional rupture and repair-planning information.
choices.temptation: Extends the correct screening modality to a suspected-rupture planning problem.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic small AAA being surveilled is appropriately assessed by ultrasound.

choices.label: Catheter aortography of the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels
choices.rationale: Initial catheter luminal imaging does not replace CT mapping of the sac, surrounding hemorrhage and access anatomy in this stable setting.
choices.temptation: Treats proximity to an endovascular procedure as a reason to skip cross-sectional planning.
choices.counterfactual: Catheter angiography is useful during an intervention or for an unresolved post-EVAR leak source.

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: All choices specify approach and urgency at the same definitive-treatment stage. Availability of both approaches is a necessary resource constraint that privileges neither. Device suitability is documented rather than fabricated from an invented neck cutoff; actual dimensions are not supplied as unsourced eligibility rules.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Definitive repair approach and timing after completed hospital CTA.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the wall-defect/hematoma relationship as rupture despite maintained pressure.
Apply documented endovascular suitability to an emergency repair strategy.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: open-first reflex and treating a contained leak as elective are plausible but separable errors.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A wall defect with contiguous retroperitoneal blood plus verified graft suitability.
authorGate.closestError: Emergency open repair regardless of suitable endovascular anatomy.
authorGate.consequence: Choosing a less-favored approach for this supported anatomy, or dangerously delaying repair if containment is mistaken for an intact aneurysm.
authorGate.deletionTest: Rupture evidence determines urgency; suitability and hospital capabilities determine the comparison between the emergency approaches. Each changes the decision.
authorGate.counterfactual: Keep rupture but replace the planning record with no usable proximal seal or iliac access: the offered emergency open approach becomes appropriate. Remove the wall defect/hematoma and make the case asymptomatic: an elective pathway becomes reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback teaches the role of CT, not the EVAR preference. The new scan changes both the diagnosis boundary and treatment selection.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed unsupported anatomy numbers and any claim that the game executes hospital repair. Retained an explicit limitation: the device suitability judgment is outside the scored objective and must be checked by clinical reviewers.

explanation.text: The wall defect and contiguous hematoma establish rupture. Preserved pressure does not make it elective. With documented suitable anatomy and treating-hospital expertise, the guideline favors emergency EVAR over open repair.

choices.label: Emergency endovascular aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The record demonstrates rupture and device-suitable anatomy; guideline recommendations favor EVAR in that setting.
choices.temptation: Recognizes containment as rupture rather than a reason to delay and uses the documented anatomic suitability.
choices.counterfactual: An unsuitable proximal seal or access anatomy could favor open repair instead.

choices.label: Emergency open aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: Open repair is a real alternative, but the guideline favors EVAR for the documented suitable anatomy.
choices.temptation: Treats rupture as an automatic indication for open exposure.
choices.counterfactual: Inability to achieve an endovascular seal or obtain access could make open repair the appropriate choice.

choices.label: Elective endovascular aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The wall defect and retroperitoneal hematoma establish rupture despite current preserved pressure.
choices.temptation: Misinterprets containment and stable circulation as an intact elective aneurysm.
choices.counterfactual: An intact asymptomatic qualifying aneurysm could undergo elective repair planning.

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: The CTA relationship is described without naming type A or assigning an author interpretation. The tear and flap extent deliberately conflict. Every option is a definitive hospital treatment plan; the medical plan's imaging component has timing metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Definitive plan after a completed acute aortic CTA; impulse control remains background stabilization for surgical patients.
reasoningSteps: Separate entry-tear location from ascending involvement in classification.
Apply the ascending extent to immediate operative management despite stable physiology.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: both the distal tear and normal pressure can wrongly steer an otherwise knowledgeable resident toward a type-B strategy.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The flap extends into the ascending aorta, not merely through the descending segment.
authorGate.closestError: Descending TEVAR directed at the entry tear as the complete treatment.
authorGate.consequence: Failure to treat the dangerous acute ascending segment.
authorGate.deletionTest: The distal tear creates the meaningful competing error; ascending extent changes the answer. Preserved perfusion keeps a separate contested malperfusion-first question out of this item.
authorGate.counterfactual: Confine the flap to the descending aorta and preserve the uncomplicated physiology: the offered medical plan becomes correct.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; no other dissection case's feedback is assumed visible. No new ICU setting, bedside treatment execution or live consultation is required.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed an initial pure Stanford-label task and made classification consequential to treatment. The explanation does not claim every distal tear with retrograde extension can be managed with one generic operation.

explanation.text: Ascending involvement determines the type-A pathway even when the entry tear is distal. Stable current pressure does not remove the need for emergency surgical treatment of acute ascending dissection.

choices.label: Emergency open ascending aortic repair
choices.rationale: Ascending involvement places this in the type-A pathway despite a descending entry tear.
choices.temptation: Classifies by the involved segment and applies its urgent surgical consequence.
choices.counterfactual: A flap confined distal to the left subclavian without complications would favor initial medical treatment.

choices.label: Urgent descending thoracic endovascular repair
choices.rationale: Treating the distal tear as a type-B problem does not address the acute ascending involvement.
choices.temptation: Classifies the dissection by the tear location alone.
choices.counterfactual: A complicated dissection confined to the descending aorta with suitable anatomy can favor TEVAR.

choices.label: Intravenous esmolol with CT angiographic follow-up
choices.rationale: Impulse control is background stabilization but not definitive treatment of acute ascending dissection.
choices.temptation: Uses normotension and absence of malperfusion to choose an uncomplicated type-B pathway.
choices.counterfactual: An uncomplicated dissection confined to the descending aorta initially receives medical therapy and monitoring.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.
decisionNodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?

answerChoices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.

answerChoices.label: Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
answerChoices.rationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.

answerChoices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.

decisionNodes.explanation: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.
decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
answerChoices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

answerChoices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
answerChoices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: No type-B or 'uncomplicated' label is visible. The key is not the only specific plan: all labels identify actual hospital treatments. Organ findings and beta-blocker safety checks are retained because they determine management and the named regimen, rather than merely decorating a high blood pressure.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Initial hospital treatment strategy for newly evaluated acute dissection.
reasoningSteps: Infer descending-only dissection without demonstrated organ compromise or rupture.
Choose monitored impulse therapy and appropriate infusion sequence rather than immediate repair.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: applying an all-dissection surgical reflex or calling an untreated first high pressure 'refractory' are credible errors. The named drug sequence is an additional treatment detail, not a separate scored question.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Descending confinement with preserved kidney enhancement, urine output and limb/abdominal examination before treatment.
authorGate.closestError: Urgent TEVAR for the first high-pressure reading.
authorGate.consequence: Premature invasive treatment or failure to institute appropriate impulse control.
authorGate.deletionTest: Extent and organ-perfusion observations determine the strategy. Conduction, bronchospasm and heart-failure checks earn their place because the key names a beta blocker. Numeric vitals are fictional observations, not new cutoffs.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace preserved renal perfusion with new oliguria, falling renal enhancement and true-lumen collapse despite treatment: urgent endovascular repair becomes the preferred offered strategy.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The explanation does not name the later kidney complication or its intervention. Later anatomy and response are not visible at admission.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: An initial pure infusion-order question was rejected as too narrow. The revised neutral treatment-plan task requires extent/perfusion interpretation before drug selection. No dose or numeric treatment target is added.

explanation.text: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated.

choices.label: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
choices.rationale: The observed extent and perfusion support initial medical treatment; rate/impulse control precedes added vasodilation.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes initial hypertension from persistent complications despite adequate treatment.
choices.counterfactual: New organ malperfusion despite treatment would change the need for intervention.

choices.label: Urgent thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
choices.rationale: The admission record has not demonstrated rupture, malperfusion or failure of medical treatment that would establish an immediate repair indication.
choices.temptation: Treats every acute dissection or first elevated pressure as complicated disease.
choices.counterfactual: A suitable type-B dissection with new organ malperfusion generally warrants intervention.

choices.label: Urgent open descending aortic graft replacement
choices.rationale: An open replacement is not the initial treatment for this uncomplicated descending presentation.
choices.temptation: Overextends the acute ascending-dissection operation rule to a different extent and physiology.
choices.counterfactual: Complicated disease unsuitable for endovascular treatment can require open reconstruction.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update supplies renal function, enhancement and true-lumen geometry without using 'complicated' or 'malperfusion.' All plans include their relevant reassessment scope; the key is not a uniquely complete combined plan.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Aortic treatment strategy after a documented new complication during medical therapy.
reasoningSteps: Integrate oliguria/creatinine change with new regional inflow and enhancement changes rather than assuming nonspecific renal injury.

authorGate.difficulty: Hard prediction: symptom and pressure improvement can falsely reassure, while contrast exposure can divert interpretation of the renal trajectory.
authorGate.decidingObservation: New renal dysfunction co-localized with true-lumen compression and weaker kidney enhancement despite achieved impulse control.
authorGate.closestError: Continue the prior infusions and observe renal function because pain and pressure improved.
authorGate.consequence: Prolonged renal ischemia despite a treatable inflow obstruction.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the regional CTA relationship makes nonspecific renal injury more credible; deleting the functional trajectory leaves an image without demonstrated organ consequence. Both are needed.
authorGate.counterfactual: If renal function, output and enhancement stayed preserved after treatment, continued monitored medical management would remain appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The admission explanation does not identify this organ complication or promise that TEVAR will solve all branch disease. This node's feedback states reassessment but not the next fixed branch intervention.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a bowel operation outside this scored lane and balanced reassessment across the operative options. TEVAR suitability is documented by the outside team; no exact device thresholds are fabricated.

authorGate.cueAttack: No static/dynamic diagnosis is supplied. The current response, branch anatomy and persistent gradient must be read together. All three choices are specific endovascular actions and have comparable length; none adds explanatory warnings.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Adjunctive endovascular treatment after a completed central repair, with ongoing documented organ inflow compromise.
reasoningSteps: Use central lumen expansion plus unchanged intrabranch narrowing to distinguish a residual fixed lesion from the earlier central mechanism.
Select the branch target rather than repeat central sealing or pressure equalization.
authorGate.difficulty: Hard: recognizing the initial mechanism does not establish the cause of the residual deficit; the current response must revise the anatomic target.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Central expansion and entry sealing coexist with fixed renal flap narrowing and persistent gradient.
authorGate.closestError: Distal septal fenestration for presumed continued dynamic obstruction.
authorGate.consequence: Additional intervention at the wrong target while renal ischemia persists.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the post-TEVAR response and the initial central strategy may still be appropriate. Delete the persistent functional/pressure defect and an incidental branch flap would not establish a need for treatment.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the branch were patent but central true-lumen collapse and cycling flap prolapse persisted, a pressure-equalizing fenestration could become reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The previous explanation warns to reassess without teaching that this specific branch is fixed or naming renal stenting. This node requires new response interpretation.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced an implausible dialysis-as-repair foil with a credible dynamic-obstruction procedure. Kept renal anatomy in the aortic-complication lane and left non-aortic AKI management unscored.

explanation.text: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

choices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
choices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.
choices.temptation: Localizes the residual obstruction after observing the central repair response.
choices.counterfactual: If branch flow recovered after central true-lumen expansion, an additional renal stent would not follow from these findings.

choices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
choices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.
choices.temptation: Carries forward the original dynamic-compression mechanism despite the documented response.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent dynamic aortic flap-related obstruction after entry treatment can merit fenestration.

choices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
choices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.
choices.temptation: Assumes every perfusion failure after TEVAR reflects inadequate central sealing.
choices.counterfactual: An incompletely sealed entry with persistent central compression could require graft revision.

authorGate.cueAttack: The CABG anatomy is necessary raw conduit information; the presentation does not state that bypass is required. The transposition foil is a real durable revascularization, while deferred rescue is a separate timing policy. The first label is not uniquely cautious or longer than the alternatives.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: LSA management strategy around an elective covering repair.
reasoningSteps: Trace the patent LIMA-to-LAD graft's dependence on the LSA with an occluded native LAD.
Choose pre-coverage inflow preservation that avoids the proximal clamp required for transposition, rather than waiting for arm symptoms.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a durable transposition is tempting until its clamp sequence is considered alongside the pedicled coronary conduit.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Patent LIMA-to-LAD graft with native LAD occlusion and planned LSA-origin coverage.
authorGate.closestError: Choose transposition without accounting for interruption of the pedicled LIMA during proximal clamping.
authorGate.consequence: Loss of coronary graft inflow during an otherwise elective procedure.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the CABG conduit or native LAD finding and the key's patient-specific urgency weakens. Elective timing distinguishes this from unavoidable emergency coverage.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the LIMA were a free graft arising from the aorta rather than a patent pedicled subclavian conduit, transposition could become a reasonable pre-coverage technique; the specific bypass-over-transposition constraint would be removed.
authorGate.sequenceReview: This explanation focuses on coronary supply and does not teach spinal-cord rescue. A later postoperative neurologic event is revealed only in the next record.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Rejected the initial low-value post-coverage assessment foil. Targeted STS guideline verification established the transposition-clamp issue; replaced the foil with pre-coverage transposition and re-solved the exact three strategies.

explanation.text: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.
choices.temptation: Follows the coronary conduit back to its inflow origin.
choices.counterfactual: If no LSA-dependent coronary or other critical inflow existed, timing and need could differ, particularly in an emergency.

choices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
choices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.
choices.temptation: Treats upper-extremity symptoms as the only meaningful consequence of LSA interruption.
choices.counterfactual: Selective delayed revascularization may fit some emergency coverings without critical LSA-dependent inflow.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.
choices.temptation: Chooses a durable LSA revascularization while overlooking its proximal clamp sequence.
choices.counterfactual: Without a patent pedicled LIMA or another clamp-dependent inflow, transposition can be a reasonable LSA revascularization technique.

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: The update contains no spinal diagnosis or target pressure. Warm pulses and preserved upper-body examination are necessary localization data, not blanket exclusions. All labels name an immediate medication/procedure pathway; no option says 'alone' or labels its own error.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Immediate postoperative rescue strategies after a new neurologic deficit.
reasoningSteps: Localize the deficit to spinal perfusion rather than limb inflow or a focal cerebral syndrome.
Reverse the low-perfusion state and consider intrathecal-pressure reduction rather than continuing the earlier impulse goal.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: the conflict between protecting an aortic repair from pressure and maintaining cord perfusion creates a consequential treatment-direction error.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Bilateral leg deficit after hypotension with warm pulsed feet and preserved face/arm function.
authorGate.closestError: Continue esmolol pressure reduction because the patient has an aortic repair.
authorGate.consequence: Worsening potentially reversible cord hypoperfusion.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the hypotensive trigger or localization findings and the rescue target is less defensible. Coagulation data inform drain safety; they do not guarantee that placement has no risk.
authorGate.counterfactual: Change the record to cold pulseless legs with confirmed aortoiliac occlusion: the offered limb-ischemia pathway becomes appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The prior LSA explanation concerns LIMA coronary supply and does not give this neurologic rescue plan. The actual postoperative trigger changes the decision.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a numeric MAP/CSF target because source protocols differ. The label activates a rescue pathway, with specialist drain safety assessment in feedback; this is not automatic drain placement or routine prophylactic drainage.

explanation.text: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.

choices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
choices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.
choices.temptation: Links bilateral motor findings with the hypotensive trigger and preserved limb inflow.
choices.counterfactual: A focal cerebral syndrome or arterial inflow loss would require a different rescue target.

choices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
choices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.
choices.temptation: Carries an acute aortic impulse-reduction plan into a phase where low pressure is the precipitating problem.
choices.counterfactual: An unrepaired hypertensive acute aortic syndrome without cord hypoperfusion supports impulse control.

choices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
choices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.
choices.temptation: Interprets leg weakness after endovascular repair as an access or limb-occlusion complication.
choices.counterfactual: Sudden cold pulseless legs with demonstrated aortoiliac occlusion could require this pathway.

decisionNodes.stem: Which aneurysm plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s right popliteal lesion?

answerChoices.label: Plan popliteal aneurysm exclusion and bypass
answerChoices.rationale: The thrombus and distal embolic findings make size-only observation inadequate despite a diameter below 20 mm.

answerChoices.label: Arrange annual popliteal duplex surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A diameter-only policy overlooks the repeated embolic complications documented here.

answerChoices.label: Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Medical suppression does not remove the aneurysmal thrombus source; the supported next strategy includes repair consideration.

decisionNodes.explanation: The relevant problem is distal embolization from a thrombus-containing PAA, not diameter alone. Repair is considered even below 20 mm when embolic complications are present; the exact operation still depends on operative assessment and conduit anatomy.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After outside popliteal exclusion and vein bypass, he develops progressive calf swelling and plantar numbness. Duplex shows a widely patent bypass and persistent flow within an enlarging excluded sac. The sac displaces the popliteal vein and tibial nerve. Venous duplex shows compression without thrombus.
decisionNodes.stem: Which procedure should have addressed {patientName}'s new postoperative problem?

answerChoices.label: Surgical decompression of the excluded aneurysm sac
answerChoices.rationale: The symptomatic enlarging sac is the compressive target even though bypass inflow and outflow remain patent.

answerChoices.label: Revision of the popliteal bypass graft
answerChoices.rationale: The bypass is patent; revising it does not remove the compressive sac.

answerChoices.label: Embolization of residual genicular branch inflow
answerChoices.rationale: Inflows can contribute to sac persistence, but the demonstrated symptomatic compression calls for decompression of the enlarged sac.

decisionNodes.explanation: A patent bypass does not remove an enlarging excluded sac. When that sac causes neural or venous compression, surgical decompression addresses the current problem rather than revising a patent conduit.
sourceLabels: Alik Farber et al. (2022). SVS clinical practice guidelines on popliteal artery aneurysms.

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: The presentation gives symptoms, distal occlusions and aneurysmal thrombus rather than calling the lesion symptomatic or high-risk. All options are vascular management plans. The key is shorter than the two surveillance labels; every testing plan has duplex metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Nonemergent source management of a PAA with embolic findings, not acute threatened-limb salvage.
reasoningSteps: Connect digital occlusions and episodic blue toes with the mural-thrombus source despite palpable foot pulses.
Override an asymptomatic diameter-only surveillance rule and plan source repair.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a remembered 20-mm threshold and normal pedal pulses both invite reassurance despite distal embolization.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Repeated distal embolic findings linked to thrombus in the 18-mm popliteal lesion.
authorGate.closestError: Annual surveillance because the diameter is below the usual asymptomatic repair threshold.
authorGate.consequence: Continued distal embolization and possible limb injury.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without digital findings the small lesion could be observed; without the mural-thrombus source an alternative embolic workup would be needed. Normal strength/sensation keeps acute limb-threat treatment out of scope.
authorGate.counterfactual: Remove thrombus and embolic symptoms while keeping a small stable PAA: annual surveillance becomes reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The next node concerns a new record's survey coverage, not another repair threshold. No contralateral screening answer appears in this feedback.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Changed a simple size-threshold recall draft into an embolic-complication decision. The key states a repair plan, not a claim that open bypass is invariably superior; the exact conduit/procedure is a clinical-review boundary.

explanation.text: The relevant problem is distal embolization from a thrombus-containing PAA, not diameter alone. Repair is considered even below 20 mm when embolic complications are present; the exact operation still depends on operative assessment and conduit anatomy.

choices.label: Plan popliteal aneurysm exclusion and bypass
choices.rationale: The thrombus and distal embolic findings make size-only observation inadequate despite a diameter below 20 mm.
choices.temptation: Recognizes the symptomatic source while preserving the distinction from a threatened limb emergency.
choices.counterfactual: A small asymptomatic lesion without thrombus or poor runoff could remain under surveillance.

choices.label: Arrange annual popliteal duplex surveillance
choices.rationale: A diameter-only policy overlooks the repeated embolic complications documented here.
choices.temptation: Applies the usual asymptomatic small-PAA pathway to a symptomatic source.
choices.counterfactual: A small asymptomatic PAA without thrombus or embolic findings can be monitored.

choices.label: Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up
choices.rationale: Medical suppression does not remove the aneurysmal thrombus source; the supported next strategy includes repair consideration.
choices.temptation: Treats the embolic event without addressing its persistent source.
choices.counterfactual: A patient in whom repair must be deferred for prohibitive risk may require an interim specialist-directed medical plan.

Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up

reviewRound1Drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: No sentence says 'the left side was not done.' Acquisition labels and the available original studies establish coverage. Each choice is a named arterial imaging study with a wait profile, and the key has no uniquely comprehensive bundle.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Complete associated-aneurysm imaging after reviewing existing acquisitions.
reasoningSteps: Identify the relevant associated aneurysm territories for a PAA.
Subtract the adequately imaged territory and choose the remaining targeted study.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: rote recall of an AAA association can lead to duplicate abdominal imaging rather than actual survey completion.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A complete abdominal CTA paired with a unilateral right-leg arterial acquisition.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat abdominal ultrasound after recalling the AAA association.
authorGate.consequence: Duplicate testing while leaving the contralateral aneurysm site unassessed.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the acquisition record and both aortic and opposite-leg screening could be needed; the update determines which single study completes the current workup.
authorGate.counterfactual: Provide adequate bilateral popliteal imaging but only a pelvis-only CT: abdominal aortic ultrasound becomes the appropriate additional survey study.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first feedback concerns embolic repair below a diameter boundary; it does not teach associated-site screening. The new acquisition record is necessary to select one study.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a one-step 'what is associated with PAA' question with survey-completeness reasoning. A missing exported image is not equated with an unperformed acquisition; original acquisition records are explicitly available.

explanation.text: PAA prompts an opposite-leg and abdominal-aortic aneurysm survey. Review what was actually acquired: a complete abdominal CTA already evaluates the aorta, but a right-leg-only duplex does not evaluate the left popliteal artery.

choices.label: Left popliteal arterial duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: The abdominal aorta has been assessed, while the associated contralateral popliteal site is outside the documented unilateral acquisition.
choices.temptation: Combines the PAA association with the actual tested territory.
choices.counterfactual: If the left popliteal artery were already imaged adequately and the aorta were not, an abdominal aortic study would be appropriate.

choices.label: Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: The complete adequate abdominal CTA already addresses the aortic component of the associated-aneurysm survey.
choices.temptation: Recalls the AAA association but ignores the existing acquisition's scope.
choices.counterfactual: An incomplete abdominal assessment would support a dedicated aortic study.

choices.label: Thoracic aortic CT angiography
choices.rationale: The specific routinely recommended associated sites are the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta, not a substitute thoracic survey.
choices.temptation: Generalizes aneurysm association into an unrestricted whole-arterial imaging search.
choices.counterfactual: An independent thoracic aneurysm or heritable-aortopathy indication could justify thoracic imaging.

Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
Thoracic aortic CT angiography

authorGate.cueAttack: Raw duplex geometry links sac, vein and nerve without labeling a compression syndrome. The options are three actual procedures of comparable scope; the key is not a combined diagnosis-plus-treatment label.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Procedure for a new post-exclusion sac complication with known graft patency.
reasoningSteps: Localize the new swelling/numbness to the expanding sac rather than venous thrombus or bypass occlusion.
Select decompression for symptomatic mass effect instead of treating patency or inflow alone.
authorGate.difficulty: Hard prediction: a resident may stop at the successful bypass result or regard residual flow as a purely embolization problem.
authorGate.decidingObservation: An enlarging sac visibly displaces vein and nerve while the bypass is patent and the vein has no thrombus.
authorGate.closestError: Genicular inflow embolization as the entire treatment for the current compressive symptoms.
authorGate.consequence: Persisting venous/neurologic compression despite attention to blood flow.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without symptomatic displacement, sac-flow management could differ. Without demonstrated bypass patency, graft revision would remain a genuine contender.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the patent bypass with a flow-limiting graft lesion and remove mass effect: bypass revision becomes the appropriate offered procedure.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Earlier PAA feedback does not teach that exclusion may leave a symptomatic mass. This new postoperative anatomy creates a distinct decision.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a venous thrombolysis foil that was already ruled out by the duplex. The remaining embolization comparator is clinically plausible; the exact preference for decompression is supported by SVS recommendation 6 and needs clinician confirmation for this version.

explanation.text: A patent bypass does not remove an enlarging excluded sac. When that sac causes neural or venous compression, surgical decompression addresses the current problem rather than revising a patent conduit.

choices.label: Surgical decompression of the excluded aneurysm sac
choices.rationale: The symptomatic enlarging sac is the compressive target even though bypass inflow and outflow remain patent.
choices.temptation: Separates revascularization success from continued local aneurysm effects.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic stable excluded sac would not establish a decompression indication.

choices.label: Revision of the popliteal bypass graft
choices.rationale: The bypass is patent; revising it does not remove the compressive sac.
choices.temptation: Treats new postoperative limb symptoms as graft failure.
choices.counterfactual: A demonstrated flow-limiting graft stenosis or occlusion could require revision.

choices.label: Embolization of residual genicular branch inflow
choices.rationale: Inflows can contribute to sac persistence, but the demonstrated symptomatic compression calls for decompression of the enlarged sac.
choices.temptation: Focuses on recurrent sac flow while overlooking the current compressive effect.
choices.counterfactual: Residual flow without symptomatic mass effect can prompt assessment of an inflow-directed strategy.

authorGate.cueAttack: The context never labels graft infection or fistula. The endoscopy's actual examined territory is specified rather than saying 'all tests negative.' Every option is a named bleeding/graft investigation with complete wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Next diagnostic investigation after a completed unrevealing proximal endoscopy in a stable hospital assessment.
reasoningSteps: Integrate graft history, infection and bleeding as a possible linked vascular complication.
Choose cross-sectional graft-interface evaluation rather than re-examining the same mucosal territory or only localizing bleeding.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: melena invites a standard luminal workup, while intermittent stability and an unrevealing endoscopy can falsely reassure.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Unexplained infection and bleeding months after aortic grafting, with only proximal mucosa examined.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat the same upper-endoscopic territory to explain the melena.
authorGate.consequence: Delayed recognition of a dangerous graft-related infection or bowel communication.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the graft/culture history this could be an ordinary obscure-bleeding workup. Precise endoscopic scope preserves provenance; no hidden fourth-duodenal examination is assumed.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the prior endoscopy instead showed a recurrent treatable proximal ulcer with no graft-related infection concern, repeat endoscopy would become reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation indicates the diagnostic target but does not choose a source-control operation. Definitive graft findings appear only next.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a generic 'urgent review' key and used actual investigations. The CTA preference is a targeted application of a single checked guideline; it is flagged for exact clinical review rather than claiming that every intermittent GI bleed must have this scan.

explanation.text: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal.

choices.label: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
choices.rationale: The graft history plus infection and bleeding warrants cross-sectional assessment of the reconstructed aorta and its bowel interface.
choices.temptation: Does not treat a negative proximal endoscopy as exclusion of a graft complication.
choices.counterfactual: A directly demonstrated ordinary mucosal bleeding lesion without graft-related findings could redirect the workup.

choices.label: Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
choices.rationale: Repeating the same examined mucosal territory does not evaluate the prosthetic graft or its extraluminal interface.
choices.temptation: Anchors on melena as necessarily a lesion within the already examined lumen.
choices.counterfactual: Recurrent bleeding from a known treatable proximal mucosal lesion could warrant repeat endoscopy.

choices.label: Tagged-red-cell scintigraphy for gastrointestinal bleeding
choices.rationale: Bleed localization does not assess the graft infection concern raised by the combined history and cultures.
choices.temptation: Seeks the intermittent bleeding site while treating bacteremia as an unrelated problem.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent intermittent bleeding after graft pathology has been excluded may need a separate bleeding-localization strategy.
