authorGate.cueAttack: All options are concrete source-control strategies and have comparable scope. Operative physiology and functional context are necessary ranking information; no vague individualized-care option carries the key.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Definitive source-control strategy after diagnostic confirmation, with antimicrobials common background care.
reasoningSteps: Recognize persistent prosthesis/bowel infection despite directed treatment rather than an isolated bloodstream episode.
Use current operative suitability to choose removal/reconstruction over bridging or suppression.
authorGate.difficulty: Hard: rapid endovascular control and antibiotic response can be mistaken for definitive treatment of an infected prosthesis.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A communicating perigraft collection, persistent same-organism cultures and no prohibitive operative condition.
authorGate.closestError: Covered relining as definitive treatment because it may arrest bleeding.
authorGate.consequence: Persistent infected material and bowel contamination.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without operative suitability, suppression or endovascular treatment may become defensible; without the persistent source, an immediate major reconstruction would not be established.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace stable operability with uncontrolled hemorrhage and shock: covered relining as a bridge may become appropriate. Replace it with prohibitive permanent operative risk: suppression may be considered.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding answer does not supply the operation, and new anatomy/culture response determines this stage. The clinic reviews a hospital operation plan rather than performing it.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Did not rank in-situ against extra-anatomic reconstruction or invent an antibiotic duration. Both belong to specialist/clinician decisions beyond the scored source-control objective.

explanation.text: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

choices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes definitive source control from bridging or suppression.
choices.counterfactual: Prohibitive operative risk could change the balance toward nonoperative suppression or a limited strategy.

choices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
choices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.
choices.temptation: Uses rapid bleeding control as though it establishes durable infection source control.
choices.counterfactual: Uncontrolled hemorrhage in an unstable patient can make an endovascular bridge reasonable.

choices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
choices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Equates a temporary physiologic response to antibiotics with eradication of an infected prosthesis.
choices.counterfactual: A patient who cannot tolerate reconstruction may need a suppression-based strategy after specialist review.

authorGate.cueAttack: The known genetic diagnosis is a legitimate prerequisite for this management objective; no approach is named as preferred in the presentation. All options are specific thoracoabdominal reconstructions of comparable scope, not an operation versus an obviously premature scan.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Definitive repair approach after the need for repair is established.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that native aortic sealing regions in heritable tissue disease differ from the degenerative anatomy commonly used for endovascular repair.
Apply that durability boundary and current operability to the approach preference.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: technical feasibility and lower initial invasiveness make branched repair credible, and hybrid debranching may appear to remove the endograft durability issue.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Confirmed Marfan syndrome with native sealing regions and no prohibitive open risk.
authorGate.closestError: Branched endovascular repair because both procedures are technically feasible.
authorGate.consequence: Extending a degenerative-aneurysm procedural preference without accounting for the heritable substrate.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the genetic/native-aorta findings, the preference is not established. Fitness and an already accepted repair indication prevent this becoming an unsupported size-threshold or surveillance question.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace Marfan with a degenerative aneurysm and substantially elevated open operative risk: branched endovascular repair becomes a reasonable preferred alternative after aortic-team assessment.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone exact context. No root/ascending threshold, prophylactic family surgery or traumatic injury objective is imported.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed an unverified exact diameter and a surveillance foil. Kept three actual reconstructions. The newer ESVS 2026 PDF was inaccessible; this single-guideline preference requires exact clinician review rather than claiming exhaustive current agreement.

explanation.text: For an intact TAAA requiring repair in Marfan syndrome, the checked multisociety guideline favors open repair. Native-aortic tissue disease and long-term durability matter even when branched or hybrid reconstruction is technically possible.

choices.label: Open thoracoabdominal graft replacement
choices.rationale: Heritable native-aorta disease in an operable patient favors open reconstruction when repair is required.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes the tissue disease from an ordinary degenerative aneurysm.
choices.counterfactual: Severe operative prohibitions or emergency bridging needs can change the balance.

choices.label: Branched endovascular thoracoabdominal repair
choices.rationale: Technical feasibility does not erase the guideline preference for open repair in this heritable native-aorta setting.
choices.temptation: Generalizes the lower initial invasiveness of endovascular repair to all aneurysm substrates.
choices.counterfactual: An appropriate degenerative TAAA patient with higher open risk may be considered for branched repair.

choices.label: Visceral debranching with thoracic endografting
choices.rationale: A hybrid operation still relies on endograft sealing in the diseased native aorta rather than providing the preferred open reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Assumes adding open visceral bypasses resolves the native-seal concern.
choices.counterfactual: Selected patients unsuitable for conventional open repair can require alternative hybrid strategies.

authorGate.cueAttack: The context does not use pseudoaneurysm or announce a rupture risk. All options are specific lesion-management plans. The correct label specifies assessment because exact embolization technique depends on vascular anatomy; both imaging alternatives receive equal CT wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Whether to proceed toward treatment or imaging surveillance after a defined new visceral arterial lesion.
reasoningSteps: Infer an acquired contained wall disruption rather than a chronic small true aneurysm from serial anatomy and the inflammatory setting.
Apply the pseudoaneurysm treatment boundary rather than a true-aneurysm diameter rule.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: the small size and lack of active bleeding are credible reasons to delay if the lesion mechanism is misclassified. The two imaging plans represent different delay rationales; independent review must confirm their discriminating value.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A new extra-organ cavity connected through a focal arterial wall defect after pancreatitis.
authorGate.closestError: Annual size surveillance after applying a small true-aneurysm rule.
authorGate.consequence: Leaving an acquired wall defect at risk while waiting for size growth.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the wall/serial findings, the mechanism and prompt-treatment boundary are not established. Extra-organ location excludes the cited narrow intraparenchymal observation exception; small size and stability deliberately test the competing rule.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the lesion with a small contained intraparenchymal defect selected by specialists for strict observation: interval imaging can become appropriate. A stable small true aneurysm would require a separate policy decision, not this pseudoaneurysm rule.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; pancreatitis treatment is background. No drain, pancreatic operation or new acute-care runtime setting is proposed.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Kept the specific embolization assessment rather than claiming a universal embolization technique. True splenic/renal aneurysm size thresholds are withheld because CIRSE and SVS differ. This item does not choose between those thresholds.

explanation.text: A newly acquired cavity communicating through an arterial wall defect after pancreatitis supports a pseudoaneurysm mechanism. Its extra-organ location and wall disruption favor prompt vascular treatment assessment, despite small diameter and current stability.

choices.label: Prompt splenic-artery embolization assessment
choices.rationale: A new extra-organ contained leak through a wall defect is not governed by small true-aneurysm surveillance thresholds.
choices.temptation: Integrates the acquired wall defect and inflammatory setting with the rupture-risk management boundary.
choices.counterfactual: A small stable true aneurysm without symptoms can require a different surveillance decision.

choices.label: CT angiographic surveillance after inflammation resolves
choices.rationale: Waiting for inflammatory resolution leaves the demonstrated arterial wall defect unaddressed.
choices.temptation: Treats the cavity as a transient inflammatory change that can be reassessed with the collection.
choices.counterfactual: Selected small intraparenchymal pseudoaneurysms may be observed only under strict specialist follow-up; this is not that anatomy.

choices.label: Annual CT angiographic surveillance of lesion size
choices.rationale: A diameter-only true-aneurysm policy does not apply to an acquired extra-organ wall disruption.
choices.temptation: Lets the small 12-mm diameter override the lesion's mechanism.
choices.counterfactual: A stable small true visceral aneurysm in an appropriate patient may be surveilled after specialist assessment.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later CTA measures the sac at 7.0 cm using the same method. Contrast appears near a graft-limb junction and a lumbar branch, but metal artifact prevents tracing its origin despite arterial and delayed acquisitions. He remains hemodynamically stable without pain.
decisionNodes.stem: Which angiographic assessment should precede targeted leak treatment for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Aortography across the seal zones and graft junctions
answerChoices.rationale: The enlarging sac and uncertain source require reassessment for direct graft or attachment inflow before targeting a branch.

answerChoices.label: Selective mesenteric-to-inferior-mesenteric collateral angiography
answerChoices.rationale: This maps a branch route but does not resolve the possible attachment or component defect producing the current sac growth.

answerChoices.label: Selective iliolumbar-to-lumbar collateral angiography
answerChoices.rationale: The lumbar branch near the contrast focus does not establish that it is the only source.

decisionNodes.explanation: Do not carry forward a branch-leak label when a growing sac has an uncertain current inflow source. Problem-solving aortography can assess the attachments and modular junctions before choosing a branch-directed treatment.
sourceLabels: Joo-Young Chun et al. (2024). CIRSE Standards of Practice on Management of Endoleaks Following Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Aortography shows contrast passing through a gap between the main body and right iliac limb into the sac during the arterial phase. Both attachment sites remain sealed. Adequate overlap can be obtained between the existing components with an additional covered limb.
decisionNodes.stem: Which endovascular repair should have been selected for {patientName}'s demonstrated defect?

answerChoices.label: Bridge the separated components with a covered graft
answerChoices.rationale: The source is the modular gap; a bridging covered component restores continuity.

answerChoices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
answerChoices.rationale: Branch embolization does not close the direct connection through the separated graft components.

answerChoices.label: Extend the proximal attachment with an aortic cuff
answerChoices.rationale: The proximal seal is intact; extending it does not cover the limb junction gap.

decisionNodes.explanation: The direct component gap is a type III mechanism and requires prompt repair. A covered bridge across the separation closes the source; branch embolization or a remote proximal extension would not.

answerChoices.rationale: Ascending involvement places this in the type-A pathway despite a descending entry tear.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial hospital treatment plan should have been selected for {patientName} at that assessment?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
answerChoices.rationale: The observed extent and perfusion support initial medical treatment; rate/impulse control precedes added vasodilation.

answerChoices.label: Urgent thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
answerChoices.rationale: The admission record has not demonstrated rupture, malperfusion or failure of medical treatment that would establish an immediate repair indication.

answerChoices.label: Urgent open descending aortic graft replacement
answerChoices.rationale: An open replacement is not the initial treatment for this uncomplicated descending presentation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.
decisionNodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?

answerChoices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.

answerChoices.label: Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
answerChoices.rationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.

answerChoices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.

decisionNodes.explanation: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.
sourceLabels: Eric M. Isselbacher et al. (2022). 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.
decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
answerChoices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

answerChoices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
answerChoices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.
decisionNodes.stem: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?

answerChoices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.

answerChoices.label: Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
answerChoices.rationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.

answerChoices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.

decisionNodes.explanation: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.
sourceLabels: Eric M. Isselbacher et al. (2022). 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

Thomas E. MacGillivray et al. (2022). STS/AATS Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Type B Aortic Dissection.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.
decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
answerChoices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

answerChoices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
answerChoices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.
sourceLabels: Yuri Gupta et al. (2026). CIRSE Standards of Practice on the Endovascular Management of Descending Thoracic Aortic Disease.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, visits clinic to review an outside elective descending thoracic aneurysm repair. decisionNodes.stem: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
answerChoices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.

answerChoices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
answerChoices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
answerChoices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.

decisionNodes.explanation: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The later outside ICU record describes new bilateral leg weakness after a hypotensive episode following long-segment TEVAR. Both feet remain warm with palpable pulses. Speech, face and arm movement are unchanged. Platelet count and coagulation studies are normal, and no neuraxial drain is present.
decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?

answerChoices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
answerChoices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
answerChoices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.

answerChoices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.

decisionNodes.explanation: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.
sourceLabels: Eric M. Isselbacher et al. (2022). 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should have followed {patientName}'s unrevealing upper endoscopy during that admission?

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
answerChoices.rationale: The graft history plus infection and bleeding warrants cross-sectional assessment of the reconstructed aorta and its bowel interface.

answerChoices.label: Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the same examined mucosal territory does not evaluate the prosthetic graft or its extraluminal interface.

answerChoices.label: Tagged-red-cell scintigraphy for gastrointestinal bleeding
answerChoices.rationale: Bleed localization does not assess the graft infection concern raised by the combined history and cultures.

decisionNodes.explanation: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal.
sourceLabels: Eric M. Isselbacher et al. (2022). 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CTA demonstrates a perigraft fluid-and-gas collection with a channel to adjacent duodenum. The same organism persists in repeated blood cultures despite directed intravenous antibiotics. He has preserved pressure and organ function, remains functionally independent, and the multidisciplinary hospital assessment finds no prohibitive operative condition.
decisionNodes.stem: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?

answerChoices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.

answerChoices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
answerChoices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.

answerChoices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.
sourceLabels: Eric M. Isselbacher et al. (2022). 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.
Yuri Gupta et al. (2026). CIRSE Standards of Practice on the Endovascular Management of Descending Thoracic Aortic Disease.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use total dissection extent rather than entry-tear location to identify the need for emergency ascending repair.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A distal entry tear can distract from acute ascending involvement; the resulting operative pathway is consequential.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Failure to treat the dangerous acute ascending segment.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old woman, visits clinic after hospitalization for abrupt chest and back pain. The founder reviews her initial CTA: the entry tear lies distal to the left subclavian artery, but the flap extends backward through the arch into the ascending aorta. At that assessment she was alert and normotensive, without abdominal pain or limb deficits.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which definitive hospital plan should have been selected from {patientName}'s initial CTA?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Descending TEVAR directed at the entry tear as the complete treatment.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The flap extends into the ascending aorta, not merely through the descending segment.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Confine the flap to the descending aorta and preserve the uncomplicated physiology: the offered medical plan becomes correct.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose urgent cross-sectional planning in a stable suspected rupture without misusing a repeat size-only study.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Detection, physiology and repair planning must be separated in a time-critical aneurysm problem.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Failing to define the repair anatomy or contained hemorrhage needed for the definitive strategy.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 73-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for abrupt abdominal and back pain. At the recorded initial assessment, bedside ultrasound showed a 7-cm infrarenal AAA. He remained alert with systolic pressures between 108 and 116 mm Hg over repeated assessments. The hospital aortic team was preparing definitive treatment.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which imaging study should have been selected at {patientName}'s recorded stable assessment?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Repeat duplex because it already identified the AAA and avoids contrast.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Preserved serial circulation after a large aneurysm is demonstrated in a painful presentation.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the painful admission with an asymptomatic small-AAA surveillance visit: duplex becomes the best offered study. Refractory shock would invalidate the entire stable-imaging task and require immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Integrate contained rupture and documented device-compatible anatomy to select an emergency repair approach.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Contained rupture and suitable anatomy test two competing errors: elective delay and automatic open repair.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Choosing a less-favored approach for this supported anatomy, or dangerously delaying repair if containment is mistaken for an intact aneurysm.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 73-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for abrupt abdominal and back pain. At the recorded initial assessment, bedside ultrasound showed a 7-cm infrarenal AAA. He remained alert with systolic pressures between 108 and 116 mm Hg over repeated assessments. The hospital aortic team was preparing definitive treatment.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: CTA shows retroperitoneal hematoma continuous with a posterior aortic-wall defect. The infrarenal neck is parallel-sided, the iliac access vessels are patent, and the vascular planning record confirms the selected graft's instructions-for-use requirements are satisfied. He remains alert with unchanged pressure. The treating hospital performs both open and endovascular aortic repair.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which definitive repair approach should have been selected for {patientName} at that point?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Emergency open repair regardless of suitable endovascular anatomy.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A wall defect with contiguous retroperitoneal blood plus verified graft suitability.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Keep rupture but replace the planning record with no usable proximal seal or iliac access: the offered emergency open approach becomes appropriate. Remove the wall defect/hematoma and make the case asymptomatic: an elective pathway becomes reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize new dissection-related renal malperfusion despite achieved impulse control and escalate to repair.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Treatment response can improve one target while organ perfusion deteriorates.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Prolonged organ ischemia.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: After monitored infusion treatment, his heart rate and pressure fall and chest pain improves. Urine output then drops and creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. Repeat CTA shows a compressed aortic true lumen at the renal origins and much weaker left renal enhancement. There is no rupture. The treating aortic team documents usable proximal sealing and iliac access anatomy for TEVAR.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aortic plan should have been selected after {patientName}'s new renal findings?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Continue the prior infusions and observe renal function because pain and pressure improved.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: New renal dysfunction co-localized with true-lumen compression and weaker kidney enhancement despite achieved impulse control.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If renal function, output and enhancement stayed preserved after treatment, continued monitored medical management would remain appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Distinguish persistent static branch obstruction from resolved central dynamic compression to choose the next endovascular target.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: An apparently successful central repair can leave a distinct fixed branch lesion requiring another target.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Additional intervention at the wrong target while renal ischemia persists.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: After TEVAR, angiography shows the thoracic entry sealed and the central true lumen expanded. Left renal inflow remains narrow: the flap extends into the renal artery and the narrowed branch segment does not change during the cardiac cycle. A persistent pressure gradient across that segment accompanies weak renal enhancement.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Distal septal fenestration for presumed continued dynamic obstruction.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Central expansion and entry sealing coexist with fixed renal flap narrowing and persistent gradient.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the branch were patent but central true-lumen collapse and cycling flap prolapse persisted, a pressure-equalizing fenestration could become reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize when new attributable symptoms override the prior small-AAA surveillance plan.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A change in symptoms can overturn a previously correct diameter-based plan.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Delay in evaluating an aneurysm that may be clinically unstable despite an intact image.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, comes to clinic to review serial outside aortic studies. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the surveillance visit. The prior CTA measured 4.6 cm perpendicular to the aortic centerline; the new report lists 5.3 cm on an axial image across a curved segment. Both original CT datasets are available.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: A later outside admission documents persistent new deep abdominal and back pain, focal tenderness over the aorta and no relation to movement. CTA shows a 4.9-cm intact fusiform AAA; the hospital evaluation identifies no competing abdominal or spinal cause. He is normotensive and otherwise fit for repair.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which hospital aortic plan should have replaced surveillance for {patientName} during that admission?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Annual surveillance based on the earlier 4.7-cm classification.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A new persistent localized pain syndrome without another identified cause, rather than size change alone.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the pain were reproducible with movement and a separate spinal cause were established, size-based outpatient surveillance could again be appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize a direct attachment leak and repair the seal despite stable current sac size.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A dangerous direct-pressure leak should not inherit stable-sac observation rules.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Leaving a direct-pressure leak untreated.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 74-year-old woman, attends clinic to review a later outside CTA after EVAR. The sac diameter is unchanged, but contrast passes directly between the proximal graft edge and native aortic wall during the arterial phase. Modular junctions remain continuous. A healthy neck segment remains between the graft edge and the renal arteries.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s proximal attachment finding?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Surveillance because the sac has not enlarged.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Direct flow at the proximal attachment with an available healthy neck segment.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If contrast arrived through lumbar branches on delayed images with intact seals and a stable sac, continued surveillance would become correct.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use direct junctional flow and component separation to choose a repair that closes the actual graft defect.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Correct leak recognition must lead to repair at the actual failed graft segment.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: An unclosed sac-pressure source with continuing rupture risk.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: Aortography shows contrast passing through a gap between the main body and right iliac limb into the sac during the arterial phase. Both attachment sites remain sealed. Adequate overlap can be obtained between the existing components with an additional covered limb.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which endovascular repair should have been selected for {patientName}'s demonstrated defect?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Proximal cuff extension after correctly recognizing a high-pressure leak.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Flow traverses the main-body/limb gap, with intact seals and a feasible bridging overlap.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the junction gap with direct inflow at the proximal attachment and an available healthy landing segment: proximal cuff extension becomes appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Reassess an old leak attribution when sac growth and current imaging no longer establish the source.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: An old leak attribution can become unreliable when the sac trajectory changes.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Missing a direct-pressure leak and treating the wrong pathway.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: A later CTA measures the sac at 7.0 cm using the same method. Contrast appears near a graft-limb junction and a lumbar branch, but metal artifact prevents tracing its origin despite arterial and delayed acquisitions. He remains hemodynamically stable without pain.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which angiographic assessment should precede targeted leak treatment for {patientName} now?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Targeted lumbar angiography as if the original attribution were still established.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Large interval sac expansion plus artifact-limited origin near a graft junction despite an adequate multiphase acquisition.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If multiphase imaging conclusively established isolated lumbar inflow with no attachment or junction defect, selective iliolumbar mapping would become reasonable for treatment planning.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Combine branch-flow origin and sac trajectory to avoid unnecessary treatment of an isolated stable type II endoleak.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Avoid treating every persistent post-EVAR contrast focus when the source and trajectory favor observation.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Unnecessary intervention while teaching a mechanism-insensitive rule.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old man, comes to clinic to review outside follow-up after infrarenal EVAR. He has no abdominal or back pain. The first surveillance CTA shows delayed posterior sac filling continuous with lumbar branches; the proximal and distal attachments and modular overlaps are intact.

exhibit.caption: Constructed outside-record measurements; not a reproduced clinical image

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s later surveillance study?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Lumbar/sac embolization for a persistent but stable leak.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Lumbar continuity with identical full sac diameters and intact attachments/overlaps.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace branch filling with direct proximal attachment inflow: prompt seal treatment replaces surveillance even if size has not yet grown.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Recognize an unaddressed graft-related source when bleeding and infection coexist after aortic reconstruction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Aortic graft history changes the interpretation of otherwise familiar gastrointestinal bleeding and infection.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Delayed recognition of a dangerous graft-related infection or bowel communication.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 75-year-old man, comes to clinic after hospitalization several months after open infrarenal AAA grafting. His outside record describes fever, recurrent positive blood cultures and intermittent melena. Upper endoscopy examined the esophagus, stomach and first two duodenal portions without finding a bleeding source. He was alert with preserved pressure between bleeding episodes.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which investigation should have followed {patientName}'s unrevealing upper endoscopy during that admission?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Repeat the same upper-endoscopic territory to explain the melena.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Unexplained infection and bleeding months after aortic grafting, with only proximal mucosa examined.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the prior endoscopy instead showed a recurrent treatable proximal ulcer with no graft-related infection concern, repeat endoscopy would become reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose definitive source control for an infected aortic prosthesis in a patient who can undergo reconstruction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Definitive infection source control differs from hemostatic bridging or suppression.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Persistent infected material and bowel contamination.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 75-year-old man, comes to clinic after hospitalization several months after open infrarenal AAA grafting. His outside record describes fever, recurrent positive blood cultures and intermittent melena. Upper endoscopy examined the esophagus, stomach and first two duodenal portions without finding a bleeding source. He was alert with preserved pressure between bleeding episodes.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: CTA demonstrates a perigraft fluid-and-gas collection with a channel to adjacent duodenum. The same organism persists in repeated blood cultures despite directed intravenous antibiotics. He has preserved pressure and organ function, remains functionally independent, and the multidisciplinary hospital assessment finds no prohibitive operative condition.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Covered relining as definitive treatment because it may arrest bleeding.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A communicating perigraft collection, persistent same-organism cultures and no prohibitive operative condition.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace stable operability with uncontrolled hemorrhage and shock: covered relining as a bridge may become appropriate. Replace it with prohibitive permanent operative risk: suppression may be considered.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Localize a new post-TEVAR neurologic deficit and reverse impaired spinal perfusion rather than extending pressure reduction.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: The required direction of pressure treatment changes when postoperative cord perfusion is threatened.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Worsening potentially reversible cord hypoperfusion.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, visits clinic to review an outside elective descending thoracic aneurysm repair. The planned proximal sealing segment spans the left subclavian origin. His CABG record shows a patent pedicled left internal mammary graft arising from the left subclavian artery to the LAD; the native LAD is chronically occluded. Both carotid arteries are patent.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The later outside ICU record describes new bilateral leg weakness after a hypotensive episode following long-segment TEVAR. Both feet remain warm with palpable pulses. Speech, face and arm movement are unchanged. Platelet count and coagulation studies are normal, and no neuraxial drain is present.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Continue esmolol pressure reduction because the patient has an aortic repair.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Bilateral leg deficit after hypotension with warm pulsed feet and preserved face/arm function.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Change the record to cold pulseless legs with confirmed aortoiliac occlusion: the offered limb-ischemia pathway becomes appropriate.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Trace LSA-dependent coronary inflow and preserve it before an elective covering graft.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Conduit origin and clamp sequence make a familiar revascularization technique hazardous in a specific patient.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Loss of coronary graft inflow during an otherwise elective procedure.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, visits clinic to review an outside elective descending thoracic aneurysm repair. The planned proximal sealing segment spans the left subclavian origin. His CABG record shows a patent pedicled left internal mammary graft arising from the left subclavian artery to the LAD; the native LAD is chronically occluded. Both carotid arteries are patent.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Choose transposition without accounting for interruption of the pedicled LIMA during proximal clamping.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Patent LIMA-to-LAD graft with native LAD occlusion and planned LSA-origin coverage.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the LIMA were a free graft arising from the aorta rather than a patent pedicled subclavian conduit, transposition could become a reasonable pre-coverage technique; the specific bypass-over-transposition constraint would be removed.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use embolic complications rather than diameter alone to choose repair evaluation for a small PAA.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Complications override a memorized asymptomatic diameter rule.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Continued distal embolization and possible limb injury.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aneurysm plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s right popliteal lesion?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Annual surveillance because the diameter is below the usual asymptomatic repair threshold.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Repeated distal embolic findings linked to thrombus in the 18-mm popliteal lesion.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Remove thrombus and embolic symptoms while keeping a small stable PAA: annual surveillance becomes reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Identify symptomatic sac compression after successful exclusion/bypass rather than treating graft patency as resolution of the entire lesion.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Conduit patency does not establish that an excluded aneurysm no longer causes harm.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Persisting venous/neurologic compression despite attention to blood flow.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: After outside popliteal exclusion and vein bypass, he develops progressive calf swelling and plantar numbness. Duplex shows a widely patent bypass and persistent flow within an enlarging excluded sac. The sac displaces the popliteal vein and tibial nerve. Venous duplex shows compression without thrombus.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which procedure should have addressed {patientName}'s new postoperative problem?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Genicular inflow embolization as the entire treatment for the current compressive symptoms.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: An enlarging sac visibly displaces vein and nerve while the bypass is patent and the vein has no thrombus.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the patent bypass with a flow-limiting graft lesion and remove mass effect: bypass revision becomes the appropriate offered procedure.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose an iliac repair configuration that preserves the only remaining internal-iliac inflow.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Repair planning must account for the only remaining pelvic inflow and real landing anatomy.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Avoidable pelvic ischemia risk or failure to seal in a healthy segment.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 71-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside vascular consultation. She was asymptomatic and independent in daily activities. Serial orthogonal measurements showed a fusiform infrarenal AAA of 5.1 cm, unchanged from the preceding study. No major life-limiting illness was identified.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The outside repair-planning CTA shows both common iliac arteries enlarged through their bifurcations. The left internal iliac artery is chronically occluded. The right internal iliac and both external iliac arteries are patent, with nonaneurysmal distal landing segments. A standard bifurcated infrarenal main body can be used.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which iliac configuration should have been selected for {patientName}'s planned endovascular repair?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Bilateral external extension with embolization of the remaining internal iliac.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Left internal-iliac occlusion plus right internal-iliac and external-iliac distal landing segments.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Restore nonaneurysmal distal common iliac landing zones: standard common-iliac limb landings become appropriate. Remove the right branch landing zone: the exact chosen branch configuration is no longer established.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose a durable repair approach for an operable heritable native-aorta TAAA rather than extending routine degenerative-aneurysm EVAR preferences.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A heritable substrate changes the applicability of an ordinary degenerative endovascular preference.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Extending a degenerative-aneurysm procedural preference without accounting for the heritable substrate.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 43-year-old man with genetically confirmed Marfan syndrome, attends clinic to review an outside aortic-team plan. An enlarging intact thoracoabdominal aneurysm includes the visceral origins; both potential endograft sealing regions are native aorta. He is active without major cardiac, pulmonary or renal dysfunction. Repair has been recommended, and both open and branched endovascular reconstruction are technically possible.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which repair approach should have been preferred for {patientName}'s intact thoracoabdominal aneurysm?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Branched endovascular repair because both procedures are technically feasible.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Confirmed Marfan syndrome with native sealing regions and no prohibitive open risk.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace Marfan with a degenerative aneurysm and substantially elevated open operative risk: branched endovascular repair becomes a reasonable preferred alternative after aortic-team assessment.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Resolve noncomparable serial dimensions before treating an apparent diameter increase as rapid growth.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Measurement-plane validity must precede a growth-based treatment conclusion.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Radiation/contrast exposure while leaving the growth inference unresolved.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, comes to clinic to review serial outside aortic studies. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the surveillance visit. The prior CTA measured 4.6 cm perpendicular to the aortic centerline; the new report lists 5.3 cm on an axial image across a curved segment. Both original CT datasets are available.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which imaging action should precede a growth-based repair decision for {patientName} at that visit?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Repeat contrast CT under the same new axial protocol.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Different planes across a curved segment, with both datasets available.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: If the original acquisitions were unavailable or inadequate for the needed landmarks, new appropriate cross-sectional acquisition would become reasonable.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Apply the female repair-assessment threshold without treating stable size or female sex as a reason to defer assessment.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: A stable aneurysm can still cross a sex-specific repair-assessment boundary.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Delayed specialist repair evaluation.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 71-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside vascular consultation. She was asymptomatic and independent in daily activities. Serial orthogonal measurements showed a fusiform infrarenal AAA of 5.1 cm, unchanged from the preceding study. No major life-limiting illness was identified.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aortic plan should have been offered after {patientName}'s 5.1-cm result?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Six-month surveillance until the male repair threshold is reached.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm full sac in a woman without a life-limiting condition.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Change the diameter to 4.7 cm while retaining the asymptomatic female profile: six-month ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use full sac size rather than a thrombus-lined lumen to determine referral for an intact 6-cm AAA.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Residual flowing lumen is not the full aneurysm diameter used for repair assessment.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Deferring assessment of an aneurysm already warranting repair consideration.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic to review his outside preventive-care records. He stopped smoking after 20 pack-years. At the first visit he had no abdominal or back symptoms. His previous chest CTA ended at the diaphragm; he had never had abdominal aortic imaging.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The next outside record contains an ultrasound with an outer-wall infrarenal aortic diameter of 6.0 cm and a flowing lumen of 3.1 cm surrounded by mural thrombus. He had no pain, remained independent, and had no life-limiting illness or major cardiopulmonary impairment.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which plan should have followed {patientName}'s ultrasound result at that asymptomatic visit?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Annual surveillance based on the patent lumen.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The 6.0-cm outer wall surrounds a smaller lumen and mural thrombus.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Change the full sac to 4.7 cm with documented stability: annual ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use matched serial diameter and symptom status to select an appropriate small-AAA follow-up interval.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Reconciled dimensions, population and adequate modality determine a concrete follow-up plan.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Unnecessary short-interval testing; a three-year error would under-surveil.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, comes to clinic to review serial outside aortic studies. He had no abdominal or back symptoms at the surveillance visit. The prior CTA measured 4.6 cm perpendicular to the aortic centerline; the new report lists 5.3 cm on an axial image across a curved segment. Both original CT datasets are available.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: Matched outer-wall orthogonal measurements are 4.6 cm on the prior CTA and 4.7 cm on the current study. He remains free of abdominal or back symptoms. The entire infrarenal sac is consistently visualized on ultrasound.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which aortic surveillance schedule should have been selected for {patientName} after that comparison?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Six-month ultrasound based on the original 5.3-cm report.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A reproducible 4.7-cm sac in an asymptomatic man with an adequate ultrasound window.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: A matched 5.2-cm sac in the same asymptomatic man changes the preferred offered interval to six months.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Interpret descending extent and preserved organ perfusion to choose initial impulse control instead of immediate repair.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Extent and current organ function distinguish initial impulse therapy from immediate repair.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Premature invasive treatment or failure to institute appropriate impulse control.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which initial hospital treatment plan should have been selected for {patientName} at that assessment?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Urgent TEVAR for the first high-pressure reading.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: Descending confinement with preserved kidney enhancement, urine output and limb/abdominal examination before treatment.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace preserved renal perfusion with new oliguria, falling renal enhancement and true-lumen collapse despite treatment: urgent endovascular repair becomes the preferred offered strategy.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Distinguish inflammatory wall disruption from a small true aneurysm when choosing whether to treat a visceral arterial lesion.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Wall-disruption mechanism changes management despite a small apparent lesion.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Leaving an acquired wall defect at risk while waiting for size growth.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside pancreatitis admission. Follow-up CTA shows a new 12-mm contrast-filled cavity outside the pancreas, continuous with the splenic artery through a focal wall defect beside an inflammatory collection. Earlier imaging showed that arterial segment without a cavity. He is stable and has no active bleeding.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which vascular plan should have been selected for {patientName}'s new splenic-artery lesion?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Annual size surveillance after applying a small true-aneurysm rule.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A new extra-organ cavity connected through a focal arterial wall defect after pancreatitis.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the lesion with a small contained intraparenchymal defect selected by specialists for strict observation: interval imaging can become appropriate. A stable small true aneurysm would require a separate policy decision, not this pseudoaneurysm rule.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use the associated aneurysm pattern and actual prior imaging coverage to complete an aneurysm survey without repeating an adequate examination.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: An association becomes useful when combined with the actual coverage of prior studies.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Duplicate testing while leaving the contralateral aneurysm site unassessed.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic to review an outside vascular course. He had repeated brief episodes of painful blue right toes. The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses and normal strength and sensation. Right-leg duplex showed an 18-mm focal popliteal dilation containing mural thrombus; distal imaging showed small digital arterial occlusions.
rawEvidence.currentUpdate: The same outside workup includes a complete abdominal-aortic CTA with outer diameters under 3 cm throughout the abdominal aorta. The arterial duplex acquisition is labeled right lower extremity from common femoral to pedal vessels. The clinic receives the original images and acquisition records.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which additional aneurysm study should have completed {patientName}'s survey after review of these records?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Repeat abdominal ultrasound after recalling the AAA association.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: A complete abdominal CTA paired with a unilateral right-leg arterial acquisition.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Provide adequate bilateral popliteal imaging but only a pelvis-only CT: abdominal aortic ultrasound becomes the appropriate additional survey study.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

rankedConcepts.objective: Apply ever-smoker eligibility and the actual scope of prior imaging to choose an initial abdominal aortic screen.
rankedConcepts.expectedTestingRelevance: Preventive eligibility and prior scan coverage are a more useful application than repeating a modality label.
rankedConcepts.practicalImportance: Missing an indicated abdominal-aortic screen.

rawEvidence.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic to review his outside preventive-care records. He stopped smoking after 20 pack-years. At the first visit he had no abdominal or back symptoms. His previous chest CTA ended at the diaphragm; he had never had abdominal aortic imaging.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Which imaging plan should have been selected at {patientName}'s asymptomatic preventive visit?
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: No additional imaging because an aortic CTA already exists.
rankedConcepts.decidingObservation: The prior acquisition stops at the diaphragm and he has never had abdominal imaging.
rankedConcepts.counterfactual: Replace the chest study with a documented completed adequate abdominal aortic screen: no additional one-time screen becomes the best offered plan.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate, not an exam-frequency or measured performance claim.

answerChoices.label: Preserve right internal-iliac inflow during bilateral external-iliac extension

explanation.text: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

choices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
choices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes definitive source control from bridging or suppression.
choices.counterfactual: Prohibitive operative risk could change the balance toward nonoperative suppression or a limited strategy.

choices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
choices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.
choices.temptation: Uses rapid bleeding control as though it establishes durable infection source control.
choices.counterfactual: Uncontrolled hemorrhage in an unstable patient can make an endovascular bridge reasonable.

choices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
choices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Equates a temporary physiologic response to antibiotics with eradication of an infected prosthesis.
choices.counterfactual: A patient who cannot tolerate reconstruction may need a suppression-based strategy after specialist review.

decisionNodes.stem: Which endovascular repair should have addressed {patientName}'s demonstrated leak?

answerChoices.label: Covered stent-graft bridging at the modular junction
answerChoices.rationale: A fabric gap provides a direct route into the sac. A covered bridge restores the missing barrier between the aligned components.

answerChoices.label: Balloon remodelling at the modular junction
answerChoices.rationale: Expansion can improve apposition where fabric overlaps, but cannot supply the absent covering between separated ends.

answerChoices.label: Bare-metal stent reinforcement at the leaking segment
answerChoices.rationale: Radial scaffolding does not add a covering across the demonstrated open channel to the sac.

decisionNodes.explanation: The problem is loss of covered continuity, not simply insufficient expansion. A covered bridge can close a separated modular junction. Balloon remodelling or bare-metal reinforcement addresses other apposition/support problems but does not itself cover a fabric gap.

record.title: Reassessing an enlarging EVAR sac with uncertain inflow
fairness: The meaningful decision is to question the earlier branch-leak attribution when a larger sac and indeterminate graft-junction flow appear, then investigate a potential direct graft-related source before selective branch treatment.

The three choices are angiographic assessments at the same stage. Aortography is a defensible first offered assessment; selective collateral studies might subsequently be needed but do not replace assessment of the uncertain graft interface.

suggestions: Retain the distinction between an earlier documented pattern and an uncertain current source. Do not convert the task into an unsupported universal rule that selective studies are never useful.

decisionNodes.stem: Which study should have completed {patientName}'s current aortic surveillance assessment?

answerChoices.label: MRI of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The current ultrasound does not define full sac size; MRI provides cross-sectional assessment without requiring the iodinated-contrast exposure implicated in his prior reaction.

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging addresses the inadequate ultrasound, but this proposed contrast examination disregards the serious prior immediate reaction when MRI is a supported alternative.

answerChoices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The prior success of ultrasound does not establish a usable current outer-wall measurement through the documented acoustic limitation.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During a later outside admission he reports new deep abdominal and back pain beginning at rest and persisting through changes in position. Palpation over the pulsatile abdominal mass reproduces the pain. MR angiography measures the infrarenal sac at 4.9 cm without extravasation. answerChoices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.

answerChoices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional endovascular action should have addressed {patientName}'s persistent renal perfusion defect?

answerChoices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
answerChoices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
answerChoices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.

answerChoices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
answerChoices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

case.learningSummary: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated. Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. case.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. His pressure is 184/96 mm Hg and rhythm is sinus at 108/min. Both kidneys enhance, urine output is maintained, and the abdominal and limb examinations show no ischemic findings. He has no conduction disease, active bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure.

decisionNodes.stem: Which study should have completed {patientName}'s current aortic surveillance assessment?

answerChoices.label: MRI of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The current ultrasound does not define full sac size; MRI provides cross-sectional assessment without requiring the iodinated-contrast exposure implicated in his prior reaction.

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging addresses the inadequate ultrasound, but this proposed contrast examination disregards the serious prior immediate reaction when MRI is a supported alternative.

answerChoices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The prior success of ultrasound does not establish a usable current outer-wall measurement through the documented acoustic limitation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Current ultrasound adequacy matters more than the fact that ultrasound was useful previously. Cross-sectional assessment is needed when the sac is not defined, and MRI is reasonable when CT is contraindicated. The earlier matched measurements do not establish the current sac size after an inadequate examination.

answerChoices.label: Reconstruct the serial CT volumes for matched measurements
answerChoices.rationale: The apparent increase uses different planes. Adequate source volumes permit a valid comparison before using enlargement to determine repair assessment.

answerChoices.rationale: Applying a surveillance band to the unreconciled latest value does not resolve whether a consequential interval change occurred.

decisionNodes.explanation: The reported 0.7-cm difference spans different measurement planes. Use the adequate acquired volumes to establish a matched comparison before interpreting growth. record.title: Surveillance after inadequate ultrasound and severe contrast reaction
fairness: MRI is the best offered study. The resident must recognize that an untraceable posterior sac boundary prevents a current diameter assessment, then account for the severe prior iodinated-contrast reaction when choosing cross-sectional imaging.

The prior CT measurements do not substitute for a current examination. Repeat duplex is less persuasive after the documented positional attempts, and routine CTA is less attractive after wheezing, hives and hypotension requiring epinephrine. These observations are decision-critical and should not be removed merely because they distinguish the choices.

The sequence advances explicitly to the following annual visit, repeats the pertinent matched measurements and states the absence of new pain. It can be answered from the shared presentation and current update without recalling the previous key. This is a practical, high-yield surveillance-modality decision.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation should not be read as declaring all CT techniques categorically contraindicated: the offered comparator is iodinated-contrast CTA, and the safety and feasibility of alternative protocols are not tested.
suggestions: For editorial precision, remove the unsupported historical aside that ultrasound was useful previously; the visible earlier measurements were CT measurements. State the reusable adequacy principle directly. This aside does not change the offered best answer.
