decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The matched CT measurements are 4.6 and 4.7 cm, six months apart. At the following annual surveillance visit, ultrasound displays the anterior wall but cannot trace the posterior sac boundary through bowel gas on the acquired supine and lateral views. During the last iodinated-contrast injection he developed wheezing, generalized hives and hypotension requiring epinephrine. He has no new pain.
decisionNodes.stem: Which study should have completed {patientName}'s current aortic surveillance assessment?

answerChoices.label: MRI of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The current ultrasound does not define full sac size; MRI provides cross-sectional assessment without requiring the iodinated-contrast exposure implicated in his prior reaction.

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging addresses the inadequate ultrasound, but this proposed contrast examination disregards the serious prior immediate reaction when MRI is a supported alternative.

answerChoices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
answerChoices.rationale: The prior success of ultrasound does not establish a usable current outer-wall measurement through the documented acoustic limitation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Current ultrasound adequacy matters more than the fact that ultrasound was useful previously. Cross-sectional assessment is needed when the sac is not defined, and MRI is reasonable when CT is contraindicated. The earlier matched measurements do not establish the current sac size after an inadequate examination.
sourceLabels: Society for Vascular Surgery (undated). Patients with Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA).
Eric M. Isselbacher et al. (2022). 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During a later outside admission he reports new deep abdominal and back pain beginning at rest and persisting through changes in position. Palpation over the pulsatile abdominal mass reproduces the pain. MR angiography measures the infrarenal sac at 4.9 cm without extravasation. A chronic lumbar wedge deformity has the same appearance as on older imaging. His pressure and lower-limb strength remain preserved.
decisionNodes.stem: Which plan should have been selected for {patientName} during that admission?

answerChoices.label: Inpatient vascular assessment for aneurysm repair
answerChoices.rationale: New focal aortic tenderness and persistent nonmechanical pain change the previously asymptomatic premise despite an intact image and smaller diameter.

answerChoices.label: Inpatient lumbar MRI before vascular assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The unchanged structural spine finding does not establish that it explains the new rest pain and focal pain reproduced over the aorta.

answerChoices.label: Clinical observation with scheduled aortic ultrasound follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Routine observation and surveillance do not address the new aneurysm-localized symptoms simply because the scan shows no leak.

decisionNodes.explanation: The pain pattern and focal tenderness make the aneurysm clinically concerning even though MR imaging shows no extravasation. The unchanged lumbar finding does not by itself explain this new syndrome. Inpatient vascular repair assessment is appropriate; a size-based asymptomatic surveillance rule does not settle this admission.

authorGate.cueAttack: The neutral task no longer demands an imaging correction. A compact acquisition table supplies the actual planes and source-series adequacy; the key does not repeat a distinctive perpendicular phrase. Repair assessment and surveillance are genuine competing responses to the apparent change.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Next aortic management plan after discordant serial reports, before a growth claim is accepted.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the relationship between vessel curvature, measurement plane and reported change.
Decide whether to verify the change now, apply a growth-based repair policy or apply a size-based surveillance band.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: both the apparent growth over six months and a subthreshold latest diameter invite defensible-looking but incompatible policies. Neither can be applied correctly until measurement validity is resolved.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Different image planes despite adequate complete source volumes from both time points.
authorGate.closestError: Repair referral based on the apparent six-month enlargement as if it were confirmed.
authorGate.consequence: Escalating care on an invalid comparison or overlooking a consequential trajectory by merely rescheduling surveillance.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing the plane or source-volume rows changes the validity of the comparison. Removing the interval would make a growth-rate interpretation unfair; six months is now explicit.
authorGate.counterfactual: Make both values matched orthogonal outer-wall measurements at the same landmark: the confirmed six-month increase supports the offered repair-evaluation plan.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Later v2 nodes receive a reconciled comparison and a separate change in ultrasound adequacy, then a new pain episode. The explanation gives no later MRI or pain-attribution answer.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the deliberately repeated bad CT protocol foil with actual growth-versus-surveillance decisions. Added only the directly checked ACC/AHA growth boundary; no new automatic operation rule.

choices.temptation: Separates a changed number from established biological growth.
choices.counterfactual: Comparable orthogonal measurements confirming the same change over six months could support vascular repair evaluation.

choices.label: Refer for repair evaluation based on serial enlargement
choices.rationale: The amount and interval would matter if the measurements were comparable, but the plane discrepancy prevents treating the reported difference as confirmed growth.
choices.temptation: Correctly recognizes a potentially important rate but assumes the two report values are interchangeable.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed increase from 4.6 to 5.3 cm using the same reproducible method over six months makes repair evaluation reasonable.

choices.label: Schedule ultrasound follow-up using the latest reported size
choices.rationale: Applying a surveillance band to the unreconciled latest value does not resolve whether a consequential interval change occurred.
choices.temptation: Uses the current diameter band while overlooking a potentially important but unvalidated trajectory.
choices.counterfactual: Once comparable imaging establishes a stable unrepaired male AAA near the repair threshold, six-month ultrasound may be appropriate.

authorGate.cueAttack: Removed the supplied adequate-ultrasound conclusion and the three interval labels. The raw acoustic-window observations and immediate contrast reaction are necessary constraints; all options are named aortic investigations with their own wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Complete a current nondiagnostic surveillance examination with an appropriate imaging modality.
reasoningSteps: Determine that the current examination cannot establish the full aneurysm dimension despite the prior stable comparison.
Select cross-sectional imaging while accounting for the serious prior iodinated-contrast response.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: repeating the customary surveillance modality and automatically escalating to CTA are each credible errors. The new clinical meaning is modality adequacy, so the old interval concept/history is retained separately.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The posterior sac boundary is not measurable on the current views, and the prior iodinated injection produced an immediate systemic reaction.
authorGate.closestError: Order CTA after correctly recognizing that ultrasound is inadequate.
authorGate.consequence: Unnecessary repeat exposure to the implicated contrast class, or failure to establish an interpretable aneurysm dimension.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the contrast reaction and CT becomes a supported alternative; remove the acoustic limitation and ordinary ultrasound remains appropriate. The actual six-month interval eliminates the original rate-assessment ambiguity.
authorGate.counterfactual: Provide complete reproducible current ultrasound visualization of the sac: duplex becomes the appropriate offered study despite the contrast history.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding measurement feedback does not teach MRI selection. The later pain record uses MR angiography, maintaining the contrast-history chronology rather than silently performing another routine iodinated CTA.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Changed the scored meaning explicitly instead of claiming that a corrected diameter creates two new inferences. Verified ACC/AHA ultrasound/CT/MRI recommendations and retained the old meaning without FSRS transfer.

authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a generic 'urgent referral' key with a concrete inpatient vascular repair assessment. Retained pain attribution and urgent warning observations; no exact deadline or drug regimen invented.

case.learningSummary: The reported 0.7-cm difference spans different measurement planes. Use the adequate acquired volumes to establish a matched comparison before interpreting growth. Confirmed enlargement of that amount over six months could change repair assessment, so the discrepancy should not simply be deferred to routine surveillance. Current ultrasound adequacy matters more than the fact that ultrasound was useful previously. Cross-sectional assessment is needed when the sac is not defined, and MRI is reasonable when CT is contraindicated. The earlier matched measurements do not establish the current sac size after an inadequate examination. The pain pattern and focal tenderness make the aneurysm clinically concerning even though MR imaging shows no extravasation. The unchanged lumbar finding does not by itself explain this new syndrome. Inpatient vascular repair assessment is appropriate; a size-based asymptomatic surveillance rule does not settle this admission.

authorGate.cueAttack: Removed 'should have replaced surveillance' from the task and the blanket claim excluding every alternative cause. The record instead gives a genuine competing lumbar observation, its chronology and the pain localization. Both alternative plans involve real assessment or follow-up.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Current inpatient aortic-versus-spine/observation plans after a new pain evaluation.
reasoningSteps: Use the pain behavior, focal examination and unchanged lumbar image to assess the competing attribution.
Apply that attribution to inpatient vascular repair assessment rather than the earlier asymptomatic size policy.
authorGate.difficulty: Fair moderate prediction: an incidental spine abnormality and an intact aneurysm image are credible anchors. Diagnostic attribution remains a clinical judgment; the draft does not pretend that imaging alone proves the pain source.
authorGate.decidingObservation: New persistent rest pain is reproduced over the aortic mass while the competing lumbar structural finding is unchanged.
authorGate.closestError: Spine MRI first because a lumbar deformity appears in the imaging record.
authorGate.consequence: Delaying aortic assessment after a meaningful change in symptoms.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the actual competing lumbar finding this is a simpler symptom-trigger rule. Without chronology and focal localization, choosing the vascular pathway would be less defensible. No blanket negative supplies the interpretation.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace aortic tenderness/rest pain with reproducible mechanical back pain and new corresponding spinal findings: the spine-directed investigation becomes reasonable before attributing symptoms to the AAA.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback concerns imaging adequacy and does not rehearse pain as a repair indication. MR angiography preserves the serious iodinated-contrast history established in the preceding v2 node.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Re-solved the neutral task after deleting the cue and broad exclusion. Kept the supported moderate attribution problem rather than adding an unsourced imaging sign or compulsory operation deadline.

authorGate.cueAttack: Sex and full measured size are necessary eligibility data, not deterministic risk language. The stem does not ask for a sex association or announce a lower threshold. All choices name concrete plans, and both surveillance choices have ultrasound wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Elective aortic management after an established intact aneurysm result.
reasoningSteps: Separate absence of growth from being below a size threshold.
Apply the female diameter boundary to repair assessment rather than borrowing the male band.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: stable size and remembered male thresholds are two credible competing errors. This is a practical replacement for repeating an epidemiologic association.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm full sac in a woman without a life-limiting condition.
authorGate.closestError: Six-month surveillance until the male repair threshold is reached.
authorGate.consequence: Delayed specialist repair evaluation.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing sex or the measured diameter makes the interval/referral ranking indeterminate. Ordinary function supplies fitness context without assigning an invented mortality score.
authorGate.counterfactual: Change the diameter to 4.7 cm while retaining the asymptomatic female profile: six-month ultrasound becomes the best offered plan.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The subsequent iliac decision uses a new CTA planning record. This explanation does not teach hypogastric preservation.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Created a separate meaning; no FSRS history from the approved sex-outcome association is transferred. Replaced unqualified mandatory EVAR with assessment rather than asserting that diameter determines the operation.

authorGate.cueAttack: The presentation no longer announces an established 5.1-cm aneurysm as a completed interpretation. The constructed table provides competing measured structures. All labels are concrete management plans with comparable grammar; no mandatory-operation or generic shared-decision key is used.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Elective aortic management after a measurement record, before selecting any repair technique.
reasoningSteps: Identify the maximum full sac dimension rather than the residual flow channel.
Apply the female assessment boundary rather than the male threshold or the female interval for a smaller sac.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: each surveillance choice follows a different credible error, so the learner must resolve both dimension and population. It is not claimed to be a universal mandatory operation rule.
authorGate.decidingObservation: A 5.1-cm outer contour surrounds a smaller flowing channel in a woman.
authorGate.closestError: Use the full size but apply a male threshold and defer assessment for six months.
authorGate.consequence: Postponing repair assessment or following the wrong sac-size band.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing the contour/channel distinction leaves only threshold recall; removing sex makes the assessment-versus-six-month choice different. Extra fitness statements were not added to manufacture difficulty.
authorGate.counterfactual: Change the patient to a man with the same asymptomatic full dimensions: six-month ultrasound becomes an appropriate offered plan. Change the female full sac to 4.2 cm: annual follow-up becomes appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: No earlier feedback is visible in this case. The next node receives new iliac anatomy and tests preservation strategy; this explanation gives no side-specific configuration answer.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Added a consequential measurement interpretation and explicitly distinguished the two societies' recommendation strength in feedback. The source-supported endpoint is assessment, not automatic EVAR or a universal policy for every woman.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update gives each relevant vessel's patency and landing-segment anatomy without naming pelvic ischemia or a preserving technique. Every option is a graft configuration; no uniquely cautious counseling label appears.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Distal graft configuration after an elective EVAR plan, not selection of whether to repair.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that the right internal iliac is the remaining direct pelvic inflow and that both usual distal landing regions are aneurysmal.

authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a technically simple bilateral external extension is tempting, as is retaining common-iliac landings to avoid branch work.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Left internal-iliac occlusion plus right internal-iliac and external-iliac distal landing segments.

authorGate.deletionTest: The entire new vessel map is needed; without it, no configuration is uniquely preferred. No arbitrary device dimension is imposed.
authorGate.counterfactual: Restore nonaneurysmal distal common iliac landing zones: standard common-iliac limb landings become appropriate. Remove the right branch landing zone: the exact chosen branch configuration is no longer established.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding size decision does not disclose this vessel map or preservation rule. A new clinical decision is made at the planning stage.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a fourth implausible remote-vessel operation. Kept three actual configurations and a source limitation: final device suitability requires the treating vascular team, not this synthetic map.

authorGate.cueAttack: Removed the device-specific key and the clearly aneurysmal common-iliac landing foil. The arterial/delayed observations must be interpreted to locate usable current inflow. Each option specifies the same distal-seal configuration and a distinct side-specific preservation policy.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Pelvic-inflow strategy accompanying an established distal exclusion plan, before selecting a device or conduit.
reasoningSteps: Infer the remaining direct hypogastric inflow from opacification and occlusion observations.
Determine what the planned bilateral external-iliac seals would interrupt and choose the preservation target.
authorGate.difficulty: Fair moderate prediction. It retains the useful side/patency inference and avoids fabricating device criteria to make technical selection appear hard. The final hardware choice is deliberately outside the scored meaning.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Right internal-iliac opacification with an occluded left channel, coupled with distal seals beyond both origins.
authorGate.closestError: Apply a nominal left-sided preservation policy while the patent right origin is excluded.
authorGate.consequence: Losing the remaining direct pelvic inflow or assuming unverified collateral protection.
authorGate.deletionTest: Patency observations determine which side matters; planned seal positions make that patency consequential. No unsupported branch-device suitability conclusion remains.
authorGate.counterfactual: Reverse the observed patency so the left side supplies the pelvis and the right channel is occluded: left-sided preservation becomes the appropriate offered strategy.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding v2 explanation concerns size assessment and does not name the inflow side. The current CTA supplies the new operative planning information.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Resolved the fairness issue by narrowing the task to the supported inflow-preservation strategy. All three policies address the same planned seals; no arbitrary neck, diameter or angulation criterion is supplied.

explanation.text: The current imaging leaves the right internal iliac as the remaining direct pelvic inflow. Preserve that route as part of exclusion planning when feasible. This is a strategy decision: the scan does not by itself establish eligibility for a particular iliac branch device, and the final preserving reconstruction requires separate anatomic planning.

choices.label: Preserve right internal-iliac inflow during bilateral external-iliac extension
choices.rationale: The right internal iliac is the remaining direct pelvic inflow. An exclusion strategy should preserve it when feasible rather than intentionally eliminating that route.
choices.temptation: Maps the opacified vessel and planned exclusion to the remaining pelvic supply.
choices.counterfactual: If the right side were occluded and the left internal iliac supplied the pelvis, left-sided preservation would be the relevant goal.

choices.label: Preserve left internal-iliac inflow during bilateral external-iliac extension
choices.rationale: The left channel is already occluded; assigning preservation to that side does not protect the patent right pelvic supply from the planned coverage.
choices.temptation: Reverses the side or counts a formerly named artery as current patent inflow.
choices.counterfactual: A patent left internal iliac with an occluded right side would make left-sided preservation the appropriate goal.

choices.label: Exclude both internal-iliac origins during bilateral external-iliac extension
choices.rationale: This would intentionally interrupt the remaining right-sided route instead of preserving at least one direct hypogastric inflow when feasible.
choices.temptation: Prioritizes a simple distal exclusion configuration and relies on unspecified collateral compensation.
choices.counterfactual: When both direct routes are already lost or preserving inflow is truly infeasible, the clinical team must consider a different risk/strategy balance rather than assuming this draft's preserving reconstruction.

decisionNodes.stem: Which endovascular repair should have addressed {patientName}'s demonstrated leak?

answerChoices.label: Covered stent-graft bridging at the modular junction
answerChoices.rationale: A fabric gap provides a direct route into the sac. A covered bridge restores the missing barrier between the aligned components.

answerChoices.label: Balloon remodelling at the modular junction
answerChoices.rationale: Expansion can improve apposition where fabric overlaps, but cannot supply the absent covering between separated ends.

answerChoices.label: Bare-metal stent reinforcement at the leaking segment
answerChoices.rationale: Radial scaffolding does not add a covering across the demonstrated open channel to the sac.

decisionNodes.explanation: The problem is loss of covered continuity, not simply insufficient expansion. A covered bridge can close a separated modular junction. Balloon remodelling or bare-metal reinforcement addresses other apposition/support problems but does not itself cover a fabric gap.

authorGate.cueAttack: The record never calls the flow benign or supplies a type label. The table requires the learner to compare diameter across time. Each option names one plan; the key is not the most detailed or only cautious phrase. Its ultrasound wait is explicit.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Management of a known post-EVAR sac-flow finding at surveillance.
reasoningSteps: Infer retrograde side-branch inflow from phase and continuity.
Use unchanged serial sac size to favor surveillance rather than treating every leak.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: embolization feels appropriate when contrast persists, and a proximal cuff is a real treatment for the competing leak mechanism.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Lumbar continuity with identical full sac diameters and intact attachments/overlaps.
authorGate.closestError: Lumbar/sac embolization for a persistent but stable leak.
authorGate.consequence: Unnecessary intervention while teaching a mechanism-insensitive rule.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the diameter comparison, the branch leak might coexist with enlargement and the management ranking would be incomplete. Attachment observations exclude a different dangerous source without interpreting them for the learner.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace branch filling with direct proximal attachment inflow: prompt seal treatment replaces surveillance even if size has not yet grown.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Feedback does not name component separation or its treatment. Subsequent growth and new angiographic anatomy are withheld until their nodes.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the label 'isolated type II' from the visible context and replaced it with raw phase/continuity observations. The constructed table is numerical evidence rather than a promised scan asset.

explanation.text: Delayed branch-associated flow with an unchanged sac supports continued surveillance. A visible leak is not enough to choose its treatment; source and sac behavior matter.

choices.rationale: The branch origin and unchanged sac support observation with continued imaging.
choices.temptation: Interprets both the leak route and sac behavior.
choices.counterfactual: A direct attachment leak or a growing sac would require a different evaluation or intervention.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: A visible branch leak does not by itself establish a treatment benefit when the sac is stable.
choices.temptation: Treats persistence of any contrast outside the graft as a repair indication.
choices.counterfactual: A persistent proven branch leak with consequential sac growth can merit embolization after other sources are excluded.

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: The observed inflow is from lumbar branches, not the proximal attachment.
choices.temptation: Confuses every leak with a proximal seal failure.
choices.counterfactual: A proximal attachment leak with a usable extra landing segment would favor cuff extension.

authorGate.cueAttack: All three choices are equally specific catheter-angiographic assessments and share a wait profile. The update describes both candidate sites and actual acquired phases; it does not say a series is missing or name an omitted action.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Define the inflow source during catheter workup before selecting targeted treatment.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that a new expanding sac invalidates automatic reassurance from prior stable branch flow.
Choose central graft/seal assessment before committing to one collateral route.
authorGate.difficulty: Hard prediction: the earlier correct surveillance decision and branch finding create a credible anchoring error; nearby lumbar contrast is not proof of causal inflow.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Large interval sac expansion plus artifact-limited origin near a graft junction despite an adequate multiphase acquisition.
authorGate.closestError: Targeted lumbar angiography as if the original attribution were still established.
authorGate.consequence: Missing a direct-pressure leak and treating the wrong pathway.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the growth and new uncertainty restores the earlier surveillance rationale. Phase acquisition details distinguish actual ambiguity from a merely missing export.
authorGate.counterfactual: If multiphase imaging conclusively established isolated lumbar inflow with no attachment or junction defect, selective iliolumbar mapping would become reasonable for treatment planning.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation teaches source/trajectory assessment but does not identify this new source. This node's explanation names possible categories but gives no repair configuration for the later demonstrated defect.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced 'obtain more information' versus repair options with three same-stage angiographic targets. No universal growth threshold is inferred from the constructed large change.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update supplies raw defect anatomy instead of a type-III label. 'Covered graft' is one specific repair among parallel actual endovascular actions; no uniquely elaborate plan or rationale appears in its label.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Select the site-specific endovascular repair after definitive angiography.
reasoningSteps: Infer a direct-pressure modular graft failure from arterial-phase passage through the component gap.
Choose a covered bridge across that site rather than a branch or attachment procedure.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: prior branch attribution can persist, while a resident may identify a dangerous leak yet choose a proximal cuff for the wrong anatomic defect.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Flow traverses the main-body/limb gap, with intact seals and a feasible bridging overlap.
authorGate.closestError: Proximal cuff extension after correctly recognizing a high-pressure leak.
authorGate.consequence: An unclosed sac-pressure source with continuing rupture risk.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the actual gap and there is no basis to select bridging over the two other repairs; intact seal observations distinguish the closest wrong repair.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the junction gap with direct inflow at the proximal attachment and an available healthy landing segment: proximal cuff extension becomes appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback requires source confirmation but never gives this bridging answer. The new angiographic relationship, not a repeated type label, determines the repair.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Kept attachment and overlap facts because they establish one feasible repair. Did not use an unsafe default that every component defect can be managed with a generic new limb.

authorGate.cueAttack: Removed the sentence naming an additional covered limb and asserting successful overlap. The record now describes separation, alignment and intact adjacent fabric. All options are concrete endovascular repair methods of comparable scope; the previous proximal-cuff foil is gone.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Select the repair mechanism after diagnostic angiography localizes the actual defect.
reasoningSteps: Infer a direct-pressure loss of graft continuity from arterial flow through separated fabric ends.
Distinguish adding a covered barrier from radial remodelling or uncovered scaffolding.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: the closest error is a real intraprocedural leak manoeuvre applied to the wrong mechanical failure. This is more consequential than matching the words additional covered limb to its repeated option.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The fabric ends have separated and no overlap remains across the leak route.
authorGate.closestError: Balloon remodelling because the contrast focus lies at a modular junction.
authorGate.consequence: Manipulating the junction without restoring the missing exclusion barrier.
authorGate.deletionTest: If separation versus maintained overlap is removed, balloon remodelling cannot be ranked fairly. Native attachment observations preserve source localization but no longer directly delete a proximal-cuff option.
authorGate.counterfactual: Maintain a fabric overlap and show incomplete expansion at that junction without an open gap: balloon remodelling becomes an appropriate offered repair.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding two PASS nodes, their presentations, exhibits and feedback remain exactly unchanged. New findings appear only after them; neither earlier explanation names the covered-bridge manoeuvre. Full original v1 cases are also retained.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Re-solved the new method comparison using CIRSE's component-gap, overlap-remodelling and attachment-adjunct distinctions. Final device sizing is not inferred from an invented numeric overlap rule.

explanation.text: The problem is loss of covered continuity, not simply insufficient expansion. A covered bridge can close a separated modular junction. Balloon remodelling or bare-metal reinforcement addresses other apposition/support problems but does not itself cover a fabric gap.

choices.label: Covered stent-graft bridging at the modular junction
choices.rationale: A fabric gap provides a direct route into the sac. A covered bridge restores the missing barrier between the aligned components.
choices.temptation: Uses the observed mechanical defect to select a repair that actually excludes the channel.
choices.counterfactual: If the components still overlapped and the problem were remediable incomplete expansion, balloon remodelling could be appropriate.

choices.label: Balloon remodelling at the modular junction
choices.rationale: Expansion can improve apposition where fabric overlaps, but cannot supply the absent covering between separated ends.
choices.temptation: Treats every junctional leak as incomplete expansion of an existing overlap.
choices.counterfactual: An intraoperative leak from incomplete expansion within a maintained overlap can be treated by balloon remodelling.

choices.label: Bare-metal stent reinforcement at the leaking segment
choices.rationale: Radial scaffolding does not add a covering across the demonstrated open channel to the sac.
choices.temptation: Confuses mechanical support with reconstruction of the exclusion barrier.
choices.counterfactual: Selected attachment-apposition leaks can use bare-metal reinforcement as an adjunct when the covered fabric and sealing anatomy are present.

authorGate.cueAttack: The unchanged diameter is a real competing datum, not reassurance supplied by the author. No type label or urgency phrase appears before answering. All choices are post-EVAR management plans with similar specificity.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Treat or observe a documented late leak, using its anatomic source.
reasoningSteps: Infer a sealing failure from direct arterial-phase attachment flow.
Apply its pressure-risk significance rather than letting stable sac size determine observation.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: a resident may correctly remember stable-sac observation but apply it to the wrong leak origin.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Direct flow at the proximal attachment with an available healthy neck segment.
authorGate.closestError: Surveillance because the sac has not enlarged.
authorGate.consequence: Leaving a direct-pressure leak untreated.
authorGate.deletionTest: The source and healthy landing anatomy are necessary; removing them prevents selecting the cuff. Stable diameter earns its role as the competing misconception.
authorGate.counterfactual: If contrast arrived through lumbar branches on delayed images with intact seals and a stable sac, continued surveillance would become correct.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone exact context; not dependent on the other endoleak case or its explanation. No cross-case exposure is assumed.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced 'repair immediately' with a concrete anatomically possible cuff plan. Restricted the case to an established late leak rather than a transient intraoperative blush.

explanation.text: This arterial-phase attachment route represents a type I sealing failure. Prompt seal repair is appropriate even before the sac enlarges; the available healthy neck makes proximal extension a supported option.

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff

choices.temptation: Distinguishes a sealing defect from a stable branch leak.
choices.counterfactual: Absent a usable neck, a more complex reconstruction would need consideration.

choices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance

choices.counterfactual: A confirmed isolated branch leak with stable sac size supports surveillance.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity

choices.temptation: Treats contrast in the sac as a branch-leak problem regardless of its observed source.
choices.counterfactual: A growing isolated branch leak could support branch/sac embolization.

authorGate.cueAttack: The care frame is a retrospective clinic review. Serial pressure and alertness are constructed physiologic observations, not an invented stability cutoff. No sentence promises that CT is available or will not delay care. Every option names a vascular imaging study and has a wait profile.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Imaging to plan hospital repair after aneurysm detection, not initial screening or the final repair procedure.
reasoningSteps: Interpret preserved serial perfusion as allowing urgent planning despite a possible contained rupture.
Choose imaging that supplies surrounding hemorrhage, sealing and access anatomy.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: equating rupture with inevitable immediate collapse or reusing ultrasound after detection are credible errors.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Preserved serial circulation after a large aneurysm is demonstrated in a painful presentation.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat duplex because it already identified the AAA and avoids contrast.
authorGate.consequence: Failing to define the repair anatomy or contained hemorrhage needed for the definitive strategy.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing physiologic trajectory makes a CT-planning decision unsafe; removing the completed ultrasound changes the stage from planning to initial evaluation.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the painful admission with an asymptomatic small-AAA surveillance visit: duplex becomes the best offered study. Refractory shock would invalidate the entire stable-imaging task and require immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation avoids the later EVAR-versus-open ranking. CTA findings appear only after answering, and no hospital service is executed by the clinic runtime.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a transfer-permission sentence with serial physiology and removed 'most informative' from the task. Timing estimates are placeholders, not authorization to delay real emergency care.

authorGate.cueAttack: Removed stable from the task and removed the restriction to choosing an imaging modality. The alternatives now represent actual current pathways: planning CT, direct control or continued stabilization. The presentation gives observations without declaring the stability classification.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Immediate hospital next-step plans after a painful large AAA is detected, before definitive repair anatomy is known.
reasoningSteps: Interpret an initially low pressure followed by sustained current perfusion as a changing trajectory rather than a fixed category.
Choose urgent planning imaging versus direct control or further stabilization at this actual time point.
authorGate.difficulty: Fair moderate prediction. Direct open control is a credible nearest competitor after the initial hypotension. The item does not claim high difficulty from merely recalling CTA, nor does it require a fabricated shock threshold.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Repeated current pressure and mental-status recovery after initial resuscitation, rather than one isolated reading.
authorGate.closestError: Direct open control based solely on the first low pressure despite the subsequent trajectory.
authorGate.consequence: Skipping useful repair-planning anatomy, or delaying the supported next step while waiting for normal numbers.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the serial observations, whether CT is appropriate cannot be decided fairly. The completed bedside ultrasound establishes the current stage but does not supply the repair anatomy.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the recovered trajectory with recurrent loss of consciousness and falling pressure despite initial resuscitation: direct hemorrhage control becomes the appropriate offered pathway.
authorGate.sequenceReview: This v2 case is standalone because the subsequent repair-approach item is parked. No specific endovascular device or final repair preference is disclosed by its feedback.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the three-modality recall set with a neutral actual-stage decision. Kept the supported moderate version; exact suitability and reperfusion strategies require evidence not invented here.

explanation.text: Use the current serial perfusion observations, not the initial pressure in isolation. At this recorded point urgent CT can define rupture and repair anatomy while definitive aortic care is prepared. Persistent or renewed circulatory collapse would change that balance toward immediate aortic control.

choices.label: Urgent CT angiography during aortic-team preparation
choices.rationale: Repeated preserved pressure and mentation after initial resuscitation support urgent cross-sectional repair planning rather than another detection-only examination.
choices.temptation: Uses the current trajectory instead of classifying the patient solely from the first low reading.
choices.counterfactual: A renewed collapse or inability to sustain perfusion would make a direct hemorrhage-control pathway appropriate instead.

choices.label: Direct operating-room transfer for open aortic control
choices.rationale: Immediate control can be necessary in collapse, but the current serial observations support obtaining repair-planning CT first.
choices.temptation: Treats an initially low pressure and large aneurysm as proof that planning imaging is no longer possible.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent deterioration in circulation despite initial resuscitation would favor proceeding to hemorrhage control rather than delaying for CT.

choices.label: Further resuscitation before any cross-sectional planning
choices.rationale: The record already shows restored mentation and sustained pressure over repeated assessments; further normalizing physiology before defining the repair anatomy unnecessarily postpones the next supported step.
choices.temptation: Waits for entirely normal vital signs rather than judging whether current perfusion permits urgent planning.
choices.counterfactual: If perfusion remained inadequate for safe movement to CT, immediate resuscitation alongside a hemorrhage-control plan would be necessary.

authorGate.cueAttack: The CTA relationship is described without naming type A or assigning an author interpretation. The tear and flap extent deliberately conflict. Every option is a definitive hospital treatment plan; the medical plan's imaging component has timing metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Definitive plan after a completed acute aortic CTA; impulse control remains background stabilization for surgical patients.
reasoningSteps: Separate entry-tear location from ascending involvement in classification.
Apply the ascending extent to immediate operative management despite stable physiology.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: both the distal tear and normal pressure can wrongly steer an otherwise knowledgeable resident toward a type-B strategy.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The flap extends into the ascending aorta, not merely through the descending segment.
authorGate.closestError: Descending TEVAR directed at the entry tear as the complete treatment.
authorGate.consequence: Failure to treat the dangerous acute ascending segment.
authorGate.deletionTest: The distal tear creates the meaningful competing error; ascending extent changes the answer. Preserved perfusion keeps a separate contested malperfusion-first question out of this item.
authorGate.counterfactual: Confine the flap to the descending aorta and preserve the uncomplicated physiology: the offered medical plan becomes correct.
authorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone; no other dissection case's feedback is assumed visible. No new ICU setting, bedside treatment execution or live consultation is required.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed an initial pure Stanford-label task and made classification consequential to treatment. The explanation does not claim every distal tear with retrograde extension can be managed with one generic operation.

explanation.text: Ascending involvement determines the type-A pathway even when the entry tear is distal. Stable current pressure does not remove the need for emergency surgical treatment of acute ascending dissection.

choices.temptation: Classifies by the involved segment and applies its urgent surgical consequence.

choices.rationale: Treating the distal tear as a type-B problem does not address the acute ascending involvement.
choices.temptation: Classifies the dissection by the tear location alone.
choices.counterfactual: A complicated dissection confined to the descending aorta with suitable anatomy can favor TEVAR.

choices.rationale: Impulse control is background stabilization but not definitive treatment of acute ascending dissection.
choices.temptation: Uses normotension and absence of malperfusion to choose an uncomplicated type-B pathway.
choices.counterfactual: An uncomplicated dissection confined to the descending aorta initially receives medical therapy and monitoring.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic after an aortic hospitalization. The founder reviews the admission record: CTA shows a flap beginning just distal to the left subclavian artery, with no ascending involvement or extravasation. authorGate.cueAttack: No type-B or 'uncomplicated' label is visible. The key is not the only specific plan: all labels identify actual hospital treatments. Organ findings and beta-blocker safety checks are retained because they determine management and the named regimen, rather than merely decorating a high blood pressure.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Initial hospital treatment strategy for newly evaluated acute dissection.
reasoningSteps: Infer descending-only dissection without demonstrated organ compromise or rupture.
Choose monitored impulse therapy and appropriate infusion sequence rather than immediate repair.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate: applying an all-dissection surgical reflex or calling an untreated first high pressure 'refractory' are credible errors. The named drug sequence is an additional treatment detail, not a separate scored question.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Descending confinement with preserved kidney enhancement, urine output and limb/abdominal examination before treatment.
authorGate.closestError: Urgent TEVAR for the first high-pressure reading.
authorGate.consequence: Premature invasive treatment or failure to institute appropriate impulse control.
authorGate.deletionTest: Extent and organ-perfusion observations determine the strategy. Conduction, bronchospasm and heart-failure checks earn their place because the key names a beta blocker. Numeric vitals are fictional observations, not new cutoffs.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace preserved renal perfusion with new oliguria, falling renal enhancement and true-lumen collapse despite treatment: urgent endovascular repair becomes the preferred offered strategy.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The explanation does not name the later kidney complication or its intervention. Later anatomy and response are not visible at admission.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: An initial pure infusion-order question was rejected as too narrow. The revised neutral treatment-plan task requires extent/perfusion interpretation before drug selection. No dose or numeric treatment target is added.

drafts.reviewDisplay: key shown first for review only

authorGate.cueAttack: The former unique conditional medical option versus two operations is gone. All choices are named infusion changes. Safety and treatment-response observations apply to all competing pharmacologic strategies rather than appearing as a beta-blocker permission list.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Next infusion change after initial monitored beta blockade, not whether every descending dissection requires an operation.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the discordant treatment response: rate has responded, pressure has not, with current perfusion preserved.
Select added vasodilation rather than further rate reduction or rate-agent substitution.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: an apparently incomplete response can lead to escalating the wrong target or declaring the beta blocker ineffective. Three comparably specific medication changes require the response data.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Sinus rate is now 64/min while arterial pressure remains 184/96 with preserved perfusion.
authorGate.closestError: Increase esmolol because blood pressure is still high.
authorGate.consequence: Further rate reduction without the preferred next treatment of persistent pressure elevation.
authorGate.deletionTest: Both pretreatment/current rate and current pressure are required; deleting either leaves the treatment response unclear. Current perfusion and cardiac findings support the safety of the offered strategies without assigning an invented score.
authorGate.counterfactual: Keep pressure elevated but leave the sinus rate at 108/min without a limiting beta-blocker effect: further esmolol titration becomes a reasonable offered next change before adding vasodilation.
authorGate.sequenceReview: This is a separate standalone v2 case with a new meaning. The two later type-B PASS items remain frozen with their original entire v1 case and original preceding content; no response-focused rewrite is inserted before them.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Chose the review's focused drug-response objective and gave it a new concept identity. Verified the guideline rate range, add-after-beta recommendation and regulatory nicardipine pharmacology. The old uncomplicated-disease meaning/history is retained.

explanation.text: Rate and pressure are separate treatment targets. The observed rate response is within the guideline range, while pressure remains elevated. Add an intravenous vasodilator after initial beta blockade rather than simply intensifying rate reduction or substituting another rate-control agent. Nicardipine provides additional blood-pressure reduction while beta blockade continues.

choices.label: Add intravenous nicardipine infusion
choices.rationale: Rate has entered the guideline target range while pressure remains uncontrolled; added vasodilation addresses the remaining treatment target after beta blockade.
choices.temptation: Separates the achieved chronotropic response from the persisting pressure problem.
choices.counterfactual: If heart rate remained markedly elevated before adequate beta blockade, further beta-blocker titration could precede vasodilation.

choices.label: Increase the intravenous esmolol infusion
choices.rationale: Escalating rate-slowing therapy does not best address the remaining pressure target once the recorded rate response is adequate and perfusion is preserved.
choices.temptation: Uses one infusion to pursue both goals without interpreting which goal has already responded.
choices.counterfactual: Persisting sinus tachycardia with tolerable perfusion and no limiting response could support further beta-blocker titration.

choices.label: Replace esmolol with intravenous diltiazem
choices.rationale: The record does not demonstrate beta-blocker intolerance or a rate-control failure requiring substitution; it shows persisting pressure elevation after a rate response.
choices.temptation: Treats incomplete pressure response as failure of the chosen rate-control drug class.
choices.counterfactual: A genuine beta-blocker contraindication or intolerance can favor a nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker for rate control.

decisionNodes.stem: Which left-subclavian strategy should have accompanied {patientName}'s elective TEVAR plan?

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
answerChoices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.

answerChoices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
answerChoices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.

answerChoices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
answerChoices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.

decisionNodes.explanation: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate rescue plan should have been activated for {patientName}'s postoperative findings?

answerChoices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
answerChoices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
answerChoices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.

answerChoices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.

authorGate.cueAttack: The CABG anatomy is necessary raw conduit information; the presentation does not state that bypass is required. The transposition foil is a real durable revascularization, while deferred rescue is a separate timing policy. The first label is not uniquely cautious or longer than the alternatives.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: LSA management strategy around an elective covering repair.
reasoningSteps: Trace the patent LIMA-to-LAD graft's dependence on the LSA with an occluded native LAD.
Choose pre-coverage inflow preservation that avoids the proximal clamp required for transposition, rather than waiting for arm symptoms.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a durable transposition is tempting until its clamp sequence is considered alongside the pedicled coronary conduit.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Patent LIMA-to-LAD graft with native LAD occlusion and planned LSA-origin coverage.
authorGate.closestError: Choose transposition without accounting for interruption of the pedicled LIMA during proximal clamping.
authorGate.consequence: Loss of coronary graft inflow during an otherwise elective procedure.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the CABG conduit or native LAD finding and the key's patient-specific urgency weakens. Elective timing distinguishes this from unavoidable emergency coverage.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the LIMA were a free graft arising from the aorta rather than a patent pedicled subclavian conduit, transposition could become a reasonable pre-coverage technique; the specific bypass-over-transposition constraint would be removed.
authorGate.sequenceReview: This explanation focuses on coronary supply and does not teach spinal-cord rescue. A later postoperative neurologic event is revealed only in the next record.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Rejected the initial low-value post-coverage assessment foil. Targeted STS guideline verification established the transposition-clamp issue; replaced the foil with pre-coverage transposition and re-solved the exact three strategies.

explanation.text: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.
choices.temptation: Follows the coronary conduit back to its inflow origin.
choices.counterfactual: If no LSA-dependent coronary or other critical inflow existed, timing and need could differ, particularly in an emergency.

choices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
choices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.
choices.temptation: Treats upper-extremity symptoms as the only meaningful consequence of LSA interruption.
choices.counterfactual: Selective delayed revascularization may fit some emergency coverings without critical LSA-dependent inflow.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.
choices.temptation: Chooses a durable LSA revascularization while overlooking its proximal clamp sequence.
choices.counterfactual: Without a patent pedicled LIMA or another clamp-dependent inflow, transposition can be a reasonable LSA revascularization technique.

authorGate.cueAttack: The update contains no spinal diagnosis or target pressure. Warm pulses and preserved upper-body examination are necessary localization data, not blanket exclusions. All labels name an immediate medication/procedure pathway; no option says 'alone' or labels its own error.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Immediate postoperative rescue strategies after a new neurologic deficit.
reasoningSteps: Localize the deficit to spinal perfusion rather than limb inflow or a focal cerebral syndrome.
Reverse the low-perfusion state and consider intrathecal-pressure reduction rather than continuing the earlier impulse goal.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: the conflict between protecting an aortic repair from pressure and maintaining cord perfusion creates a consequential treatment-direction error.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Bilateral leg deficit after hypotension with warm pulsed feet and preserved face/arm function.
authorGate.closestError: Continue esmolol pressure reduction because the patient has an aortic repair.
authorGate.consequence: Worsening potentially reversible cord hypoperfusion.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the hypotensive trigger or localization findings and the rescue target is less defensible. Coagulation data inform drain safety; they do not guarantee that placement has no risk.
authorGate.counterfactual: Change the record to cold pulseless legs with confirmed aortoiliac occlusion: the offered limb-ischemia pathway becomes appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The prior LSA explanation concerns LIMA coronary supply and does not give this neurologic rescue plan. The actual postoperative trigger changes the decision.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a numeric MAP/CSF target because source protocols differ. The label activates a rescue pathway, with specialist drain safety assessment in feedback; this is not automatic drain placement or routine prophylactic drainage.

explanation.text: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.

choices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
choices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.
choices.temptation: Links bilateral motor findings with the hypotensive trigger and preserved limb inflow.
choices.counterfactual: A focal cerebral syndrome or arterial inflow loss would require a different rescue target.

choices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
choices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.
choices.temptation: Carries an acute aortic impulse-reduction plan into a phase where low pressure is the precipitating problem.
choices.counterfactual: An unrepaired hypertensive acute aortic syndrome without cord hypoperfusion supports impulse control.

choices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
choices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.
choices.temptation: Interprets leg weakness after endovascular repair as an access or limb-occlusion complication.
choices.counterfactual: Sudden cold pulseless legs with demonstrated aortoiliac occlusion could require this pathway.

authorGate.cueAttack: The presentation gives symptoms, distal occlusions and aneurysmal thrombus rather than calling the lesion symptomatic or high-risk. All options are vascular management plans. The key is shorter than the two surveillance labels; every testing plan has duplex metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Nonemergent source management of a PAA with embolic findings, not acute threatened-limb salvage.
reasoningSteps: Connect digital occlusions and episodic blue toes with the mural-thrombus source despite palpable foot pulses.

authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: a remembered 20-mm threshold and normal pedal pulses both invite reassurance despite distal embolization.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Repeated distal embolic findings linked to thrombus in the 18-mm popliteal lesion.
authorGate.closestError: Annual surveillance because the diameter is below the usual asymptomatic repair threshold.
authorGate.consequence: Continued distal embolization and possible limb injury.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without digital findings the small lesion could be observed; without the mural-thrombus source an alternative embolic workup would be needed. Normal strength/sensation keeps acute limb-threat treatment out of scope.

authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Changed a simple size-threshold recall draft into an embolic-complication decision. The key states a repair plan, not a claim that open bypass is invariably superior; the exact conduit/procedure is a clinical-review boundary.

authorGate.cueAttack: Removed the unsupported commitment to exclusion and bypass. Every option is now a concrete repair, anticoagulation or surveillance strategy, with no generic individualized-plan label. The current limb findings remain necessary to distinguish embolization from acute threatened-limb salvage.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Repair-versus-medical/surveillance strategy for a viable limb with a demonstrated aneurysmal embolic source.
reasoningSteps: Connect blue toes and digital occlusions with the mural-thrombus source despite preserved pedal pulses.

authorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction, consistent with the independent review's useful two-step objective. The technique-selection question was removed rather than manufactured from unsupplied conduit or device criteria.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Repeated distal embolic findings coexist with mural thrombus in the 18-mm lesion.
authorGate.closestError: Anticoagulation and duplex as the definitive plan without a source-repair assessment.
authorGate.consequence: Continued embolic risk from the persistent aneurysmal source.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the digital findings or mural thrombus, a small lesion may be surveilled and the source inference would weaken. Normal strength/sensation defines a viable-limb decision stage.
authorGate.counterfactual: Remove thrombus and the embolic history while preserving a small stable asymptomatic PAA: annual surveillance becomes reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The next revised node examines actual imaging targets; this feedback does not give its associated-site survey answer. The later uncertain decompression item is parked and not included as a current scored node.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Resolved the key/explanation mismatch exactly as requested. Open versus endovascular repair is not ranked; named repair planning remains a specific clinical strategy requiring ordinary clinician review.

explanation.text: Digital occlusions with a thrombus-containing PAA support distal embolization even when pedal pulses remain palpable. authorGate.cueAttack: Removed repeat from the aortic label and removed a prose declaration of survey completeness. A left-leg examination actually exists, so a generic left-sided missing-counterpart shortcut no longer settles the target. All three named studies have comparable scope and complete timing metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Complete an associated-aneurysm survey by interpreting the actual vessel target of existing acquisitions.
reasoningSteps: Apply the associated contralateral-popliteal and abdominal-aortic survey to the diagnosed PAA.
Determine that venous compressibility/flow is not an arterial aneurysm assessment while the acquired aortic coverage is adequate.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: a normal left-leg ultrasound can create false completion of the contralateral survey. The key requires both the clinical association and the acquisition-target distinction, rather than a no-left-image checklist.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The apparently reassuring left-leg record consists of venous sequences, whereas the aortic outer contours were actually imaged.
authorGate.closestError: Choose abdominal ultrasound after assuming the left-leg study already assessed the contralateral aneurysm site.
authorGate.consequence: Duplicating an assessed territory while leaving the relevant opposite arterial site unexamined.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the left-leg acquisition type and the negative examination cannot be interpreted; remove aortic coverage and more than one study could be needed. No missing export is equated with an unperformed acquisition.
authorGate.counterfactual: Make the left examination a complete arterial duplex and the CT a pelvis-only acquisition: abdominal aortic ultrasound becomes the appropriate additional study.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The preceding repair explanation does not identify the screening association. The original acquired-target table is revealed only at this node and earns the new inference.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the redundant-repeat foil and unilateral-absence cue with a wrong-vascular-target problem. Preserved real original acquisition records rather than inferring nonperformance from absent exported series.

explanation.text: Screening associated with a PAA includes the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta. choices.label: Left popliteal arterial duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: The left-leg examination evaluates veins, not a contralateral arterial aneurysm; the abdominal aorta is already adequately depicted.
choices.temptation: Separates a reassuring examination at the wrong vascular target from the associated arterial survey still needed.
choices.counterfactual: An adequate left arterial examination with an unassessed abdominal aorta would instead support abdominal aortic screening.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: This is an appropriate associated site but does not address the remaining arterial target after an adequate abdominal CTA.
choices.temptation: Recalls the AAA association while mistaking the left venous examination for a completed left arterial survey.
choices.counterfactual: An abdominal acquisition that omitted the infrarenal aorta would make a dedicated aortic study appropriate.

choices.label: Thoracic aortic CT angiography
choices.rationale: A thoracic study does not complete the specifically supported opposite-popliteal and abdominal-aortic associated survey.
choices.temptation: Generalizes aneurysm association to another arterial territory while treating the recorded left-leg study as sufficient.
choices.counterfactual: An independent thoracic or heritable-aortopathy indication can justify thoracic imaging.

decisionNodes.stem: Which definitive source-control plan should have been selected for {patientName} after those findings?

answerChoices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.

answerChoices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
answerChoices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.

answerChoices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

authorGate.cueAttack: The context never labels graft infection or fistula. The endoscopy's actual examined territory is specified rather than saying 'all tests negative.' Every option is a named bleeding/graft investigation with complete wait metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Next diagnostic investigation after a completed unrevealing proximal endoscopy in a stable hospital assessment.
reasoningSteps: Integrate graft history, infection and bleeding as a possible linked vascular complication.
Choose cross-sectional graft-interface evaluation rather than re-examining the same mucosal territory or only localizing bleeding.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard: melena invites a standard luminal workup, while intermittent stability and an unrevealing endoscopy can falsely reassure.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Unexplained infection and bleeding months after aortic grafting, with only proximal mucosa examined.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat the same upper-endoscopic territory to explain the melena.
authorGate.consequence: Delayed recognition of a dangerous graft-related infection or bowel communication.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the graft/culture history this could be an ordinary obscure-bleeding workup. Precise endoscopic scope preserves provenance; no hidden fourth-duodenal examination is assumed.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the prior endoscopy instead showed a recurrent treatable proximal ulcer with no graft-related infection concern, repeat endoscopy would become reasonable.
authorGate.sequenceReview: The first explanation indicates the diagnostic target but does not choose a source-control operation. Definitive graft findings appear only next.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a generic 'urgent review' key and used actual investigations. The CTA preference is a targeted application of a single checked guideline; it is flagged for exact clinical review rather than claiming that every intermittent GI bleed must have this scan.

authorGate.cueAttack: The CTA label no longer uniquely repeats graft and bowel. The endoscopic option reaches a genuinely new distal target rather than announcing a repeat of the completed examination. All labels are specific investigations of the remaining uncertainty and all carry timing metadata.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Next diagnostic investigation in the recorded stable interval after an unrevealing limited upper endoscopy.
reasoningSteps: Integrate bacteremia, aortic prosthesis and melena as a potentially linked vascular process rather than isolated luminal bleeding.

authorGate.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction: distal enteroscopy is a credible nearest competitor because the prior scope stopped proximally. The infection/vascular relationship must change the investigation rather than the word repeat eliminating that option.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Persistent unexplained bloodstream infection accompanies bleeding after prosthetic aortic reconstruction, while only proximal mucosa has been examined.
authorGate.closestError: Push enteroscopy as the entire next workup because the earlier scope did not reach the distal duodenum.
authorGate.consequence: Delaying assessment of a potentially dangerous prosthetic vascular complication.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete cultures or prosthetic history and the balance toward a vascular/extraluminal study changes. Endoscopic coverage remains precise; its limited negative finding is not converted into an exclusion of graft-enteric pathology.
authorGate.counterfactual: Replace the unresolved prosthetic-infection concern with independently localized distal-duodenal mucosal bleeding: the offered distal enteroscopic investigation becomes appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceReview: This v2 diagnostic question is standalone. The PASS definitive-source-control node remains with its complete original v1 case and prior feedback, rather than inheriting a newly composed pre-answer context.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Re-solved three real investigations after removing the two identified wording cues. Kept the supported diagnostic objective and did not introduce an unrelated new bleeding threshold or source-control answer.
